0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
Of all the churches Paul founded, none gave him more grief — or more glory — than the church at Corinth. Corinth was one of the great cities of the ancient world: a rebuilt Roman colony on the narrow isthmus of Greece, sitting athwart the trade routes of the Mediterranean, a cosmopolitan, polyglot, ferociously commercial city where every culture, every religion, and every vice was for sale. The Greek verb korinthiazesthai — to live like a Corinthian — had become a byword for sexual immorality. Into this city Paul came on his second missionary journey around AD 50, stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11), and planted a church that would make him simultaneously the most celebrated and most embattled apostle in his own lifetime.

He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 54–55, provoked by reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. What he had heard was alarming: the church had fractured into personality factions (“I follow Paul”; “I follow Apollos”; “I follow Cephas”; “I follow Christ”); a man was openly sleeping with his stepmother and the church was proud of its tolerance; members were suing each other in pagan courts; spiritual gifts had become instruments of status and one-upmanship; the Lord’s Supper had been turned into a class exercise in social humiliation; and some were denying the bodily resurrection entirely. This is a church in crisis — not the crisis of persecution from outside, but the far more dangerous crisis of pride, worldliness, and theological confusion from within.

Paul’s answer to every single one of these crises is the same: the cross. The word of the cross (1:18) is the only wisdom that addresses human arrogance. The crucified Christ (1:23) is the only foundation (3:11) on which a community can be built. The resurrection of Christ (15:20) is the only ground on which the resurrection of the dead makes sense. Every pastoral problem in the letter — from church discipline to spiritual gifts to the collection for the Jerusalem poor — is resolved by returning to the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. This is why Martin Luther said that the theology of the cross (theologia crucis) stands against the theology of glory (theologia gloriae) at every point, and why this letter is the most searching diagnostic of the church’s recurrent temptation to dress the gospel in the clothing of worldly wisdom and power.

The commentary that follows draws on Gordon Fee’s magnificent NICNT volume, Anthony Thiselton’s exhaustive NIGTC commentary, Roy Ciampa and Brian Rosner’s Pillar NT Commentary, Calvin’s Commentary on 1 Corinthians, Thomas Schreiner, John MacArthur, and the preaching of Timothy Keller on the Corinthian epistles. The governing conviction is that this letter was written to the twenty-first century as much as the first — because the Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world simultaneously.

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Romans opens with a theological masterwork; 1 Corinthians opens with a pastoral emergency. By verse 10, Paul is already addressing the fractures tearing the Corinthian community apart. But before the rebuke comes the gospel — and in the greeting and thanksgiving of the opening nine verses, Paul quietly plants every seed he will spend sixteen chapters watering. The Corinthians are sanctified, called, enriched in speech and knowledge, not lacking in any spiritual gift, and sustained by a faithful God. They are spiritually wealthy — which is precisely what makes their quarrelling so tragic.

The great movement of the chapter is from human division (vv. 10–17) to divine wisdom (vv. 18–31). The factional loyalties at Corinth are not merely a personality problem; they are a theological problem, because they reveal that the Corinthians have been seduced by the world’s categories of wisdom, power, and prestige. Paul’s counter-move is devastating in its simplicity: the cross. The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God (v. 18). God has chosen what is foolish, weak, and despised — and thereby destroyed every human ground of boasting. The chapter ends where the entire letter must end: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s greeting is terse by ancient standards — a mere three verses — but every word is doing theological work. He identifies himself as an apostle by the will of God, not by human appointment or apostolic succession. The commission he carries belongs to Christ; it was given, not chosen. Sosthenes, named as co-sender, is almost certainly the former synagogue ruler of Corinth (Acts 18:17), now a brother in Christ — a walking testimony to the power of the gospel to transform its opponents.

The address to the Corinthians is the most remarkable thing in the greeting: they are “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints.” Sanctified — not their achievement but their location: they are holy because they are in Christ, who is holy. This matters enormously for a letter that will spend much of its time rebuking their decidedly unholy behaviour: Paul never stops addressing them as saints. He rebukes them as people who already are what he is calling them to become. The gospel pronounces identity before it issues imperatives.

The universal address — “together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” — opens the letter to the whole church catholic. This is not merely a letter to Corinth; it is a letter for every community that calls on the name of Christ. Grace and peace — the charter of the redeemed life — come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, placed on the same level of divine gift-giving with a naturalness that is one of Paul’s most powerful incidental arguments for the deity of the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul’s self-designation as an apostle “by the will of God” is not modesty but theology. The divine will is the only ground of any apostolic or ministerial commission. This will become crucial in the letter: when the Corinthians reject Paul’s apostleship, they are not rejecting a self-appointed teacher but the will of the God who sent him. The same logic applies to their own calling: they are saints not because they volunteered but because they were called (v. 2). The sovereignty of grace is the foundation of every sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s apostolic authority was contested at Corinth by those who preferred Apollos’s rhetorical polish or Cephas’s Petrine prestige. His opening — “called by the will of God” — quietly answers the challenge before it is raised. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still the same: divine calling, not human talent. The pastor who grounds his authority in his own gifts is standing on sand; the one who grounds it in the call of God can stand when the culture turns against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three words carry the weight, and each of them takes something away from Paul. Klētos — called. Thelēmatos theou — by the will of God. Apostolos — one sent, a man under orders carrying somebody else’s message. He does not write “Paul, who became an apostle”, or “Paul, who trained for this”, or “Paul, whom the church appointed”. Every one of those would have located the commission somewhere in Paul. He puts it outside himself entirely.

And he had reason to. Whatever else the Damascus road was, it was not an application Paul submitted. He was travelling in the opposite direction with warrants in his luggage, on his way to arrest Christians, when he was knocked to the ground and blinded by the very person he was persecuting. Nobody has ever entered the ministry with less enthusiasm for the job. Which is exactly why he can open a letter to a church that is questioning his authority by saying, in effect: you may take this up with me if you like, but the appointment was not mine to make and is not mine to resign.

That matters more than it first appears, because this letter is about to spend sixteen chapters correcting people who badly do not want to be corrected. If Paul’s standing rests on his personality, his eloquence, or his track record, then the Corinthians can simply decide they prefer somebody else’s — and that is precisely what they have done (v. 12). If it rests on the will of God, their preferences are beside the point.

Then the second name, which is easy to read past and is one of the quietest miracles in the New Testament. Sosthenes. Luke records that when the Corinthian Jews dragged Paul before the proconsul Gallio and the case was thrown out, the crowd seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal (Acts 18:17). He held the office Crispus had held before he became a Christian — which means he had inherited the leadership of the opposition.

We cannot be certain it is the same man; Sosthenes was not a rare name. But the coincidence is considerable: the same unusual name, the same city, and a man now described simply as our brother, sitting beside Paul as the letter is composed and sending it to the church his synagogue had tried to destroy. If it is him, then the head of the opposition became the co-sender of the correspondence, and the Christians at Corinth would have opened this letter and seen a name they remembered from the wrong side of a courtroom.

Which is worth holding on to when you pray for someone who seems entirely closed — the relative who mocks it, the colleague who has heard it all and wants none of it, the person whose hostility feels settled and permanent. Paul was the most dangerous enemy the early church had, and Sosthenes may well have been the second. Both names are at the top of this letter. The gospel does not merely survive its opponents; it has a long history of recruiting them.

And there is a test in the first word for anyone who has quietly assumed that their own Christian life was fundamentally their idea. Ask how you came to be reading this at all. Trace it back: who spoke to you, who prayed for you, why you were in that room, what made you willing to listen when a hundred other people heard the same words and did not. Follow it far enough and you will not find a decision you made. You will find a series of things that happened to you — which is the whole meaning of called, and it is the reason no Christian can boast (cf. John 15:16; Gal. 1:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The church of God that is in Corinth” — and the preposition is doing more work than any other word in the sentence. The church belongs to God; it merely has an address. That address, though, is the point of the joke, because every reader in the ancient world knew what Corinth was. A wealthy port city with harbours on two seas, rebuilt by Rome as a colony, full of new money, competitive display, imported religion and the temple of Aphrodite. The Greeks had coined a verb from the city’s name — korinthiazomai, to Corinthianise, meaning to live immorally. To write “the church of God in Corinth” was very nearly a contradiction in terms, and Paul writes it without a flicker of embarrassment.

Then comes the description, and it is the most important thing in the greeting: they are “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints”.

Take the first phrase carefully, because a great deal of Christian anxiety turns on it. Sanctified is a perfect passive — something that was done to them, at a point in the past, with results that continue. It is not a report on their conduct. It is a statement about their location. To be sanctified is to be set apart for God, and they are set apart because they are in Christ, who is holy. The holiness is his, and they are in him.

Now remember who is being described. This is the church that will shortly be rebuked for factions, for a man sleeping with his father’s wife, for suing each other in pagan courts, for getting drunk at the Lord’s Supper while poorer members went hungry, and for a chaotic scramble over spiritual gifts. Paul knows all of it — he has already had the report (v. 11) — and he still opens by calling them sanctified saints. He does not withdraw the title in order to motivate them to earn it. He states who they are, and then spends sixteen chapters telling them to become it.

That order is the gospel, and reversing it is the single commonest way to make Christianity unbearable. The world says: behave, and you will belong. Every religion of human effort says: achieve, and you may be accepted. Paul says: you have been set apart, therefore live like it. Identity first; instruction second. Nobody in this letter is being asked to work towards a standing. They are being asked to live up to one they already have.

So a word for the reader who flinches at the word saint. Most of us hear it and think of stained glass, or of somebody markedly better than we are, and conclude the word cannot honestly apply. But “saint” in the New Testament is never a rank awarded to the exceptional — it is the ordinary word for a Christian, and Paul is happily applying it to the worst-behaved congregation in his correspondence. If the Corinthians qualified, the bar is not where you think it is. The question is not whether your record has earned the description. It is whether you are in Christ, because the description follows the location.

And here is the test, which will show you what you actually believe. When you have sinned badly — not a slip, the real thing — what is your first instinct about your standing before God? Do you assume you have dropped out of the category and have to work your way back in before you can pray properly? Or do you go to him as someone who is still, at that moment, sanctified in Christ Jesus? The first instinct is nearly universal and it is not the gospel. The letter that says you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (6:11) says it to people who were still getting it badly wrong.

The address then opens outward: “together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours”. Corinth is not a self-contained religious club with its own arrangements; it is one congregation inside something worldwide. That phrase — call upon the name of the Lord — is lifted straight out of the Old Testament, where it means to invoke the name of Yahweh (Gen. 4:26; Joel 2:32). Paul applies it to Jesus without argument or apology, as though it needed no defending. It is one of the strongest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament, and it arrives disguised as an address label.

The greeting itself fuses two worlds: charis, grace, a Christian reshaping of the ordinary Greek greeting, and shalom, peace, the standard Hebrew one. And they come “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” — one preposition governing both, the Father and the Son named together as the single source of the gift. Paul is not arguing for the deity of Christ here. He is assuming it, in a throwaway line, which is a far stronger indication of what the earliest church believed than any formal argument would be (cf. Heb. 10:14; Rom. 1:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul almost always begins his letters with a thanksgiving, and the thanksgivings are never mere formality — they are theological previews of the letter’s concerns. Here the irony runs deep: he thanks God for the Corinthians’ richness in speech and knowledge, for their possession of every spiritual gift — the very things that have become sources of pride and division. Paul is not being sarcastic; he is being theological. The gifts are real. The enrichment is genuine. The problem is not that they have these gifts but that they have mistaken the gifts for the Giver, and begun to boast in their spiritual portfolio rather than in the One who gave it.

The theological pivot of the thanksgiving is v. 7: “as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Every spiritual gift is a provisional equipment for the period between the first and second coming. The gifts are not ends in themselves; they are tools for waiting and working. And underneath all of them is the foundation that cannot shift: “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord” (v. 9). The Corinthians’ security does not rest on their gifts, their eloquence, their knowledge, or their loyalty to the right apostle. It rests on the faithfulness of the God who called them.

This is the note Paul sounds before he says a single word of rebuke — and it is the most pastoral move in the letter. He does not open with accusation but with affirmation of what God has done. The gospel is gift before it is demand; identity before it is imperative.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 — “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” — is one of the great perseverance texts in Paul. The guarantee of the Corinthians’ ultimate confirmation (v. 8) is not their grip on Christ but God’s grip on them. The calling is God’s act; the fellowship is God’s gift; the sustaining is God’s work. Reformed theology has always grounded the doctrine of perseverance here: the saints persevere not because they are strong but because the God who called them is faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing before God and their superiority over others by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge. Paul’s thanksgiving subtly reorients them: the gifts are something you “were enriched in” — given, not earned. Now: The same pride attaches to spiritual accomplishment in every generation — the sense that one’s theological sophistication or spiritual experience gives one a higher standing. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. What do you have that you did not receive? (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anything else, notice what Paul does first — and remember what he already knows. Chloe’s people have reported the quarrelling (v. 11). He has heard about the immorality, the lawsuits, the disorder. He is holding a list of things that would justify opening with anger. And the first thing he does is thank God for them.

This is not a technique, and it is not flattery. It is possible because the thanksgiving is not aimed at the Corinthians at all. Read it again: I give thanks to my God… because of the grace of God that was given you. He is not congratulating them on being impressive; he is thanking God for something God did. Which is precisely why he can do it with complete sincerity about a church he is about to take apart. There is nothing here that their behaviour could invalidate, because none of it was their achievement in the first place.

The grammar carries that. The grace was given — a completed action done to them — and they were enriched, another passive. They are wealthy, and every penny of it arrived in the post. And the word for enriched, eploutisthēte, is one Paul uses again in the most famous sentence he ever wrote about Christian wealth: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). That is where the Corinthian riches came from. Their wealth is the measure of his poverty; what they have in their hands is what it cost him to put it there.

Then the specifics, and they are chosen with some care: “in all speech and all knowledge”. Logos and gnōsis. Anyone reading the whole letter will recognise both immediately, because they are the two things that have gone most badly wrong at Corinth. Speech is the arena of the tongues problem that will occupy chapters 12 to 14. Knowledge is the source of the arrogance Paul confronts at 8:1, where he says flatly that knowledge puffs up.

So Paul thanks God for the very gifts that are currently doing the damage. He does not treat them as the problem and he does not ask the Corinthians to have less of them. This is worth pausing on, because our instinct when a gift is being misused is to disparage the gift. Paul’s instinct is to trace it back to the Giver and give thanks — and then to spend the letter putting it back in its place. The trouble at Corinth was never that they had too much of God’s grace. It was that they had forgotten it was grace.

Which yields something you can actually do, and it is harder than it sounds. Think of the person in your church you find most difficult — the one whose name lowers your mood, whose contributions in a meeting you brace for. Now write down, honestly, three things God has genuinely given that person. Not three things you can tolerate about them; three evidences of grace. Most of us discover we have never once tried, and that we have been carrying a mental file on them consisting entirely of the other column.

Paul had a far longer file on the Corinthians than you have on anybody, and he opened with thanksgiving. Not because the problems were small, and not because he intended to overlook them — he does not overlook a single one. But because he could see the grace of God in them underneath the mess, and he was determined to name that first (cf. Phil. 1:3–6; Rom. 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The testimony about Christ was confirmed among you” — bebaiōthē, a word from the world of contracts and guarantees, meaning something has been ratified and made secure. The gifts at Corinth are not decorations. They are the divine signature under the apostolic message, God countersigning what Paul preached so that nobody could say it was merely one man’s opinion.

Then the statement that ought to stop any honest reader: “so that you are not lacking in any gift”. Said of this church. A congregation deficient in love, humility, unity, self-control and basic decency is told it lacks no spiritual gift whatever. Both things are true at once, and holding them together is most of the wisdom of this letter. Gifting and maturity are not the same thing, they do not arrive together, and one is no evidence of the other. It is entirely possible to be lavishly equipped and badly behaved — which is a warning to the gifted and a considerable relief to everybody else.

And there is a word here for the Christian who has quietly concluded that he has no gift at all. You watch people who teach, or sing, or organise, or seem to know instinctively what to say in a hospital room, and you can identify nothing comparable in yourself. Paul’s statement is made to a whole congregation, and he says the same thing to them individually later in the same letter: to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (12:7). Not to some. To each. The question is never whether you were given something; it is whether anyone has ever helped you find out what it was — and gifts are ordinarily discovered by serving, not by introspection.

Now the phrase that reframes all of it: “as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ”. Apokalypsis — an unveiling, the drawing back of a curtain on someone who is already there. The gifts are issued for the waiting. They are equipment for the interval between his going and his coming, provisions for a journey rather than trophies for a cabinet.

That single clause would have solved most of the Corinthian problem if they had believed it. A gift understood as a possession becomes a measure of standing, and standing invites comparison, and comparison produces the factions of the next paragraph. A gift understood as equipment for a job raises a different question entirely — not what does this say about me? but what is this for? The same gift, held two ways, builds a church or splits one.

A word is needed here about a question this verse inevitably raises, since Christians differ on it and the disagreement runs through many congregations. Do all the gifts described in this letter continue today? Some hold that the revelatory and sign gifts — prophecy, tongues, healing — belonged to the apostolic age and ceased once the New Testament was complete, pointing to 13:8–10. Others hold that they continue until Christ returns, reading the “perfect” of 13:10 as his appearing rather than the closing of the canon — and noting that this very verse ties the gifts to the period of waiting for the revealing of the Lord, which is plainly not over.

Both positions are held with conviction by people who love Scripture and submit to it, and the argument is properly conducted at chapter 13, where Paul actually addresses it. What must not be lost is what he is saying here, which neither side disputes: whatever gifts God has given you, they were given for the waiting, they will not be needed when he appears, and they were never intended to tell you or anyone else how you are doing (cf. Rom. 8:23–25; 1 Pet. 4:10).

Which leaves a test with a sharp edge. Ask what you are actually waiting for. Not what you would say in a Bible study — what genuinely functions in you as the thing that will make everything all right. For most of us it is a resolution: the diagnosis reversed, the job secured, the child settled, the debt cleared. All legitimate to want. None of them is what Paul says the Christian is waiting for, and every one of them can arrive and leave you exactly where you were. The Corinthians had every gift and were still restless, because gifts were never designed to satisfy the ache that only a Person appearing can end.

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Who will sustain you to the end” — and the subject of that verb is the last word of the previous verse. It is Christ who will do the sustaining, or God through him; it is certainly not the Corinthians. The word is bebaiōsei, the same root as “confirmed” in v. 6 — the language of legal guarantee, of a contract made secure so that it will hold. Something has been underwritten here, and the underwriter is not you.

Then the word the whole verse is built to deliver: “guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”. Anenklētous is a courtroom term, and it does not mean innocent in the sense of never having done anything. It means unaccused — no charge standing, nothing on the sheet, no case to answer. It describes a man against whom the prosecution has nothing to bring.

Now feel the force of that as the Corinthians would have. Paul is about to spend fifteen chapters listing what is wrong with them, and much of it is not trivial — incest in the congregation, drunkenness at the Lord’s table, believers dragging each other before pagan judges. And before he names a single item he tells them how the day of judgment will go for them: they will stand there with no charge against them.

How can that possibly be true? Only one way, and the letter will say it plainly at 15:3 — Christ died for our sins. The charges are not being ignored, waived, or quietly dropped for lack of evidence. They were transferred. Every accusation that could be brought against a Corinthian believer on that day was brought against Christ on a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, and answered there. The sheet is clean because someone else’s was filled in.

This is the verse for the Christian who is genuinely afraid of the last day, and there are more of them than admit it. You believe in the forgiveness of sins in general and you are not at all sure it will hold for you in particular, because you know things about yourself that nobody else knows — the thing you did that you have never told anyone, the pattern you have confessed a hundred times and returned to, the person you damaged who never got an apology. And somewhere underneath, you expect that day to be the moment it all finally comes out.

Something will indeed come out. But look at what Paul says will be true of you when it does: guiltless. Not “forgiven, but with a permanent asterisk”. Not “acquitted after a difficult hearing”. No charge standing. If a single accusation could still be brought against a believer on that day, then Christ’s death dealt with most sins and not all, and the letter that says he was raised on the third day would be describing a job half done.

And notice the tense, because the comfort is in it. Paul does not write that God may sustain you, or that he will if you hold on tightly enough. He writes who will sustain you to the end — a plain future about something already guaranteed. The delivery is outstanding; the verdict is not.

So here is a test, and it is diagnostic rather than accusing. Imagine the day arriving this evening. Notice what your mind reaches for first as the ground of your confidence. If it reaches for your record — the years of church, the things you gave up, the sins you have avoided — then whatever you believe about grace, you are functionally planning to be assessed on your own paperwork, and it will not survive the audit. The only answer that holds on that day makes no reference to you at all.

He will present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). Not with relief that the business is finally concluded, and not with the weariness of a judge who has found a technicality. With joy — because the one doing the presenting is the one who paid for the presentation, and he has wanted this from before the foundation of the world (cf. Rom. 8:33–34; Col. 1:22).

verseByVerse.quote: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pistos ho theos. God is faithful. Two words in the Greek, and they are the floor under everything Paul has just promised.

Because a reader who has taken v. 8 seriously will already have asked the obvious question. It is very well to say that God will sustain me to the end — but what if I let go? I have let go before. I know how thin my grip is on a bad week, and I have watched people who seemed far stronger than me walk away entirely. What happens then?

Paul’s answer is not to reassure you about your grip. He changes the subject away from your grip altogether, and puts the entire weight on the character of God. The guarantee is not that you are faithful; it is that he is. Which is the only guarantee that would be worth anything, because a promise is exactly as reliable as the person making it, and you already know what yours are worth.

Look at how the sentence is built. God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son. The calling is his act — a passive verb again, something done to them. The fellowship is his gift. And the faithfulness that will keep them in it is his character. There is no point in that sentence at which the Corinthians contribute anything, which is a remarkable thing to say about a church whose behaviour is about to be dismantled for fifteen chapters.

This is the ground the Reformed doctrine of perseverance stands on, and it is worth being exact about what it does and does not claim. It does not claim that a Christian cannot sin badly, or drift for years, or go through a season in which faith is barely detectable. The Corinthians are the standing proof that it claims nothing so comfortable. What it claims is that the God who began the work will not abandon it — that the calling was not experimental and the fellowship is not on probation.

The doctrine is sometimes described as “the perseverance of the saints”, and the name can mislead, because it sounds like a statement about the stamina of the saints. It is not. It is a statement about the preservation of the saints by God. Christians persevere; and the reason they persevere is that they are being kept.

And notice what they are called into: koinōnia, fellowship, partnership — a word for having something in common, holding a share in the same thing. Not called into a religion, or a set of obligations, or a moral improvement scheme. Called into a shared life with the Son of God. The Corinthians, who have divided themselves into parties over which teacher they prefer, are told in the last line of the thanksgiving that they were all called into partnership with the same Person — which quietly makes every faction in the next paragraph absurd before Paul has even named them.

So the test, for the reader who lies awake over this. Ask which of two questions you are actually asking. Am I holding on tightly enough? is a question with no answer, because there is no measurement that would settle it, and asking it repeatedly has never once produced assurance in anybody. Is he faithful? is a question with an answer, and the answer has a location: a cross, and an empty tomb, and a record of a God who has never yet abandoned anyone who called on his name.

Keller: “The most dangerous thing in the world is not a God who might abandon you. It is a God of infinite faithfulness who has committed himself to you.” Dangerous, because such a God will not leave you as you are — and safe, for exactly the same reason.

He has never broken a promise. Not to Abraham, waiting twenty-five years for a son; not to Israel, kept through four centuries of silence in Egypt; not to David, whose throne was empty for six hundred years before a child was born in Bethlehem to fill it. Every one of those promises looked, for a long time, like a promise that had failed. Not one of them did. He is faithful (cf. 1 Thess. 5:24; 2 Tim. 2:13; Phil. 1:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transition from thanksgiving to rebuke is abrupt and deliberate. Paul does not ease into the problem; he names it: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you.” The word for “divisions” is schismata — tears, splits in fabric. The church at Corinth is tearing apart along lines of apostolic loyalty: some claiming Paul, some Apollos, some Cephas, some Christ. The factions map onto real social and theological differences — Paul’s simplicity of proclamation vs. Apollos’s Alexandrian rhetorical polish vs. the Petrine prestige of Jerusalem connection — and they reveal a church that has imported the ancient world’s habit of social competition into the body of Christ.

Paul’s response is not to defend himself but to redirect attention to Christ. “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptised in the name of Paul?” The questions are rhetorical but lethal: the only person around whom a Christian community can legitimately cohere is the one who was crucified for them. Paul is actually glad he baptised so few of them — because baptism into his name would have been the precise idolatry the factions are committing. The logic of baptism is that it names the one to whom you belong; to be baptised in Christ’s name is to belong to Christ, not to any apostle.

The climax of the section is v. 17: “For Christ did not send me to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.” This is the hinge of the entire letter’s first section. The cross is the thing that is at stake. Dress it in human rhetorical eloquence and you have improved the packaging while destroying the contents. The power of the gospel is not the power of skillful persuasion; it is the power of God operating through the proclamation of a crucified Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions are a cautionary tale about what happens when human personality becomes the centre of Christian community. Calvin saw in this text a permanent warning: the church that rallies around a preacher’s gifts, style, or personality rather than around the crucified Christ has already drifted from the gospel. The preacher is, at most, a herald — the one who announces a message that does not belong to him. Paul’s refusal to preach with “eloquent wisdom” is not anti-intellectualism; it is a deliberate choice to let the gospel speak in its own register, with its own power, rather than dressing it in borrowed clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and sophistry: you attached yourself to the most impressive teacher, displayed his influence on your life, and measured your social standing by his. The Corinthian factions are simply the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity pastor culture is the contemporary version. The church that streams a famous preacher rather than investing in local pastors, or that divides over which theological tradition’s champion to follow, is still choosing Apollos over Christ — a more impressive package over the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I appeal to you” — parakalō, the verb of urging and entreating, from the same root as the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the Paraklētos, the one called alongside. Paul does not command here, though as an apostle he could. He pleads. And he pleads “by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” — the one name in Corinth that belongs equally to every person he is writing to, which is exactly the point he is about to make.

The word for divisions is schismata — tears, rents, the word for a rip in a garment. It is not the word for a difference of opinion. It is the sound of fabric giving way. And what makes it worse is what the fabric is: this letter will shortly call the church a body (12:12–27), and a tear in a body is not an untidiness. It is a wound.

What Paul asks for is easily misread: that they “be united in the same mind and the same judgment”. This is not a demand that every Christian hold identical views on every question. Paul himself makes room for genuine disagreement on real matters — food, days, disputable things (Rom. 14) — and this same letter will spend chapter 8 handling a question on which believers landed differently. What he is after is a shared orientation: a church so fixed on the same Lord that no rival loyalty can organise a party.

Then something quietly remarkable about how Paul handles the report. “It has been reported to me by Chlo’s people” — and he names them. We do not know who Chloe was; she may not even have been a Christian. Her “people” are her household — slaves, freedmen, dependants — socially the least significant witnesses available in Corinth, and precisely the sort of people whose testimony a status-conscious congregation would be inclined to discount.

Paul does two things with that, and both are instructive. He takes their report seriously, from the bottom of the social order rather than the top. And he says openly where it came from, refusing to deal in anonymous information. He will not build a rebuke on gossip he cannot attribute, and he will not pretend to a knowledge he acquired by some more dignified route. If you are going to confront a church, you say what you have heard and who told you.

Now the practical question, because most readers of this passage are living somewhere inside it. Your church has a fault line. Perhaps it is a leadership dispute, or a music argument, or two families who no longer speak, or a slow separation into those who liked the last minister and those who wanted the change. What does this verse actually ask of you on Sunday?

Four things, and none of them is dramatic. Refuse the party. The factions at Corinth were sustained by people saying “I follow” — and every division needs recruits. You are not obliged to have a side, and declining to take one is a positive act, not cowardice. Stop repeating it. A great deal of what tears a congregation is not the original disagreement but its retelling, and the sentence that begins “I probably shouldn’t say this, but…” has done more damage in more churches than any heresy. Speak to the person, not about them — which is what Paul is doing here, at some cost, rather than writing to somebody else about Corinth. And keep eating together; this letter treats a shared table as a theological act, and people who eat together find it much harder to caricature each other.

One guard, because this passage can be used as a weapon by the wrong people. A call for unity is not a call to suppress genuine concern, and “you are being divisive” is the standard reply of anyone who wishes an uncomfortable question would go away. Paul himself is prepared to break fellowship over the gospel — he publicly opposed Peter to his face when the gospel was at stake (Gal. 2:11), and told the Galatians that a different gospel is no gospel at all. The unity commanded here is unity around the crucified Christ, and it is not the same thing as quiet.

The test is whether the thing dividing your church is Christ or preference. If a congregation is splitting over the gospel, that is a grief and may be a necessity. If it is splitting over anything else — and it usually is — then what Paul says next applies without qualification, and the next three questions he asks will take the ground out from under both sides at once.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four slogans, and Paul reports them without comment before demolishing them: I follow Paul. I follow Apollos. I follow Cephas. I follow Christ.

The names are not random, and each represents a real attraction. Paul founded the church; his party is the loyalist old guard, the people who were there at the beginning. Apollos arrives in Acts 18 as an Alexandrian, eloquent and mighty in the Scriptures — the polished speaker, and in a city that paid to hear professional orators, a considerable draw. Cephas is Peter, in Aramaic: the Jerusalem connection, the man who walked with Jesus, apostolic prestige of a kind Paul could not match. And Christ — the party that has risen above parties.

Notice that nothing here is a heresy. Nobody is teaching error. Every one of these men is a genuine servant of God, and Paul will insist two chapters later that Apollos and he are simply servants through whom the Corinthians believed (3:5). The material of the division is entirely good. That is what makes it so hard to see from the inside — a congregation dividing over false teaching at least knows what it is doing, whereas a congregation dividing over preferences believes it is defending something important.

Then the three questions, and they are not rhetorical flourishes. Each one is a hammer.

“Is Christ divided?” If the church is his body, then a factional church is a dismembered Christ — the image is grotesque, and it is meant to be. There are not four Christs to distribute among four parties. Every believer at Corinth has the whole of him, which means no group holds a portion the others lack.

“Was Paul crucified for you?” Here is the only credential that could possibly justify a Christian naming himself after someone. Loyalty of this depth belongs to a person who died for you, and exactly one person qualifies. Paul is not being modest. He is pointing out that the Corinthians have offered him something he has no right to receive.

“Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” Baptism names your owner. To be baptised into the name of someone is to be publicly transferred into their possession — and every Corinthian was baptised into the name of Christ, whoever happened to be standing in the water with them.

And the fourth slogan deserves its own word, because it looks like the right answer and is rebuked alongside the others. I follow Christ — what could be wrong with that? Everything, if it is said in that tone. It is the claim to have transcended the mess: I have no time for your teachers and your traditions and your squabbling church; I have Christ, directly, and I need nothing else. It sounds like maturity and is a subtler form of the same pride, because it has still turned Christ into a party badge, and it has done it by using his name to look down on his people.

Which brings this passage uncomfortably close to home for a particular reader. You have been hurt by a church, or simply exhausted by one. You have watched Christians behave in ways that embarrassed you, and you have quietly withdrawn into a private faith — you love Christ, you read your Bible, and you have concluded you can do without the rest. Nothing in this passage doubts the hurt, and a church that damaged you owes you an apology it may never offer.

But notice where the fourth slogan sits in Paul’s list. He does not put it above the others as the one healthy option. He puts it in the same sentence and lets the same three questions fall on it. The reason is that Christ has attached himself to a body, and a man cannot take the Head and decline the rest of him. The very next chapters will make it plain: you cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you (12:21).

So a test, and it is worth answering honestly. Think of the Christian tribe you belong to — the tradition, the church, the teacher whose books you buy, the theological camp whose language you speak. Now ask what you would find harder to give up: that identity, or the company of a believer who has all of Christ and none of your tribe’s distinctives. Most of us discover our loyalties are considerably more Corinthian than we thought, and the tell is not what we say about Christ. It is who we are content to be in the same room with (cf. Eph. 4:4–6; John 17:20–21).

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is glad he baptised almost nobody — which, said by an apostle, needs explaining before anything else. He is not disparaging baptism. Christ commanded it (Matt. 28:19), Paul assumes every Corinthian has received it (v. 13), and he treats it in this very letter as the moment believers were joined into one body (12:13). What he is glad about is narrower and shrewder: the fewer people who can claim a personal bond with him through baptism, the fewer people can build a party on it. Given what is happening in vv. 12–13, his relief is entirely justified.

The three he does remember are worth knowing, because each was a person of standing. Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue who believed with his whole household (Acts 18:8) — the most prominent convert in the city. Gaius hosted not merely Paul but “the whole church” (Rom. 16:23), which means a house large enough for the entire congregation. Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia and had devoted themselves to serving the saints (16:15). These are exactly the people a personality cult would be built around, and Paul knows it.

Now the sentence that stops careful readers, and it deserves a proper answer rather than a smile. “Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.” A man writing Scripture has just admitted, in Scripture, that he cannot remember. How can that be, if the Bible is the word of God?

The question rests on an assumption worth examining: that inspiration must mean dictation — that God overrode Paul’s mind and used him as a pen, so that anything less than total recall is a flaw in the machinery. But that is not what Scripture claims for itself, and it is not how the Bible reads. Luke opens his Gospel by describing research — following all things closely, consulting eyewitnesses, writing an orderly account (Luke 1:1–4). The Psalms are full of men saying exactly what they feel, including things God then answers. The human authors are not bypassed; they are used.

What the doctrine actually holds is that the Spirit so superintended what these men wrote that the result is precisely what God intended to say, without suppressing the men themselves — their vocabulary, their temperament, their circumstances, their memories. And on that understanding this verse is not a problem at all. Ask what the sentence asserts. It asserts that Paul, at the time of writing, was not certain whether there had been others. And that assertion is entirely true. Scripture accurately records the state of the apostle’s memory, which is what it set out to do. Nothing false has been affirmed.

There is more here than a defence, though. Consider what this verse does to the character of the document. A forger tidies. A man inventing an apostolic letter to bolster his own authority does not portray himself groping after a detail and correcting himself mid-sentence, and he certainly does not leave the correction in. The little parenthesis — oh, and Stephanas’s household as well — is the sound of a real man dictating a real letter and remembering something halfway through. It is the kind of detail that no one puts in on purpose.

And it tells you something about how God works that is worth more than the apologetic. He did not require Paul to be superhuman before he would use him. The letter that contains the greatest chapter ever written on love, and the fullest account of the resurrection in the New Testament, also contains its author failing to remember who he baptised — and God saw no need to remove it. Which is a considerable encouragement to anyone who has assumed that God can only work through people whose faculties are impressive.

So the test that comes out of this paragraph is about the thing Paul was so anxious to avoid. He deliberately limited what could be traced back to him, because he had seen what happens when people attach themselves to a servant instead of the Master. Ask, then, whose name is attached to your ministry — the group you lead, the class you teach, the work you have built. If it ended tomorrow and someone else’s name went on it, and it flourished, how would you feel? Paul’s answer to that question is in the first three words of this passage: I thank God.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the hinge of the whole opening argument, and everything from v. 18 to the end of chapter 2 unfolds from it. Christ sent Paul to preach — “and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power”.

The verb is kenōthē: to be emptied, drained, made hollow. It is the same root as the great word in Philippians 2:7, where the Son emptied himself and took the form of a servant. There it describes a glorious self-emptying; here it describes a disastrous one. The cross can be hollowed out — not by attack, but by presentation. A preacher can leave every doctrine formally intact and still drain the thing of power, simply by the way he handles it.

How? By making the message a vehicle for the messenger. “Words of eloquent wisdom” is sophia logou, and in Corinth that phrase had a precise cultural meaning. Travelling orators — the sophists — made their living by public display; audiences paid, compared, took sides, and attached themselves to a favourite. Rhetoric was competitive entertainment. To preach the cross in that register is to enter the competition, and the moment you do, the audience begins assessing the performer. They may leave impressed. They will not leave undone.

Let us be careful about what Paul is not saying, because this verse has been used to defend laziness for centuries. He is not against learning: he was trained under Gamaliel, quotes Greek poets, and constructs arguments in this very letter of considerable sophistication. He is not against clarity, or preparation, or taking trouble over words — the man who wrote chapter 13 plainly took enormous trouble over words. A sermon that is muddled, dull, and badly prepared is not thereby more spiritual; it is merely worse.

What he is against is the substitution of one power for another. There are two things that can produce a response to preaching: the persuasive skill of the speaker, and the Spirit of God working through the message of a crucified Saviour. Both produce visible results. Only one produces conversions. And the tragedy is that the first is easier to obtain, quicker to measure, and immediately rewarded — which is why every generation of preachers has to be warned about it.

Calvin saw the permanent warning here: the church that gathers around a preacher’s gifts rather than around the crucified Christ has already begun to drift, however sound its doctrine remains on paper. A herald is a man carrying a message that does not belong to him. The moment the herald becomes interesting in his own right, the message has a rival.

And this is not a matter for preachers only. Every Christian who has ever tried to explain the faith to someone has felt the same pull in miniature. You are with a colleague, or a relative, and the conversation turns; and somewhere underneath the desire for them to see Christ there is a second desire — not to look foolish, to have a good answer ready, to come out of it well. That second desire is exactly what this verse is about, and it is the reason so many of our conversations about Christ are careful, clever, and curiously ineffective.

Here is the test, and it can be run on any conversation you have had in the last month. Afterwards, what did you replay in your mind? If it was chiefly your own performance — the point you made well, the thing you wish you had said better, whether they thought you were reasonable — then you already know which power you were relying on. The man who has genuinely proclaimed the cross tends to walk away thinking about the other person, because he was never the subject.

The extraordinary thing is that God has arranged it this way on purpose. He could have chosen a method that rewarded eloquence, and the gospel would have travelled through the ancient world on the strength of its orators. Instead he chose a message that no amount of skill can make respectable — a crucified man — so that when it saves anybody at all, there is no possibility of mistaking whose power did it. The weakness is not a defect in the method. It is the method.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
These eight verses are among the most concentrated theology in the Pauline corpus. Paul is not simply making a point about preaching style; he is describing a fundamental epistemological rupture between the wisdom of this age and the wisdom of God. The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing — not because it lacks logical coherence but because the natural mind, operating by the world’s categories of power, achievement, and status, cannot process a God who saves by dying. A crucified Messiah is a contradiction in terms by every available measure. The Jews expected a Messiah who would triumph over Rome; they got one who was executed by it. The Greeks prized a wisdom that could be displayed and admired; they got a God who became a spectacle of failure. The cross violated both expectations utterly.

But Paul does not simply defend the cross against these critiques; he turns the categories upside down. The “foolishness” of the cross is wiser than human wisdom; the “weakness” of the cross is stronger than human strength. This is not a paradox that resolves into something more respectable; it is a permanent inversion. God has chosen what the world counts as foolish, weak, and despised — and by that choice, destroyed every human platform of boasting. The cross is not an embarrassment to be apologised for; it is the lens through which the character of God is most fully revealed.

The citation from Isaiah 29:14 — “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise” — places the cross in the long history of God’s pattern of confounding human self-sufficiency. When Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, the wise men of Israel were helpless; God acted alone. When Babylon swept away the temple, the philosophers of the nations had no answer; God restored by promise, not strategy. The cross is the ultimate expression of this pattern: God saves not by leveraging human wisdom but by overturning it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross (Theologia Crucis)

Luther’s distinction between the theology of the cross and the theology of glory is nowhere more clearly grounded than in 1:18–25. The theologian of glory sees God in power, success, and wisdom that makes sense on human terms. The theologian of the cross sees God revealed precisely in weakness, foolishness, and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross is not the means to something better; it is the place where God is most fully known. Sproul: “The cross is not Plan B after the fall. The cross is Plan A from eternity — the place where the justice and the love of God were both satisfied at the same moment, in the same event, in the same Person.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul wrote into a culture where crucifixion was the ultimate symbol of shame, defeat, and criminal status. To preach a crucified Messiah was not merely theologically offensive but socially disqualifying. The early Christians were not brave about something trivial; they were staking their social standing and their lives on an executed criminal. Now: The pressure to make the gospel more palatable — to lead with Jesus-as-life-coach rather than Jesus-as-sin-bearer, to emphasise personal fulfilment rather than atonement — is the contemporary version of Paul’s Corinthian problem. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age. The answer is still to preach it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The word of the cross” — ho logos tou staurou. Not the cross considered as an event, but the message about it, spoken out loud by somebody. Paul locates the power in the proclamation, which is why the previous verse mattered so much: God has chosen to save people through an announcement, and the announcement is about an execution.

Then two present participles, and English translations rightly keep them moving: to those who are perishing, and to us who are being saved. Neither is a finished state. Paul is describing two directions of travel, two populations in motion, and the same sentence lands differently depending on which road you are on. The message does not change. The hearers are not in the same condition.

The word for folly is mōria — the root behind our word moron. Paul is not softening it. To the perishing, the cross is not merely unconvincing; it is idiotic, the sort of thing an intelligent person is embarrassed to be associated with. And he says this without defensiveness, because he expects it. A message that the natural mind found reasonable would not be this message.

Which brings us to the reader this passage was written for, and there are many. You have a brother, or a daughter at university, or a colleague at the next desk, who thinks your faith is beneath you. Not hostile, necessarily — often worse than hostile: kind, and faintly embarrassed on your behalf. They have read a little, they can produce the standard objections, and they leave you with the distinct impression that you are a reasonably intelligent person who has made one inexplicable exception.

This verse tells you three things about that experience, and all three are worth having. First, it is predicted. You have not stumbled into an unexpected weakness in Christianity; you have run into precisely what Paul said would happen, and if the cross were widely regarded as sensible, that would be the surprising development. Second, the issue is not that you have failed to explain it well. Paul was better at explaining than you are, and the folly verdict came in anyway. And third — the part that changes how you pray — the difference between the two responses is not intelligence. It is not that the saved are cleverer. Both groups hear the same words; what separates them is which road they are on, and that is God’s business, not yours.

One guard, because this can be twisted. Paul is not saying that stupidity is holy, or that Christians should be glad to sound ridiculous, or that any objection can be waved away with “the natural man cannot understand”. That is a lazy misuse of the verse, and this letter is itself a sustained piece of careful argument. The foolishness is in the content — a crucified God — not in the manner of the people who believe it. We are asked to be always ready to give a reason (1 Pet. 3:15). We are simply told not to be shocked when the reason is found absurd.

Then the citation, and its background repays a moment. Isaiah 29:14 comes from a passage about people whose religion had become mouth-work — this people draw near with their mouth and honour me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me — and about the political sophisticates of Jerusalem who thought they could manage the Assyrian crisis by clever alliances. God’s answer was to act in a way none of their calculations had allowed for. The wisdom of the wise perished, not because it was outargued, but because God did something outside its categories.

That is the pattern the cross completes. God has form for this. He gave Abraham a son a quarter of a century after it was biologically absurd; he took Israel out of Egypt with no army; he brought them home from Babylon by the decree of a pagan king. Every time, the experts had already established that it could not be done, and every time they were right on their own terms and wrong about the world they were living in (cf. Isa. 55:8–9; Rom. 1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions, and each names a recognised professional. The wise — sophos, the Greek philosopher, the man with an account of reality. The scribe — grammateus, the Jewish scholar of the law, master of the sacred text. The debater of this age — syzētētēs, the professional arguer of the Hellenistic lecture hall, a man who could take either side and win. Between them they represent every avenue by which the ancient world thought truth might be reached: reason, revelation as expertly handled, and rhetoric.

The form of the questions is borrowed. Isaiah taunted Egypt in exactly this way — where then are your wise men? (Isa. 19:12) — and again after Jerusalem’s deliverance: where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? (Isa. 33:18). It is the language of a battlefield after the fact, when the confident men who explained beforehand why it would go the other way are nowhere to be found.

Then v. 21, which is one of the most compressed and most profound sentences Paul ever wrote: “since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom”. Read it slowly, because it contains two different wisdoms and everything turns on keeping them apart. It was God’s wisdom that arranged matters so that human wisdom would not be able to find him. The failure is not an accident that God then worked around. It is the design.

Why would God arrange such a thing? Not because knowledge of him is unavailable — Paul argues elsewhere that the creation broadcasts it continuously, so plainly that nobody is left with an excuse (Rom. 1:19–20). The barrier was never a shortage of evidence. It is that the mind doing the looking is not neutral. Human beings do not merely fail to find God; they suppress what they find, because the God who is actually there is not one we would have chosen and does not leave us in charge. The problem is moral before it is intellectual, which is why more information has never yet converted anybody.

So God closed the route that would have let the clever arrive first, and opened one that anybody can walk. “It pleased God” — eudokēsen, it was his good pleasure, his delight — “through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe”. Note that Paul does not say God saves through folly; he says God saves through the folly of what we preach — the message the world files under nonsense. The instrument is preaching. The condition is believing. Neither requires a degree.

And that is a mercy with a very wide reach. If God had appointed philosophy as the road to himself, the entrance requirements would have excluded almost the whole human race — every illiterate believer in history, everyone without the leisure to think for a living, the woman running a household on no sleep, the man whose schooling ended at fourteen. Instead the requirement is to hear and to trust, and on that basis a professor and a child stand at exactly the same distance from the door.

Here is a test for anyone who has ever felt intellectually outmatched in a conversation about faith. Ask what would actually change if you won the argument. Suppose you had every answer perfectly ready and your friend conceded every point — would he then be a Christian? The evidence of two thousand years is that he would not, because nobody has ever been argued into the kingdom, and the cases where an argument was involved turn out on inspection to be cases where God was doing something underneath it. Answer the questions honestly, and take the trouble to answer them well. But do not mistake the argument for the power; the power is in the announcement, and it is God’s to apply.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom” — two cultures, two currencies, and the cross is legal tender in neither.

The Jewish demand was not unreasonable on its own terms. God had authenticated Moses with plagues and Elijah with fire from heaven; Scripture itself had trained them to expect that when God acts decisively, he shows his hand. What they were waiting for was a Messiah who would do something visible about Rome. And what makes the cross more than a disappointment to that expectation is a specific verse: cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Deut. 21:23). A crucified Messiah was not merely a failed one; by the plain reading of their own law he was a man under God’s curse. That is why Paul uses the word skandalon — not an intellectual objection, but a stumbling block, something you trip over and go down.

The Greek objection was different and just as total. Crucifixion was not a subject for polite society; Cicero called it a thing so degrading that the very word should be kept away from a Roman citizen’s ears. It was reserved for slaves and rebels, and designed to be obscene. To announce that the supreme revelation of God took place there was, to a philosopher, not merely false but tasteless — a category error so grotesque it did not merit a rebuttal.

So Paul had one message and two hostile audiences, and no version of the message would satisfy either. “But we preach Christ crucified.” The verb is present continuous. He kept doing it. He did not lead with the resurrection to soften the entrance, and he did not translate the cross into something more presentable. He went into the most status-obsessed city in Greece and announced an executed criminal.

Then the hinge of the sentence: “but to those who are called”. Not to those who worked it out. Not to those who were open-minded, or better educated, or more spiritually sensitive. Called.

This word needs plain handling, because it carries the doctrine the rest of the chapter depends on. There is a call that goes out to everybody — the invitation of the gospel, offered indiscriminately to all who hear, and genuinely offered. And there is what has been called the effectual call: the work of God by which a person not merely hears the invitation but is actually brought to the point of saying yes. The first can be refused, and constantly is. The second is God doing in a man what the man could not do in himself.

You can see the difference in the verse. The same Christ crucified is preached to everybody in Corinth. To some he is a stumbling block, to others nonsense — and to a third group, the identical message is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Nothing about the sermon changed. What changed was that God called them.

And notice how the categories are treated. The cross does not abolish the Jewish hunger for power or the Greek hunger for wisdom; it satisfies both, in the last place either would have looked. They wanted power: here is the power of God, in a man too weak to carry his own crossbeam. They wanted wisdom: here is the wisdom of God, in an event that looks like the collapse of every plan. The categories were not wrong. They were pointed in the wrong direction.

So consider what he did. He could have come with the signs they demanded; he had done greater things with a word, and legions were available for the asking. He could have come with the wisdom they sought, and held the lecture halls of Athens spellbound for forty years. He chose instead the one form of death designed to make a man contemptible, and went to it deliberately, in public, outside a city wall, between two criminals, for people who were at that moment shouting for it. The Jews asked for a sign and were given the only one that could have saved them. The Greeks asked for wisdom and were handed the wisdom of God with nails through it. There has never been a moment in the history of the universe when God looked less like God, or was more fully himself (cf. Gal. 3:13; Col. 2:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The foolishness of God… the weakness of God.” Read flatly, the sentence is close to blasphemy, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. God has no foolishness. God has no weakness. There is no such thing on either side of this comparison — which is the point of the sentence, and the reason it is constructed the way it is.

Paul is speaking from inside the world’s verdict. Very well: you have looked at the cross and filed it under folly and weakness. Take your own categories, then, and follow them where they lead. The thing you have called God’s foolishness is wiser than the best you have ever produced; the thing you have called his weakness is stronger than anything you can bring. He does not argue the verdict. He accepts it provisionally and detonates it from within.

And the comparison is not close. Set the cross against the accumulated wisdom of the human race — every philosophy, every ethical system, every scheme for making people good — and ask which of them has actually dealt with guilt. Not managed it, or explained it away, or advised us to be gentler with ourselves. Dealt with it. The wisest thing the world has ever devised leaves a man exactly where he was, with his record intact and his conscience intact and no remedy for either. What the world calls foolish removed the record.

The same with the weakness. Rome had the most efficient machinery of force the ancient world had seen, and it was employed that Friday to its full effect, and it worked: the man died. Three days later the thing that machinery existed to prevent had happened anyway, and within three centuries the empire that ran the machinery was naming itself after the victim. Whatever was operating in that tomb was not weakness with a good result. It was strength of a kind the categories had no room for.

Begg puts it exactly: “When God looks weak, he is about to do something the universe has never seen. Good Friday looked like the defeat of everything. Easter Sunday answered the question.”

And this is the verse to take into your own weakness, which is where most readers will need it. There is a persistent assumption in us that God works through our strong points — that he will use the areas where we are competent and impressive, and that our weaknesses are the parts of us he has to work around. This verse says the opposite about him, and Paul will later say the opposite about himself: it was in his weakness that Christ’s power rested on him, which is why he stopped asking for the thorn to be removed (2 Cor. 12:9–10).

So a test, and it may reorganise how you pray. Make two lists: the things about your life you would put forward as useful to God, and the things you have long regarded as disqualifying — the failure, the illness, the temperament, the years you cannot get back, the thing you are ashamed of. Now ask which list looks more like a cross. The pattern of this verse is not that God tolerates the second list. It is that the second list is where he has historically done his most significant work, and the first is where we are most likely to get in his way.

He saves by dying. He reigns from a cross. He conquers by being conquered. And every one of those sentences is nonsense by the world’s arithmetic, which is precisely why the world’s arithmetic has never once produced a resurrection.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now invites the Corinthians to look at themselves — and what they see should settle the theological argument definitively. They are not, for the most part, the wise, the powerful, or the well-born. Their own composition as a community is a demonstration of the thesis Paul has been arguing. God chose what is foolish, weak, low, and despised — not because these things have inherent virtue, but in order to nullify the things that do: the wise, the powerful, the strong. The method of grace is subtraction: God takes out of the equation everything that humanity might use as a basis for self-congratulation, so that the only remaining boast is in him.

The citation from Jeremiah 9:24 — “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” — is not an afterthought; it is the goal the whole chapter has been moving toward. The factional boasting of vv. 10–17, the intellectual boasting of vv. 18–25, and the social boasting implicit in the Corinthian culture — all of it is dismantled by the cross and replaced with a single, adequate boast: the Lord who became for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. Everything we need is in him; therefore all boasting must be about him.

Verse 30 is one of Paul’s most concentrated summary statements of the gospel. Christ Jesus “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.” Four nouns for what Christ is to the believer. Wisdom: in him we know God truly. Righteousness: in him we stand before God acquitted. Sanctification: in him we are set apart and progressively transformed. Redemption: in him we are bought out of every bondage. The Corinthians were seeking wisdom from Apollos and status from their gifts; Paul says they already have everything in Christ. Their problem is not poverty but ingratitude and forgetfulness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Doctrine of Boasting: Sola Gratia Applied

The logic of vv. 28–29 is the logic of grace pushed to its social conclusion: God chooses the things that are “not” to bring to nothing the things that “are” — “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” This is the pastoral and sociological outworking of sola gratia. If salvation were partly dependent on human wisdom, power, or birth, then at least some people could boast. But when God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors, and the socially marginal, the only conceivable boast is in the grace that did what human merit could never have achieved. Calvin: “God’s choosing the base things is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness, but a deliberate demolition of all grounds of human pride before him.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social hierarchy was steep and rigid: Roman citizens over freedpersons over slaves; the educated over the illiterate; patrons over clients. The church at Corinth crossed every one of these lines — and the crossing was theological, not merely sociological. It was evidence of the same gospel that the cross proclaimed. Now: The church that unconsciously mirrors the class and status structures of its surrounding culture is denying with its sociology what it affirms with its theology. The cross creates a community where the only legitimate boast is in the Lord — which means no other boast is legitimate at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Consider your calling, brothers” — blepete, look at it. Paul has been arguing the point theologically for eight verses; now he tells them to check it against the evidence in the room. The proof of everything he has said about God’s method is sitting in their own congregation, and they only have to look around.

“Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.” The three terms are the standard triad of ancient status: education, influence, and birth. Those were the things that determined where you sat, who returned your greeting, and what your life would be. And Paul’s observation is simply demographic: look at who has actually been converted here.

Note the precision of “not many”. He does not say “none”, and the church at Corinth is the proof of that too — Crispus the synagogue ruler, Gaius with a house big enough for the whole congregation, and Erastus the city treasurer (Rom. 16:23), a man holding public office. The gospel is not a movement of the poor that excludes the comfortable; God saves treasurers as well as slaves. But they were the exceptions, and everybody in the room knew it.

The outside world certainly knew it. Two centuries later the pagan critic Celsus was still sneering that Christianity was a religion of wool-workers, cobblers and laundry-workers, who would say nothing in front of educated men but got hold of children and women in the back rooms.
