He meant it as a demolition. He was describing, with reasonable accuracy, the thing Paul says here God did on purpose.

Because the choosing is deliberate and the purpose is stated: God chose the foolish “to shame the wise”, the weak “to shame the strong”. Not to bypass them. Not merely to demonstrate that he could manage without them. To shame them — and the shaming happens by the simple fact of the outcome. When the people who could not have found God by wisdom are manifestly full of God, the whole apparatus of wisdom stands exposed as having been useless for the one thing that finally mattered.

Now the pastoral weight, which is considerable. There is a particular kind of Christian who reads a chapter like this and feels quietly outside it. You are not a leader. You have no platform and no obvious gift. You did not do well at school, or your career went nowhere, or your life has been spent on work nobody records — and somewhere in you is the settled belief that you are one of the ordinary ones, that the real work of God is done by other people, and that your part is to make up the numbers and be grateful.

Read the verse again. That is not a description of your limitations. It is a description of God’s preference. He did not accept the unimpressive because nobody better applied. He chose them, and he chose them for a reason that has nothing to do with their inadequacy and everything to do with what he intends to prove.

And it is not a new policy. He picked a family with no children to found a nation, a shepherd boy over seven older brothers, a stammerer to confront Pharaoh, and a teenage girl in a village nobody respected to carry the Son of God. When he wanted twelve men to take the gospel to the whole world he passed over the entire religious establishment of Jerusalem and took fishermen off a beach. The pattern is so consistent that the surprising thing would be if he had chosen otherwise.

So a test worth running honestly. Think of what you would need to become before you would consider yourself genuinely useful to God — more articulate, more confident, better taught, further on. Now notice that you have just described a person God has repeatedly declined to use. The qualification he looks for is not on that list at all, and the reason is in the next two verses (cf. 1 Sam. 16:7; Luke 1:52; Matt. 11:25).

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is building to a climax and the language intensifies. Not merely the foolish and the weak now, but “the low and despised” — and then a phrase that goes past every social category: “even things that are not”. Ta mē onta. The things that do not exist.

He means the people who do not register. Not the poor, who at least appear in a census; the ones who make no impression at all — whose names are on no list, whose absence would alter nothing, who are, as far as the world’s accounting goes, simply not there. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank, this was not a metaphor. A slave had no legal personality. Paul reaches for the strongest word available and says: those are the ones God chose.

And the phrase is not chosen at random, because it is God’s signature. He is the God who “calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Rom. 4:17). He made the universe out of nothing at all. So when he builds a church out of nobodies, he is not making the best of poor material; he is doing the thing he has always done, in the way he has always done it. Creation out of nothing is not an emergency measure. It is his ordinary method.

The purpose is then stated without any softening, and it is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking towards: “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God”.

Look at the logic, because it explains everything that has puzzled the Corinthians. If God saved by strength, the strong could boast. If by wisdom, the wise could. If by birth, breeding, achievement, effort, or sincerity, then in every case somebody would arrive with a contribution and a reason to be pleased with himself. God has closed every one of those doors — not because he dislikes achievement, but because a saved man boasting in the presence of God would be a lie about what happened, and God will not build his kingdom on a lie.

This is the doctrine of grace pressed to its social conclusion. It is not merely that boasting is unattractive; it is that boasting has been rendered impossible by the design of salvation. Calvin: God’s choosing the base things is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness, but a deliberate demolition of every ground of human pride before him.

And here is where this lands for the person who has been quietly carrying the opposite conviction. Some readers do not struggle with pride at all. They struggle with the settled sense of being a nothing — a life that has not amounted to anything, a name nobody would recognise, years that produced nothing anyone could point to. If that is you, this verse is not a general encouragement. It is addressed to you specifically, and it says two things you should not miss.

The first is that God knows the category exists and did not look away from it. He did not choose people despite their being nothing, as if he had to overlook something; the text says the nothingness is what he chose. The second is what he chose it for — “to bring to nothing things that are”. He is not collecting the overlooked in order to keep them safely at the back. He is deploying them to dismantle everything the world has been impressed by. That is not a consolation prize. It is a commission.

So a test, and it is uncomfortable for both kinds of reader. Complete the sentence honestly: the thing I would most want said about me at my funeral is ______. Then ask whether that thing is on the list God has just declared he is bringing to nothing. Most of us find our deepest ambitions are for exactly the wise, powerful, well-born register that this passage says God passed over — which is worth knowing now, while there is still time to want something else.

Nobody will boast in his presence. Not the philosopher who explained the universe, not the emperor whose name is on the arch, not the Christian who served for sixty years. When that room is finally full, there will be one figure in it who is not there by grace, and every voice will be occupied with him (cf. Eph. 2:8–9; Rom. 3:27; Rev. 5:11–13).

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Because of him you are in Christ Jesus.” Four words in the Greek — ex autou, out of him, from him as source — and they settle the question of who did this. Not because you found him. Not because you were searching and happened to look in the right place. Your being in Christ traces back to God, and every one of the four gifts that follow arrives by that route.

Then Paul says something he says nowhere else in quite this way. He does not write that Christ gives us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He writes that Christ became them to us. These are not commodities dispensed from a distance by a generous benefactor. They are a Person, handed over. You do not receive four parcels; you receive him, and he turns out to be all four.

That distinction is the whole cure for Corinth. They were shopping — wisdom from Apollos, status from their gifts, standing from their faction — and Paul’s answer is not that they were shopping in the wrong places but that the shopping was over before it began. Everything they were assembling piecemeal was already theirs in one Person.

Wisdom. The city was full of it for sale, and the Corinthians were paying. Paul says the wisdom of God is not a body of teaching you acquire but a man you belong to, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3). Which does not mean a Christian knows more about everything. It means he knows the one thing on which everything else finally depends — who God is, and how a guilty man may stand before him — and there is no philosopher in history who worked that out.

Righteousness. This is the great Reformation word, and it must be plain. It does not mean God has made you a good person and now accepts you. It means that in Christ you are counted right with God — his record credited to you, your record charged to him. Luther called it an alien righteousness: not produced in you, but reckoned to you, and therefore not subject to how your week has gone. It is the answer to the question that lies underneath all religion: how can I possibly be all right with God? You cannot. He became it for you.

Sanctification. The same word that appeared in v. 2, and it is doing the same work. Christ is our holiness. We are set apart because we are in the holy one, before ever we begin to grow holier — which is why this letter can call the Corinthians sanctified while telling them to stop sleeping with prostitutes. The status comes first and the change follows from it; a Christian does not become holy in order to be accepted, but works out a holiness he has already been given.

Redemption. Apolytrōsis — the word for buying a slave out of bondage. It looks back to a price paid, and it looks forward to a deliverance not yet complete, when the body itself is finally free (Rom. 8:23). It is the last word of the four because it is the last thing to arrive.

Set them side by side and they cover the whole of a Christian’s existence: wisdom for the mind that could not find God, righteousness for the guilt that could not be removed, sanctification for the life that could not be cleaned, redemption for the body that will not last. Past, present and future, and all four located in one place.

So the test is simple and searching. Take the thing you are most anxious about tonight — the standing you are trying to establish, the guilt you are still carrying, the change in yourself you have failed to produce, the future you cannot secure — and ask which of the four it belongs to. Then ask why you have been looking for it anywhere other than in him.

He became these things. That is the astonishing verb. He did not send them; he became them, which means the wisdom has a face, and the righteousness has hands with holes in them, and the sanctification was purchased by a man who was himself made sin, and the redemption cost the redeemer everything he had. There is nothing a soul requires that is not, at this moment, sitting at the right hand of the Father in a body that still bears the marks of what it cost to obtain it.

verseByVerse.quote: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends where it was always going: a quotation, and one adequate boast.

Paul is citing Jeremiah 9:24, and it repays looking up, because he has abbreviated it and the full sentence is the whole argument of this chapter written six centuries earlier. Jeremiah says: Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches; but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me.

Wisdom, might, riches. Set that beside v. 26 — wise, powerful, of noble birth — and you can see why Paul reached for this text. He has been preaching Jeremiah’s sermon to Corinth. The three grounds of human boasting have not altered in six hundred years, and they have not altered in the two thousand since; only the vocabulary moves.

Notice what the verse does not say. It does not say: stop boasting. Paul could have written that, and it would have been a lesser thing. The instinct to boast — to have something to point to, some answer to the question of whether your life amounts to anything — is not surgically removed when a person becomes a Christian. It is redirected. The verb kauchaomai covers glorying, exulting, taking pride in; and Paul uses it of himself freely elsewhere. The question is never whether you will glory in something. It is what.

Which makes this the most practical sentence in the chapter, because everybody has an answer to it, and most of us have never said ours out loud.

So a test, and it is more revealing than asking what you believe. Think of the last time you felt genuinely diminished — overlooked in a conversation, outperformed by someone younger, made to feel small at a family gathering. Now notice what your mind reached for to restore itself. Everyone has a reserve, a fact about themselves they return to when their standing feels threatened: a qualification, a competence, a moral comparison, a child doing well, a hardship endured, a theological position more rigorous than the other person’s. That reserve is your boast, whatever you would say in church. And the trouble with every one of them is that they can be taken from you, usually by nothing more dramatic than time.

The boast Jeremiah names cannot. And notice what he says it consists of — not that you have achieved anything, but that you understand and know me. Even the boast is not about you. It is about being on terms with someone.

There is one more thing, easy to miss. Jeremiah wrote “boast in the LORD”, and in his sentence the LORD is the covenant name of God, the name too holy to be spoken. Paul quotes it and applies it, without a syllable of explanation, to the crucified man he has been preaching since v. 18. He does not argue for it or flag it as a development. It is simply where the sentence lands.

So the chapter that began by addressing people who were boasting in Paul, in Apollos, in Cephas, in their own eloquence and knowledge and rank, ends by taking every one of those props away and putting a single name in the empty space. Not a system, not a teacher, not a tradition, and not an achievement of yours. A Person — who became wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption for people who had none of the four, and who is worth boasting about for ever, by a church that had nothing whatever to bring him.

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Paul’s extended reflection on why he preached the way he preached when he came to Corinth — and on what kind of wisdom the Spirit actually brings. He came, he says, “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (v. 3). This is not a confession of inadequacy but a theological posture: the deliberate refusal to trust in rhetorical performance, so that the faith of his converts would rest not on human eloquence but on the power of God. The cross, preached without ornament, must do its own work.

The second half of the chapter then opens into one of Paul’s most majestic passages on the Spirit’s role in revelation. There is a wisdom, Paul insists, that is not the wisdom of this age — a hidden wisdom, decreed before the ages, that the rulers of this age did not understand (for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory). This wisdom is revealed by the Spirit alone, because only the Spirit searches the depths of God. The natural person, operating without the Spirit, cannot receive it; the spiritual person, indwelt by the Spirit of God, has the mind of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s self-description in the opening verses of chapter 2 is one of the most important passages in the New Testament on the nature and method of gospel ministry. He came to Corinth without superiority of speech or wisdom. He decided — a deliberate, wilful choice — to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified. He stood before them weak, fearful, trembling. His speech and message were not in plausible words of wisdom.

Why? Not because Paul was incapable of eloquence — his letters prove otherwise — but because the medium must not overwhelm the message. If the Corinthians had been converted by the brilliance of Paul’s rhetoric, their faith would rest on human skill. It would last as long as Paul’s reputation and no longer. But Paul wanted a faith that rested on something sturdier: “the power of God” (v. 5). So he stripped away everything that could have been mistaken for the source of power, and let the cross speak in its own register, authenticated by the Spirit.

The “demonstration of the Spirit and of power” in v. 4 refers not primarily to miracles but to the convicting, converting work of the Holy Spirit through apostolic preaching. When a person hears the message of the cross and believes, something has happened that no human rhetoric could have produced. That is the only demonstration Paul wanted — because it is the only demonstration that cannot be attributed to anything other than God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s deliberate simplicity in proclamation is not a pastoral strategy; it is a doctrinal commitment. The power of the gospel is the power of the Spirit working through the word of the cross — not the power of the preacher, the brilliance of the argument, or the emotional manipulation of the audience. Reformed theology has always insisted on this: it is the Spirit who regenerates, convicts, and converts; the preacher is the instrument, not the cause. Spurgeon: “If men are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything I can add.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth, the travelling sophist was a celebrity figure — a rhetorical virtuoso who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee, and move on. The Corinthians expected their teacher to perform at that level. Paul’s refusal to do so was not incompetence but protest: he would not compete on the sophists’ terms. Now: The contemporary equivalent is the pressure to make church services “compelling” through production values, platform charisma, and emotional manipulation. Paul’s counter-word is not to be deliberately boring, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: actually save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I decided” — ekrina, I judged, I reached a verdict. Paul did not drift into a plain style because he had nothing better available. He weighed it and came to a decision, and this is him defending that decision to a congregation which has since heard Apollos and concluded it would have preferred something with more polish.

A popular reading says Paul is repenting here — that he had tried philosophy at Athens, quoting their poets on the Areopagus (Acts 17), found it a failure, and arrived at Corinth chastened and determined never to try it again. It is a memorable story and it is almost certainly wrong. Luke does not present Athens as a failure: some joined him and believed, including a member of the council. Paul goes on quoting pagan writers for the rest of his ministry. And he is not describing a change of tactics here but a settled resolve about content.

Which raises the obvious question about that content, because “nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified” cannot be taken with wooden literalism. This very letter deals with lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts and the resurrection body. Paul plainly talked about a great deal more than the crucifixion at Corinth.

What he means is that the cross is the centre from which everything else is taught, and the standard by which everything else is measured. It is not the only subject; it is the subject that governs all the others. Notice how he actually does this later in the letter: when the Corinthians squabble over food, he ends with the brother for whom Christ died (8:11). When they abuse the Supper, he takes them back to the night he was betrayed. Every practical problem in this church is finally settled by reference to a cross.

And note the sharpness of the phrase. Not “Jesus Christ” alone, which could have been made respectable — a great teacher, a moral example, a figure of light. Him crucified. Paul deliberately keeps the offensive part in the centre of the frame, because the moment you remove it you have a religion the world can admire and nobody needs saving by.

Two guards, since this verse is regularly conscripted for causes Paul would not recognise. It is not a defence of anti-intellectualism: the man writing it had the best education available to a Jew of his generation and is in the middle of constructing a sustained argument. And it is not a rule that preaching must never address anything but the atonement — a congregation fed only on the mechanics of justification, never told how to be a husband or handle money or forgive, is not being fed the way this letter feeds.

So here is the test for anyone who teaches anything — a sermon, a class, a Bible study, a conversation with a child. Take the last thing you taught, and ask how many steps it took to get from your subject to the cross. If the honest answer is that it never got there, or that the connection was decorative rather than load-bearing, then whatever you delivered, it was not what Paul decided to do at Corinth. The test is not whether you mentioned Jesus. It is whether the thing you said would collapse if the crucifixion were removed from underneath it (cf. Gal. 6:14; 1 Cor. 15:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling.” This is the apostle Paul describing his own arrival at Corinth, and it is worth refusing to spiritualise it into something more dignified than it was.

Consider what had just happened to him. He had been stripped, beaten with rods and jailed at Philippi. He had been run out of Thessalonica by a mob, and then out of Berea. At Athens he had been politely mocked. He arrived at Corinth alone, without Silas and Timothy, into a city with a reputation for eating people alive — and Luke records that at some point during that stay the Lord appeared to him in a vision at night and said: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent (Acts 18:9). You do not say that to a man who is not afraid.

So the fear was real, it was not a rhetorical device, and Paul puts it in writing to a church that had begun to prefer more impressive speakers. He is not embarrassed by it. He is arguing from it.

Because the argument is this: “my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power”. Apodeixis was a technical term — the word for a compelling proof, a demonstration that settles a matter. Paul has chosen it deliberately. The sophists produced persuasion; Paul claims something better, and locates it entirely outside himself. What proved his message was not the performance of the speaker but the Spirit doing something in the hearers that no speaker can do.

And then the purpose, which is the whole point of the paragraph: “so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God”. The word for rest is the word for a foundation. Paul is thinking about what happens years later, under pressure, when the church is being tested.

A faith founded on a persuasive man lasts exactly as long as that man remains persuasive. If the Corinthians had been won by Paul’s brilliance, then the arrival of a better speaker would move them — which is precisely what has happened, and it is the whole trouble this letter is addressing. Worse, when a preacher falls, or is exposed, or simply turns out to be ordinary, everyone whose faith was built on him discovers there was nothing underneath. Every generation has watched this happen and been surprised by it.

Now the pastoral weight, because most readers need this verse more than they need the argument it serves. There is a very common Christian assumption that the people God uses are the confident ones — that if you were more assured, better spoken, less prone to going hot and cold and dry-mouthed when the conversation turns to Christ, you would be useful. And that your nervousness is evidence that this is not your gift and probably not your job.

This verse says the founding missionary of the Gentile world arrived at the most important church of his career weak, frightened and shaking. Not once, in an off week. It is how he describes the whole visit. Fear is not the opposite of usefulness, and confidence is not the qualification. If anything the reverse: a man who is not nervous may be relying on something Paul had deliberately laid down.

So a test, and it is quietly diagnostic. After you have spoken to someone about Christ, notice what you want to know. If the question in your mind is how did I come across?, then the demonstration you were relying on was your own. If it is Lord, do something in him that I cannot do, you have understood this passage. Paul trembled his way through eighteen months at Corinth and left behind a church that is still being read about two thousand years later, and not one line of it is credited to his nerve (cf. 2 Cor. 4:7; 12:9–10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established what he did not bring — worldly wisdom — Paul now describes what he does bring among the mature: a wisdom that is not of this age. This passage is one of the most profound in the New Testament on the epistemology of faith: how we come to know the things of God. Paul’s answer is startling in its radicalism. The wisdom of God is hidden, secret, decreed before the ages — and utterly inaccessible to the natural human mind. It cannot be reached by philosophical inquiry, mystical ascent, or religious achievement. It can only be revealed — and the revealer is the Spirit of God alone.

The argument moves in a careful analogy. Just as no one knows the thoughts of a person except the spirit of that person, so no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God (v. 11). God’s interior life is opaque to every created mind. But the Spirit has been given to those who believe — which means they have, not a general human spirit that reasons toward God, but the Spirit of God himself, enabling them to know what God has freely given them in Christ. This is the epistemological revolution of the gospel: the believer does not arrive at knowledge of God by ascending; God descends and gives himself to be known.

The “rulers of this age” who crucified the Lord of glory (v. 8) are either the Roman and Jewish authorities involved in the crucifixion, or the demonic powers working behind them, or (most likely) both. Their failure to recognise the Lord of glory in the person of Jesus of Nazareth is not merely a moral failure but an epistemological one: they did not have the Spirit; therefore they could not see what was there. The cross was, from the powers’ perspective, the elimination of a troublemaker; from God’s perspective, the salvation of the world. Same event, utterly different verdicts — because only one of those perspectives had the Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit (testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum). Calvin’s Institutes ground the believer’s certainty about Scripture not in external proofs but in the Spirit’s own witness to the heart. Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned; the Spirit of God alone can reveal them; the Spirit has been given to those who are in Christ. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos) is not merely unwilling but unable to receive spiritual things — a direct support for the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its noetic dimension.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for Apollos’s sophisticated rhetoric over Paul’s plain proclamation was, at root, a preference for a wisdom they could evaluate by their own natural capacities. Paul’s response: the real wisdom — the wisdom that saves — cannot be evaluated that way. It requires the Spirit to receive it. Now: The recurring temptation to evaluate the gospel by academic or cultural criteria — to ask whether Christianity can hold its own in the university seminar — misses Paul’s point. The knowledge of God is not the endpoint of human inquiry; it is the gift of the Spirit to the humble heart. This is why apologetics serves evangelism but cannot replace it: ultimately, only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom.” After two chapters of demolishing wisdom, Paul turns and says the Christian message is wisdom after all — just not of a kind the world can recognise or reach.

But the sentence needs a guard immediately, because it sounds exactly like something Paul would hate. Read carelessly, it establishes two tiers of Christian: ordinary believers who get the basic gospel, and an inner circle of the mature who are trusted with the deeper material. That is precisely how the mystery religions of Corinth were organised, and how the Gnostic teachers of the following century would organise themselves — secret knowledge for initiates, milk for the rest.

Two things rule that reading out. The first is the word itself: teleioi, the mature, the grown-up. It is not a rank; it is an age. Paul’s contrast in the very next paragraph is not initiates against outsiders but adults against infants — “I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ” (3:1). One category, at different stages.

The second is the sting the Corinthians would have felt. They regarded themselves as the mature ones; that self-assessment is the engine of the whole problem. Paul says “among the mature we impart wisdom” and then in the next breath tells them he could not do it with them, because they were still on milk and squabbling like children. This is not an invitation into an inner circle. It is a rebuke delivered by holding the door open and observing that they cannot yet walk through it.

Then the wisdom itself: “a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory”. Every word is doing something. Secret and hidden — not because God is withholding it now, but because it was concealed until he chose to disclose it; Paul’s word for that is mystērion, and in his hands a mystery is never a puzzle to be solved but a secret God has decided to tell.

Decreed before the ages — the plan was settled before there was a universe to enact it in. The cross was not God’s recovery from an unexpected disaster. It was the arrangement, made in eternity, before Adam, before the fall, before there was anybody to be saved by it.

And then the phrase that ought to stop the reader: “for our glory”. Not merely for our rescue, or our forgiveness, or our safety. The eternal decree had our glory in view — and this letter will spell out later what that means: a body raised imperishable, in glory, in power (15:42–43). Whatever God was intending before the ages, it was not simply to get us out of trouble. It was to bring us somewhere.

Which leaves a question worth sitting with rather than answering quickly. If God settled this before the ages, then the thing you are currently most anxious about — the situation you cannot see through, the outcome you are trying to secure — is happening inside a plan that was complete before the world was made. That does not tell you how it will go. It tells you that it is not being improvised, and that the same decree which reaches back before time reaches forward to a glory you have not yet seen (cf. Eph. 1:4; Rom. 8:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Who are the rulers? Commentators divide. Some take them as the human authorities — Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin, the men who actually signed the order and carried it out. Others take them as the spiritual powers, the rulers and authorities of Ephesians 6:12, working behind the human actors. The best reading is probably both, and Paul may not have felt the need to distinguish them: this letter belongs to a world in which political power and spiritual power are not separate departments, and the New Testament elsewhere shows Satan operating through named human beings at exactly this point (Luke 22:3; John 13:27).

Then the sentence that stops a careful reader: if they had known, they would not have done it. Does that mean the crucifixion was a blunder? That Satan miscalculated, and that if the powers had been better informed the atonement would never have happened and none of us would be saved?

The New Testament will not let us rest there, and the answer is one of the most important things a Christian can grasp about how God governs the world. Peter puts both halves in a single sentence on the day of Pentecost: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Not one clause qualifying the other. The plan was fixed, and the men who executed it were lawless and guilty.

The believers in Jerusalem say the same thing when they pray, and they name every party: Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel gathered together “to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:27–28). They freely did what they wanted. What they wanted had been decreed.

So the ignorance here is real and it is culpable. The powers were not victims of insufficient briefing; they were blind because they were evil, and their blindness was the very thing God used. This is the pattern of Joseph and his brothers written across cosmic history: you meant it for evil, God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The devil got exactly what he wanted, and it destroyed him — through death, the Son destroyed the one who had the power of death (Heb. 2:14).

Which yields a considerable comfort for anyone currently on the receiving end of someone else’s malice. You are not obliged to believe that what was done to you was good, or that the person who did it meant anything but harm. The cross settles that God does not require evil to be innocent in order to make it serve him. The worst act in the history of the world is the one he used to save it.

And then the title, which is the most audacious thing in the verse. The Lord of glory. It comes from Psalm 24, where the gates are commanded to lift up their heads so that the King of glory may come in — and the psalm asks twice, who is this King of glory?, and answers: the LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD of hosts.

Paul takes that title and attaches it, without a word of explanation, to a man his readers knew had been flogged and nailed up outside a city wall between two criminals. The King of glory came to his own gates and they did not lift up their heads; they crucified him. He made the wood. He made the iron in the nails, and the men who drove them, and held their hearts beating through every hour of it. And he did not come down — because coming down would have saved him and lost us, and he had decreed before the ages which of those he would choose (cf. Ps. 24:7–10; John 1:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, and the misquotation turns it inside out.

You will have heard it at funerals, and on cards: eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for them that love him — offered as a beautiful statement that heaven is beyond imagining, that we cannot know what awaits us, and that we must simply trust. It is used to close a subject.

But look where the sentence actually ends. Verse 9 finishes on a dash, not a full stop, and the main clause is in verse 10: “these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit.” Paul is not saying we cannot know. He is saying that what was once unreachable by any human faculty has now been told to us. The quotation is the setup; the revelation is the point. Quoting v. 9 without v. 10 makes Paul say the opposite of what he wrote.

And notice the three faculties the citation rules out, because they cover every route a person might take. No eye has seen — so it cannot be observed; empirical investigation will not find it. Nor ear heard — so it cannot be picked up by report; no tradition preserved it. Nor the heart of man imagined — so it cannot be arrived at by intuition, or mysticism, or the religious imagination working at full stretch. Sight, hearsay and inspiration all fail. Which leaves exactly one possibility, and it is the one Paul names: God had to say it himself.

Then the reason he was able to: “the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God”. The word is bathē — the deep places. Searching here does not mean investigating, as though the Spirit were exploring a God he does not yet fully know. It is the language of complete access. The Spirit is at home in the depths of God, because he is God.

Which is the thing to hold on to. The Spirit who has full access to the interior life of God is the same Spirit given to ordinary believers — and that is how a person with no education and no religious pedigree can read a page of Scripture and genuinely meet God there, while a hostile expert reads the identical page and finds nothing but literature.

So there is a correction here for how we speak about the Christian hope, and it matters at exactly the moment the verse is usually misused. Standing at a graveside, we are not reduced to saying that we cannot imagine what has happened to the person we loved. We can say a great deal, because God has told us: that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:8); that the dead in Christ will rise (1 Thess. 4:16); that this perishable body will put on the imperishable (15:53); that he will wipe away every tear. The Christian at a funeral is not the person who knows nothing. He is the only person in the room who has been told.

Here is a test worth running on yourself. Ask what you actually expect after death, and notice whether your answer comes from Scripture or from the culture — clouds, a vague reunion, a light, becoming a memory in other people’s heads. Most of us discover that our functional hope is far vaguer than the one we have been given, and the reason is not that God was reticent. It is that we have taken the words eye has not seen as permission not to look up what he said (cf. Isa. 64:4; Eph. 1:17–18).

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now supplies an analogy so ordinary that it is easy to miss how much it settles.

“Who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?” Think about someone you have lived alongside for thirty years. You know their face better than your own, you can predict what they will order and how they will react — and they still surprise you. You still cannot get inside. There is a room in every human being that no one else has ever entered, and the only occupant is the person themselves.

Now scale that up. If one finite creature is finally opaque to another, what possible route is there into the interior life of God? None from the outside. However clever the investigator and however long he works, he is standing outside a door with no handle on his side.

Which is what makes the next sentence extraordinary: “Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God.” The door was opened from within. God has not merely sent information about himself; he has given the one person who has always been inside — and he has given him to us, to ordinary believers in a fractious congregation in a port city.

Note the contrast Paul draws. The alternative is “the spirit of the world”, and it is worth being clear what that means. It is not a demon; it is the whole outlook a person absorbs simply by living here — the instincts about what matters, what success looks like, what is worth fearing, what is faintly ridiculous. It is the air. And it is perfectly competent within its own range; it can assess a career, a house, a reputation. It simply has no equipment for the things of God, and never will.

Then the purpose: “that we might understand the things freely given us by God”. The verb is charisthenta, from the same root as grace — the things graced to us. And notice the double gift, which is the heart of the matter. God gives, and then God gives the capacity to know what he has given. Without the second gift the first would sit unrecognised, like a man holding a deed in a language he cannot read.

Which explains something every Christian has watched happen. A new believer with no theological education reads a chapter of Paul and comes away genuinely fed, having met God in it. A scholar who has spent a career on the same chapter, and knows far more about it, comes away having met nothing. The difference is not intelligence and it is not diligence. One of them has the Spirit and the other does not, and this passage says that is the entire explanation.

So a word for the reader who feels disqualified from Scripture — who was never taught, finds the Bible hard, and assumes the real understanding belongs to people with training. Training helps and is worth having, and God gives teachers to his church for a reason. But the decisive qualification is not education. It is that the Spirit who lives in the depths of God lives in you, and he is entirely capable of showing an ordinary person what he has freely given. Ask him before you read. That is not a pious formality; it is the exact application of this verse (cf. Ps. 119:18; John 16:13–15).

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“We impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit.” The claim has moved a step further than most readers notice. Paul is no longer saying merely that the Spirit gave him the message; he is saying the Spirit was involved in the wording.

That is a considerable claim and it is the foundation of what the church has meant by inspiration. Not that God gave the apostles a general impression which they then dressed in whatever language came to hand, but that the Spirit superintended the expression as well as the substance. It is why Scripture can be studied at the level of a single word, and why translators labour over particles and tenses that would not matter in an ordinary document. If the ideas alone were inspired, the words would be packaging. Paul says the words were taught.

This should not be pressed into a claim that the human authors were suppressed. They plainly were not — Paul’s Greek does not read like Luke’s, John writes with a vocabulary a child could follow, and this same letter contains its author failing to remember whom he baptised (1:16). The Spirit used real men, with their own styles and limitations, and the result is exactly what he intended to say. Both halves must be held, and dropping either produces a doctrine the Bible itself contradicts.

The last clause is genuinely difficult, and honesty requires saying so. The Greek — pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes — can be rendered several ways: interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual; comparing spiritual things with spiritual things; or expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words. The grammar permits all three, and good commentators land differently.

What is not in doubt is the direction of Paul’s argument, which has been consistent since v. 6: spiritual realities require spiritual means at every stage. A spiritual message, given in Spirit-taught words, received by Spirit-indwelt people. There is no point in the chain at which unaided human capacity is sufficient.

And the second rendering — comparing spiritual things with spiritual — describes something practical that Christians do constantly, whether or not it is what Paul meant here. Scripture is interpreted by Scripture. An obscure verse is read in the light of a clear one; a difficult passage is checked against the whole. That is why the Bible is its own best commentary, and why the man who has read all of it will understand any part of it better than the man who knows three favourite chapters very well.

So there is a practical consequence worth acting on. If the words were taught by the Spirit, then the actual wording of Scripture rewards attention in a way no other book’s does. Slow down. Notice the tense, the conjunction, the little word but. A great deal of what people call deep Bible study is simply the willingness to read what is actually on the page rather than the summary of it we are carrying in our heads (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the verse that explains the whole chapter, and it is one of the hardest sayings in Paul.

“The natural person” is psychikos anthrōpos — the human being as he comes into the world, equipped with everything natural birth supplies and nothing more. Not a wicked person particularly; not a stupid one. Simply a man without the Spirit.

And Paul says two things about him, and they are different. He does not accept the things of the Spirit — ou dechetai, does not welcome them, will not have them. And he is not able to understand them — ou dynatai, lacks the capacity. Unwilling and unable, and the second is the more uncomfortable claim.

It needs stating carefully, because it is easily caricatured. Paul is not saying that unbelievers cannot follow the words, or that they are less intelligent, or that an atheist cannot give an accurate account of Christian doctrine — many can do it better than most churchgoers. What he says is that such a person cannot receive these things as true and desirable, cannot see them for what they are, because they are “spiritually discerned” and he has no organ for that discernment. It is like describing a colour to a man born blind; the failure is not in his reasoning, and giving him a better explanation will not help.

This is what the Reformed tradition means when it speaks of the effect of sin on the mind. The damage is not only to the will, so that we will not come; it reaches the understanding, so that we do not see anything worth coming for. And the root of it is moral rather than intellectual: the cross looks foolish to a man not because he has thought hard and found a flaw, but because he is estranged from the God it reveals.

Which raises the question this verse always raises, and it deserves a straight answer: if that is true, why say anything to anybody? If my brother-in-law is constitutionally unable to receive it, what exactly am I doing at Christmas dinner?

The answer is that God has appointed the message as the very instrument by which he gives the capacity. He does not wait for people to become able and then send a preacher; he sends the preacher and makes them able. Luke records it in a single line about a businesswoman at Philippi: Paul spoke, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14). Two things happened, in that order, and only one of them was Paul’s.

Ezekiel is the picture. Told to preach to a valley of dry bones — the least promising congregation in Scripture — he is not asked whether they are capable of responding. He is told to prophesy, and while he is prophesying the bones come together (Ezek. 37). The preacher’s job was never to produce life. It was to speak, while God produced it.

So this verse, far from discouraging evangelism, is the reason it is bearable. It takes the outcome off your shoulders. It explains why your best arguments have not worked and why your relative is not persuaded by evidence he cannot fault — not because you argued badly, but because argument was never the missing ingredient. And it tells you what to do instead: keep speaking, and pray for the one thing you cannot supply.

Which is worth turning into practice this week. Take the person you have been trying to convince for years. Stop preparing the better argument, and start asking God to open their eyes — by name, specifically, and often. You have been attempting the one part of the job that was never yours, and neglecting the part that was (cf. 2 Cor. 4:4–6; John 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.” This is among the most abused sentences in the New Testament, and the abuse is always in the same direction.

It has been used by leaders to place themselves beyond accountability, by teachers to dismiss every objection as carnal, and by ordinary Christians who simply do not wish to be corrected — you are not in a position to assess me; I am spiritual and you are judging. Used that way it is a trump card that ends every conversation, and it has protected a great deal of harm.

So begin with what it cannot mean, and the proof is in this very letter. Paul, three chapters later, delivers a verdict on a Corinthian believer’s conduct in the strongest terms, saying he has “already pronounced judgment” on the man (5:3). He then tells the congregation flatly that it is their business to judge those inside the church (5:12), and asks whether there is really no one among them wise enough to settle a dispute between brothers (6:5). Whatever v. 15 means, it does not mean that Christians are immune from the assessment of other Christians — the same author says the opposite within a few pages.

What it means is set by the argument it belongs to. Paul has spent nine verses establishing that spiritual things require the Spirit to be discerned. The conclusion follows: a man with the Spirit can evaluate reality in a dimension the natural man has no access to — and by the same token, the natural man is simply not qualified to return a verdict on him. It is a statement about who has standing, and the point is not the Christian’s superiority but the world’s incompetence in this particular court.

And “judges all things” is not a claim to omniscience or to being right about everything. Anakrinei is the word for examining, sifting, weighing something up — the discernment that sees beneath the surface of things to what they actually are before God. A Christian is not guaranteed to be correct about politics or medicine or his own motives. He is given the capacity to see what the world is, what a life is for, and what the cross means, and no amount of natural brilliance supplies that.

Where this genuinely helps is with a particular kind of pain. There are Christians whose families think they have thrown their lives away — the son who turned down the career for the mission field, the woman whose relatives regard her faith as a phase she should have outgrown, the man whose colleagues have quietly filed him under harmless and rather sad. The verdict is delivered constantly, sometimes kindly, and it lands.

Paul’s word is that the verdict is being handed down by people who, on this subject, are not competent to reach one. That is not arrogance; it is the same thing he has been saying since 1:18 about the message itself. They are not being obtuse. They are assessing a spiritual matter with equipment that does not extend to it, and their conclusion tells you about their instruments rather than about you.

But hold that alongside the guard, because the two must travel together. The world’s opinion of your faith is not the final word. Your brother’s opinion of your behaviour very often is, and a Christian who uses this verse to deflect correction from other believers has taken a sentence about the world’s incompetence and used it against the very people God gave him for the purpose. The test is simple: when you last reached for the idea that people do not understand you, was your critic outside the faith, or was it a Christian who loves you and had noticed something true?

verseByVerse.quote: “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul closes the argument with a question from Isaiah and an answer that ought to be impossible.

The quotation is Isaiah 40:13, and its setting matters. Isaiah is at his most soaring, describing a God who measures the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighs the mountains in scales, before whom the nations are a drop from a bucket and dust on the balance. Into that he drops the question: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? The expected answer is nobody, ever, and the effect is to flatten the reader.

Paul quotes it, lets it do its work — and then writes: “But we have the mind of Christ.”

It is one of the boldest sentences he ever wrote, and it should not be softened. He is not claiming that Christians know everything, or that we can second-guess God, or that any believer’s opinion carries divine authority. The whole chapter has been arguing that God’s thoughts are unreachable from below. What he is claiming is that the unreachable has been given — that through the Spirit, believers have been let into the way Christ sees things.

Which is a real participation, not a figure of speech, and it has a shape you can recognise. To have the mind of Christ is to begin valuing what he values and to find yourself unimpressed by what impressed you before. It is to look at a difficult person and see someone he died for. It is to hear about a decision at work and instinctively ask what would be honest rather than what would be advantageous. It is to feel the pull of the poor, the awkward, the unimportant, in a way that has no natural explanation. None of that is achieved by effort; it grows, and it grows because someone else’s mind has been given to you.

And it is worth saying what it is not, because the phrase gets used to end arguments. Having the mind of Christ does not mean your convictions are automatically his, and it is not a claim to be exercised against other Christians. Paul elsewhere describes the mind of Christ at length, and what he describes is not a set of superior opinions but a disposition: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death (Phil. 2:5–8). A man who says he has the mind of Christ and is chiefly using it to win is describing something other than what Paul means.

So the chapter ends where it began, and the distance travelled is enormous. It opened with a frightened man arriving in a hostile city, shaking, refusing to be impressive, determined to talk about nothing but an execution. It ends by claiming that such people — not the philosophers, not the rulers of this age, not the mature of Corinth’s own estimation — have been given access to the mind of God.

Nobody has instructed him. Nobody has advised him, or improved his plan, or contributed a single thought he did not already hold. He measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and he decreed before the ages a wisdom hidden from every ruler and every power — and then he came, and was not recognised, and was crucified by the men he was dying for. And he has given his own mind to a church at Corinth that could not stop arguing about which preacher it preferred. That is what he is like (cf. Rom. 11:33–36; Phil. 2:5).

2.text: <sup>1</sup>And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom.<sup>2</sup>For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.<sup>3</sup>And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling,<sup>4</sup>and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,<sup>5</sup>so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.<sup>6</sup>Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away.<sup>7</sup>But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.<sup>8</sup>None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.<sup>9</sup>But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”—<sup>10</sup>these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.<sup>11</sup>For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.<sup>12</sup>Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.<sup>13</sup>And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.<sup>14</sup>The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.<sup>15</sup>The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.<sup>16</sup>“For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
Chapter 3 addresses the factional spirit at Corinth from a different angle: not the cross as criterion (ch. 1–2) but the nature of Christian ministry as criterion. The Corinthians are dividing over Paul and Apollos; Paul’s response is to describe what Paul and Apollos actually are in relation to each other and to God. They are co-workers in God’s field — one planting, one watering, but God alone giving the growth. They are builders on a single foundation, the only one that was ever laid: Jesus Christ.

The chapter escalates to its most searching moment in vv. 16–17: the Corinthian church is God’s temple, indwelt by God’s Spirit. This is not a private devotional truth but a corporate, ecclesiological one. The community together is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit — and whoever destroys that community destroys the temple of God. The factional fights at Corinth are not merely social dysfunction; they are an assault on the dwelling place of God. Then the final movement (vv. 18–23) circles back to the theme of wisdom and boasting: stop boasting in men, because all things belong to you, and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul returns to the carnal condition of the Corinthians, now with more explicit diagnosis. They are not spiritual but fleshly — sarkinoi, made of flesh, still operating by the instincts of unregenerate human nature. The evidence? Jealousy and strife. These are not peripheral vices; in Paul’s catalogues of the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20), they sit alongside idolatry and sorcery. A church divided by personality loyalties is not merely socially dysfunctional; it is manifesting the symptoms of a life still dominated by the flesh rather than the Spirit.

The correction Paul offers is a radical redefinition of ministry. Paul planted, Apollos watered — but God gave the growth. Therefore “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth” (v. 7). This is not false modesty; it is precise theological description. The minister is the instrument; God is the cause. The Corinthians have been treating the instruments as if they were the cause, which is why their factions are so fierce. When you understand that Paul and Apollos are servants and God is the Lord, the competition between them collapses.

The image of God’s field introduces the first of two great metaphors in the chapter. Paul and Apollos are co-workers in one field that belongs to God — fellow labourers, not competitors. The competitive individualism of the Corinthian factions has imported the values of the Roman patronage system into the body of Christ; Paul refuses the framework entirely. “We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (v. 9) — the transition to the second metaphor, the building, sets up the crucial passage that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated insistence that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is the Reformed doctrine of sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Paul preached; Apollos taught; but neither of them converted a single soul. Conversion is the work of God, not the achievement of the preacher. This means that the minister cannot take credit for results, cannot despair over apparent fruitlessness as if it were his own failure, and cannot be compared with another minister as if their different “results” reflected their different competencies. God gives where and when he wills.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions were measuring Paul and Apollos by their outputs — converts, rhetorical impact, visible results. Paul refuses this measuring rod: the results belong to God, not to the apostle. Now: The contemporary church is still tempted to evaluate ministry by attendance, conversion numbers, and cultural impact — and to attribute these to the skill and gifting of the human leader. Paul’s corrective: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God of growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul had spent eighteen months at Corinth. He is writing perhaps three or four years later, and the verdict is devastating in its plainness: I could not address you as spiritual people.

The word he uses is sarkinoi — made of flesh, fleshly. And that is precisely the opposite of what the Corinthians called themselves. They were the spiritual ones; that was the whole basis of their confidence. They had the gifts, the knowledge, the eloquence, the tongues. Paul takes the label off them in his first sentence.

Then the image: milk, not solid food. It is a common one in the New Testament — the writer to the Hebrews uses it of people who ought by now to be teachers and still need someone to go over the basics with them (Heb. 5:12–14). But notice what milk is not. It is not a different or lesser gospel, a simplified version for beginners while the mature graduate to something else. It is the same food in a form an infant can take. The Christian who moves on from the cross has not advanced; he has wandered off.

What makes the diagnosis sting is the tense: “and even now you are not yet ready”. Not merely that they were immature when he arrived — everybody is — but that years have passed and nothing has changed. That is the charge. An infant is delightful. A man who has been an infant for four years is a tragedy.

And this raises a question worth sitting with, because it applies to a great many long-standing churchgoers. How would you know? You cannot see your own growth directly, and the people who are most confident of their maturity are, in this chapter, precisely the ones who do not have it.

Paul is about to give the measurement in the next verse, and it is not the one anybody expects. But notice already that it is not knowledge. The Corinthians knew a great deal — Paul has just conceded they are enriched in all speech and all knowledge (1:5) — and it has not made them adults. It is entirely possible to accumulate information about God for thirty years and remain a spiritual toddler, because facts are the easiest thing in the Christian life to acquire and the least reliable indicator of anything.

So a test that cuts through the self-assessment. Ask what you were like ten years ago in the one area where you are hardest to live with — your temper, your tongue, your resentment of a particular person, your handling of being crossed. Not what you know about it now; what you are actually like. Growth in Christ shows up there or it has not happened, and the person best placed to answer is not you but whoever shares your house (cf. Heb. 5:12–14; 1 Pet. 2:2).

verseByVerse.quote: for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the measurement, and it is startlingly ordinary: “while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh?”

Two words. Zēlos — the heat of wanting what someone else has, of not being able to be glad about another person’s advantage. And eris — strife, the quarrelling that follows. Paul is not describing exotic wickedness. He is describing the ordinary weather of a church committee.

And he treats them with complete seriousness, because in his catalogue of the works of the flesh in Galatians these two sit in the same list as idolatry, sorcery and drunkenness (Gal. 5:20). We instinctively grade sins, and jealousy comes low on our list precisely because it is invisible and universal. Paul puts it with sorcery.

Now feel the force of the argument. The Corinthians assessed spiritual maturity by spiritual phenomena — who could speak in tongues, who had the deeper knowledge, whose teacher was most impressive. Paul assesses it by whether they can get on with each other. Everything they were counting is set aside, and the one thing they had never thought to measure is made the whole test.

That is not Paul’s invention. It is what Jesus said would identify his disciples to a watching world — not their doctrine, not their gifts, but their love for one another (John 13:35). And it is what the next chapter of this letter’s most famous section says: gifts without love are noise (13:1–3).

“Behaving only in a human way” — literally, walking according to man. It is the deadliest phrase in the verse. The church at Corinth was running on ordinary human operating principles: rank, rivalry, the instinct to be associated with the winning side. Nothing was happening in that congregation that could not be equally observed in a trade guild or a political faction. The Spirit had been given to them, and you could not tell from the outside.

So the test, and it is uncomfortably specific. Think of the person in your church whose success you find hardest to be glad about — whose gift is the one you wish you had, whose praise you find yourself qualifying, whose name you are slightly relieved to hear criticised. Now notice that you have just located the exact point at which, on Paul’s measurement, you are still an infant.

That is not said to condemn. It is said because the Corinthians did not know, and would have gone on not knowing, and a diagnosis is the first mercy. The gifts told them nothing. The jealousy told them everything (cf. Gal. 5:19–21; James 3:14–16).

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“What then is Apollos? What is Paul?” The question is not who but what — and asking what a person is rather than who reduces them, deliberately, to a function. Paul is refusing to be a personality.

His answer is one word: diakonoi. Servants. It is the ordinary word for someone who waits at table — the person who brings the food and is not the reason anyone came. Nobody leaves a dinner party discussing the waiter. The Corinthians have organised their entire church around a debate about waiters.

Then two qualifications, and both take something further away. “Through whom you believed” — the preposition is instrumental. Paul and Apollos are the channel, not the source; you do not thank the pipe for the water. And “as the Lord assigned to each” — even the differences between them, the very differences the Corinthians are quarrelling over, were handed out by the Lord. Apollos’s eloquence is not Apollos’s achievement. It was assigned.

Which quietly removes the ground from both factions at once. If Apollos is more polished than Paul, that is not a reason to prefer Apollos — it is a fact about what God gave Apollos. And if Paul founded the church and Apollos did not, that is not a reason to prefer Paul; it is a fact about what God assigned Paul to do. You cannot construct a hierarchy out of gifts that were distributed rather than earned.

“Are you not being merely human?” Paul repeats the charge from the previous verse and attaches it to the slogans. The tragedy of a personality faction is that it is so completely unremarkable. Every institution on earth divides this way. A church doing it is not displaying a distinctive failing; it is failing to display anything distinctive at all.

And this is where the passage reaches into ordinary Christian life, because most readers do not run a faction but nearly all of us make the comparison. You listen to a gifted preacher and come away either diminished or quietly competitive. You watch someone else’s ministry flourish while yours does not. You measure your church against the one down the road. The instinct is so constant that we barely notice it operating.

Paul’s cure is not to try harder at humility. It is to remember the word assigned. What another Christian has was given to him, which means envying it is a complaint about the distribution rather than about the person — and the distributor is the Lord who assigns to each. Comparison, followed all the way down, always turns out to be an argument with God about what he decided to hand out.

So the test: when you last felt the sting of someone else’s gift, did it occur to you that God gave it to them on purpose, for the good of a church you belong to? A servant does not resent another servant’s tray. Both trays are going to the same table (cf. Rom. 12:6; 1 Pet. 4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Three verbs, and the first two are ordinary work while the third is a miracle nobody can perform.

The image is exact and worth staying with. A farmer can do a great deal. He can prepare the ground, choose the seed, get the depth right, water at the correct intervals, keep the weeds down, watch the weather. Every one of those requires skill and years of learning, and a lazy farmer produces a poor crop. But no farmer in the history of the world has ever made a seed germinate. He creates conditions. Life is not among the things he supplies, and if the seed does not come up he has no further move available.

Paul is saying that is the exact shape of Christian ministry. Preaching, teaching, hospitality, patient friendship, years of prayer — all real, all demanding, all worth doing well. And not one of them can produce spiritual life in another human being. The most gifted preacher alive stands in precisely the same relation to a hard heart as a farmer to a seed.

Then the conclusion, which is more severe than we usually let it be: “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything”. The word is ouden — nothing. Not “less important than God”, not “secondary”. Nothing. Paul has just described his own life’s work and assigned it the value zero in the column that matters.

He does not mean the work was pointless; the next verse says each will receive wages. He means it contributed nothing to the one thing that had to happen. And he says it in a church where people are choosing sides between two men, because if both men are nothing, the argument is over.

This is the verse for the reader who has been praying for someone for years. A parent whose adult child has walked away. A wife whose husband has heard it all and remains politely unmoved. Someone who has explained, invited, modelled, wept, and watched nothing happen — and who has begun to suspect the failure is theirs, that a better Christian would have got somewhere by now.

Read the verse again. You were never able to give the growth. It is not that you have tried and fallen short of a standard other people meet; it is that the thing you are longing for has never once been within the power of any human being, including the apostle Paul. That does not make your planting and watering worthless — God ordinarily uses exactly such means, and your years of faithfulness are the seed and the water. It removes a burden you were never given and could not carry.

And it should change what you ask for. Most of us pray for opportunities, and then work very hard at the opportunity when it comes. Pray instead for the thing only God does. He has been giving growth to unpromising ground since the beginning, and the man writing this verse was, before Damascus, the least likely convert in the ancient world (cf. Ezek. 36:26; John 15:5).

verseByVerse.quote: He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He who plants and he who waters are one” — hen eisin, they are one thing. Not merely allies, not colleagues who have agreed not to compete. One. The factions have set Paul against Apollos; Paul says there is no gap between them for a faction to occupy.

And then a phrase that repays slow reading: “each will receive his wages according to his labour”.

Not according to his results. The word is kopos — toil, the kind of work that wears you out. And the whole logic of the preceding verses requires this: if God gives the growth, then results cannot be the measure of the servant, because the results were never his to produce. What is his is the labour. That is what will be assessed, and that is what will be paid.

Think about how completely this inverts the way ministry is actually evaluated, then and now. The Corinthians were comparing outputs — who drew the crowd, whose converts, whose impact. Every generation since has done the same with attendance figures and conversion numbers and reach. Paul says the ledger God keeps has a different column heading altogether.

Which is one of the most quietly liberating sentences in the New Testament, and it is addressed to a very large number of people. The missionary who gave forty years to a hard field and saw a handful of converts. The Sunday school teacher who taught for three decades and watched most of them drift. The man who has led a small congregation faithfully in a village where nothing has ever grown, while a church in the next town filled up. The mother who prayed and taught and did everything she knew, and whose children do not believe.

Every one of them has, at some point, done the arithmetic and concluded the life was wasted. This verse says the arithmetic is wrong — not because the results do not matter, but because they were never the thing being weighed. The Lord who gives the growth does not then charge his servants for the growth he chose not to give.

One guard, since “wages” and “reward” make some Christians nervous. This is not salvation being earned; Paul has already settled that Christ became our righteousness (1:30) and will shortly say that the man whose work burns is saved anyway (v. 15). The New Testament is entirely unembarrassed about reward for faithful service, and treats the prospect as a proper motive. What is being paid for is not your entrance. It is your labour.

So the test is a change of question. Not what have I achieved? — which is the question that produces both pride and despair, depending on the decade — but have I laboured? Have I kept planting and watering in the place I was put, for the years I was given? That question has an answer, it is answerable tonight, and it is the only one you will be asked (cf. Matt. 25:21; Gal. 6:9; 1 Cor. 15:58).

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three genitives in one short verse: God’s fellow workers, God’s field, God’s building. Paul is hammering a single point by repetition, and the point is ownership.

The first phrase is worth a moment of honesty, because it is commonly rendered “we are fellow workers with God” — a thrilling idea, and one that has launched a great deal of preaching about partnership with the Almighty. The Greek permits it. But it equally permits, and the context rather demands, “we are fellow workers belonging to God” — God’s workmen, labouring alongside each other in a field that is his. The other two phrases in the verse are plainly possessive, and the argument since v. 5 has been that the workers are nothing. Paul is not elevating Paul and Apollos to junior partners; he is putting them in the same category as the tools.

Which is not a demotion worth grieving over. The dignity of Christian work has never come from our importance to it. It comes from whose work it is.

“You are God’s field” — and this too is aimed at the factions. A field is not divided into plots belonging to different farmers. The Corinthians have been marking out territory in ground that belongs to somebody else entirely.

Then the switch: “God’s building”. Paul changes metaphor mid-sentence, and it is not carelessness. A field is organic and forgiving; if a crop fails you plough it in and sow again next season. A building is different. It goes up in a fixed order, every course rests on the one beneath, and what you put in early determines what the whole thing can bear. The stakes have just risen, and the next eight verses will explain why.

There is also a quiet reproof in the word for anyone who has ever thought of the church as an institution to be managed. Paul’s categories are agricultural and architectural, and both are categories of ownership by someone else.
