A church is not a voluntary society belonging to its members, a platform belonging to its minister, or a heritage belonging to the families who have been there longest. The deeds are not in the building.

So a test for anyone who has ever been possessive about a congregation — and most long-standing members have, usually without noticing. Listen to how you talk about it. My church, our chairs, the way we have always done this. Then ask what changes if the field and the building are God’s, and you are one of the workmen. A workman does not get a vote on the design. He gets the considerable honour of being trusted with somebody else’s property (cf. Eph. 2:20–22; 1 Pet. 2:5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The building metaphor now unfolds with architectural precision and eschatological urgency. Paul is the master builder (arch&itekton) who laid the foundation; others build on it. But — and here is the point — the foundation was not Paul’s to choose. It was given: “no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (v. 11). The church is not free to choose its foundation. The only admissible foundation for a Christian community is Christ himself: his person, his work, his death and resurrection. Everything else — programmes, traditions, personalities, institutions — is superstructure, not foundation.

The materials used in superstructure are what will be tested: gold, silver, precious stones vs. wood, hay, straw. The test is fire — the eschatological judgment of the Last Day. Fire reveals what each minister’s work actually was: whether it was built on Christ, out of the resources of the gospel, for the glory of God (it survives); or whether it was built for human applause, institutional prestige, or personal empire (it burns). The minister whose work survives receives a reward; the minister whose work burns will be saved, “but only as through fire” — with nothing to show for his life’s work. This is not a passage about purgatory (as medieval theology read it) but about the accountability of Christian workers at the judgment.

Then the passage reaches its climax: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (v. 16). This is no longer about individual ministers but about the corporate community. The church together is the new temple — the place where the living God has chosen to dwell in the new covenant age. The Corinthian faction fights are therefore not merely unseemly; they are desecrating the dwelling place of God. “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him” (v. 17) is one of the most solemn warnings in the letter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

Paul’s identification of the church as God’s temple carries enormous theological weight in a letter written to a city famous for its pagan temples. The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the temple of Aphrodite; the city was saturated with temple culture, temple prostitution, and temple feasts. Paul’s claim is that the living God has abandoned temples made of stone and taken up residence in a community of people — flawed, fractious, sin-prone people — through his Spirit. The church is not a building where God may be found; the church is the people in whom God actually dwells. This is the new covenant fulfilment of every OT temple theology: God with his people, no longer mediated through architecture and ritual, but through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were not merely social dysfunction; they were a theological emergency. A fragmented community cannot be a temple — the architectural metaphor itself requires unity, all the stones fitting together. The faction wars were, quite literally, demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live. Now: Every church split, every faction, every deliberate destruction of community is an assault on the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. This gives a theological gravity to church unity that mere social concern cannot supply: we are not trying to be nice; we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Like a skilled master builder” — architektōn, the word behind our architect: the man responsible for the whole design, who lays out the foundation and hands the site on to others. It is the only time the word appears in the New Testament, and Paul applies it to himself without embarrassment.

But look at how he introduces it: “according to the grace of God given to me”. The competence is real and it is not his. He does not say he was skilled and therefore chosen, nor pretend to a modesty he does not feel. He states the skill and assigns its origin in the same breath, which is the only way a Christian can ever speak accurately about his own gifts.

Then the warning that governs everything to the end of the chapter: “let each one take care how he builds upon it”. Not whether — everyone in a church is building something, whether or not they have noticed. The question is how, and Paul is about to say that the answer will be exposed by fire.

And the foundation is not open for discussion. “No one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.” Note the passive: which is laid. Even Paul did not choose it. He laid it in the sense that a builder lays what the architect has specified; the specification came from elsewhere.

It is worth being exact about what this rules out, because churches rarely announce a change of foundation. They shift by degrees, and the shift is always onto something good. A congregation can be founded on its history — the families, the building, the way things have always been done. On a personality, which is the Corinthian version. On a cause, however worthy. On an experience, so that the question becomes whether people felt something. On a doctrinal system, held so tightly that Christ himself becomes a topic within it rather than the thing it rests on. Every one of those can coexist with impeccable statements of faith, and every one of them is a different building.

The test Paul implies is simple to state and searching to run. Ask what would have to be removed before your church would recognise that something essential had gone. If the minister left, the music changed, the building were sold, the denomination collapsed — would the church still be there? And if the person and work of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, were quietly no longer at the centre of what is said and sung and prayed, how long would it take anyone to notice?

A congregation can survive the loss of almost anything except one thing. And that one thing was laid before any of us arrived, by an architect who did not consult us, and it is the only surface in the universe capable of taking the weight of what is being built on it (cf. Isa. 28:16; Eph. 2:20; Matt. 7:24–27).

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six materials, in two groups of three. Gold, silver, precious stones; wood, hay, straw. Every reader in the ancient world would have caught the reference: those are the materials of Solomon’s temple against the materials of a peasant’s hut. The first group is what you use when you are building a house for God; the second is what you use when you are throwing something up quickly.

And the difference that matters is not cost or beauty. It is behaviour under fire. Gold, silver and stone come through a blaze; wood, hay and straw do not merely char, they vanish.

“The Day will disclose it” — the definite article, and no further explanation needed. The Day of the Lord, the final assize. Paul says three things about it in one sentence, and each is worth separating. The work will become manifest: made visible, brought into the open. It will be revealed by fire. And the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.

Note that last phrase carefully, because it settles what is being examined. Not how much work — the fire is not weighing output. What sort. Quality, not quantity; kind, not scale.

So what makes a work gold rather than straw? Paul does not give a list, and we should be careful about inventing one. But the letter itself supplies the direction. Work that is genuinely built on the foundation — Christ crucified, not merely mentioned but load-bearing. Work done in dependence on the Spirit rather than on technique. Work aimed at people’s good rather than at the builder’s standing, which is the very thing that has gone wrong at Corinth. And, from the chapter Paul is walking towards, work done in love, since gifts exercised without it are precisely nothing (13:1–3).

Which means the distinction is very largely invisible now, and that is the point of the fire. Straw and gold look much alike at ground level, and a straw building can be considerably more impressive than a gold one if it is bigger. Two ministries can produce identical statistics, identical buildings, identical reputations, and be made of entirely different substances. Nothing available to us in this life reliably tells them apart. The fire will.

So the sobering thought is not that a Christian might be found to have done too little. It is that a Christian might be found to have done a great deal of the wrong kind — a life of visible activity, admired at the time, that turns out to have been made of hay.

A test, then, and it can be run on anything you are doing for God this week. Ask what would happen to it if nobody ever knew you had done it. Take away the credit, the recognition, the being seen to be the sort of person who does such things — would you still do it, and would you still do it that carefully? Fire has a way of settling questions of motive that introspection never quite manages, and the honest answer to that question is a fair preview (cf. Matt. 6:1–4; 1 Cor. 4:5).

verseByVerse.quote: If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two outcomes, and Paul states them without softening either. If the work survives, a reward. If it burns, “he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire”.

The image is of a man escaping a house fire with his life and nothing else. He is out, he is alive, he is not going back in — and everything he spent forty years accumulating is behind him in the flames. Saved, and with empty hands.

This verse has carried an enormous doctrinal weight it will not bear, and it must be addressed. From the medieval period onwards it became a principal text for purgatory — a fire after death through which the saved pass to be purified of the sins for which they have not yet made satisfaction. The Roman Catholic Church still cites it. And the reading is not stupid: there is a fire, there is a Christian, and he passes through it and comes out saved.

But the passage will not support it, for reasons that are in the text rather than in anybody’s tradition. The fire tests the work, not the man. Verse 13 says so twice: it will disclose each one’s work, and test what sort of work he has done. What burns in v. 15 is the work; the man is not being purified, he is being rescued from a blaze that is consuming what he built. Nothing here suggests duration, degrees, satisfaction for sin, or that the fire improves anybody. And the context is not sin in general at all — it is the quality of ministry built on the foundation, which is what the whole chapter has been about since v. 10.

Behind that lies the deeper reason, and this letter has already stated it. Christ became our righteousness (1:30). If the cross dealt with sin, there is nothing left for a fire to deal with; and if a fire is still required, the cross did not finish. Those cannot both stand. The believer’s sins were not held over pending further payment — there is now no condemnation, and the charge sheet is empty (1:8; Rom. 8:1).

So what is left is sobering enough without importing anything. A Christian can arrive at the end of his life, be undoubtedly saved, and have nothing whatever to show for the time. Not because he was a scandal — he may have been busy, respected, even prominent — but because what he built was made of the wrong stuff. That is a real possibility, and Paul puts it in writing to frighten people out of it.

And yet notice where the sentence lands, because Paul refuses to leave the man in the fire. He himself will be saved. The clause is unqualified. His life’s work is gone and he is not. Whatever else this verse does, it does not put a single believer’s salvation in question, and it was never meant to be read by an anxious Christian as a threat.

Which yields the test, and it is best run now rather than then. Take the thing you are pouring most of yourself into — the ministry, the project, the position, the thing you would most want mentioned at your funeral. Ask what it is made of. Not how large it is; what it is made of. There is still time to change materials, and that is the entire reason Paul told them about the fire in advance (cf. 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 14:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do you not know” — a phrase Paul uses ten times in this letter, always with an edge. It means: this is not new information, you have been told, and your behaviour suggests you have forgotten.

And the first thing to get right is the pronoun, because almost everyone reads this verse wrong. Every “you” here is plural. Not you are God’s temple as an individual — that is 6:19, and Paul will get there. Here it is you together. The congregation, collectively, is the temple; the Spirit dwells in the assembled community. One temple, not two hundred little ones.

That is a considerable claim in this city. Corinth was full of temples — Apollo, Asclepius, Aphrodite on the mountain above the town — buildings of stone and marble, with priests and sacrifices and processions, the visible religious furniture of the ancient world. Paul tells a group of mostly poor people meeting in somebody’s dining room that they are the place where the living God has taken up residence. The temples on the skyline are empty. The house with the shabby congregation in it is not.

Then the warning, and it is one of the most severe sentences in the letter: “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him.” The verb is the same both times — you ruin it, he will ruin you. It is deliberately symmetrical and deliberately alarming.

Notice what it does to the subject of church division. Everything Paul has said so far might be heard as a plea for better relationships. This is not that. He has been arguing that the factions are wrecking a building, and now he names the owner and states what the owner will do about it. A church split is not a management problem, a personality clash, or a regrettable difference of vision. It is demolition work on the house where God lives, and he defends his property.

Readers rightly ask whether this means a genuine believer can be destroyed. The New Testament’s warnings are real warnings, not stage effects, and they are among the means God uses to keep his people — a fence at the cliff edge is not useless because nobody has gone over. But it should also be said plainly that the person in view is one who destroys a church: not someone who has been difficult, or has held an unpopular position, or has raised a hard question, but one who is set on wrecking it. Scripture is consistent that a man who persists in that shows in the end what he always was (cf. 1 John 2:19).

The reason for the severity is in the last clause: “God’s temple is holy”. Not holy because the members are impressive — these are the people Paul has just called infants. Holy because of who lives there. You may think very little of your congregation, and you may have good reason. God has chosen to live in it, and that fact is what makes tearing at it so serious.

So a test with teeth. Think of the last conversation you had about someone in your church who was not present. Ask honestly whether that conversation was building or quietly taking something down. Most demolition in most churches is not done by anyone who would describe themselves as destroying anything. It is done a sentence at a time, by people who would be horrified to be told what they are standing in (cf. Eph. 2:21–22; 2 Cor. 6:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes by circling back to the wisdom theme. “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise” (v. 18). The path to true wisdom runs through the humiliation of acknowledged folly — through the cross. This is not anti-intellectualism but a description of the epistemological conversion required: the person who comes to God thinking they have the resources to meet him on intellectual equal terms will leave empty; the person who comes in acknowledged poverty receives the wisdom of God as gift.

The citation from Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 — “He catches the wise in their craftiness” and “the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” — ground the argument in Scripture’s own long testimony to the futility of human wisdom before God. Then the staggering positive conclusion: “all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future — all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” The Corinthians have been fighting over which apostle to claim; Paul tells them they already own all the apostles, and all things, and they own them because they belong to Christ who owns everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from Him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great catalogue texts of what it means to be in Christ. Paul’s list — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present, future — is comprehensive: every apostle, every circumstance, every temporal horizon, even death itself, belongs to the believer in Christ. The Corinthians have been acting poor — squabbling over which apostle to claim — while they are infinitely rich. This is what Calvin called the “double grace” (“duplex gratia”) of union with Christ expanded to cosmic scope: the one who is in Christ owns, in principle, everything that Christ owns. They need not cling to Paul or Apollos; they have all of them, and infinitely more besides.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming one-quarter of the apostolic inheritance — “I follow Paul,” etc. — when they could have had the whole. Their factionalism was a self-imposed poverty in the middle of infinite wealth. Now: The Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing — claiming a slice when the whole belongs to him. The traditions are real and valuable; they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let no one deceive himself.” Paul does not warn them about being deceived by someone else. The danger is self-administered, and it is the hardest kind to detect, because the person doing the deceiving is entirely trusted by the person being deceived.

“If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise.” The instruction is deliberately shocking, and it describes a real and painful step. It is not a recommendation to stop thinking. It is the requirement to accept a verdict on your thinking — to agree that the equipment you have been relying on cannot reach God, and to accept from him what you could not work out.

Everybody who becomes a Christian does this, and for some it costs a great deal more than for others. The person who has never had much confidence in their own cleverness has less to lay down. The person whose whole standing rests on being the one who understands things — the academic, the professional, the man who is used to being the most informed person in the room — is being asked to walk into the kingdom by a door marked fool, and to keep walking through it afterwards.

Then two citations, and they are chosen to show that this is not a new policy. “He catches the wise in their craftiness” comes from Job 5:13 — and the exquisite irony is that Paul is quoting Eliphaz, one of Job’s comforters, whose confident wisdom God will himself expose before the book ends. The man who said it was caught by it. And “the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” is Psalm 94:11, where the psalmist writes the thoughts of man; Paul sharpens it to the wise, since that is the group in question at Corinth.

The word rendered futile is mataios — empty, leading nowhere. God is not described as outwitting the clever in an argument. He knows their reasoning, and knows it goes nowhere — which is a far more devastating assessment than being contradicted.

What Paul is asking for is not a one-off act but a permanent posture, and it is easy to state and hard to keep. It is the willingness to let Scripture correct your categories rather than trimming Scripture to fit them. Every Christian who reads seriously meets passages that offend his instincts — about judgment, about sexuality, about money, about God’s sovereignty, about hell. At that point one of two things happens, and which one happens is the whole subject of this verse.

So the test, and it is answerable. Name a conviction you have changed in the last five years because Scripture required it, against your preference and against the opinion of people whose respect you wanted. If nothing comes to mind, it is worth asking whether you have been reading the Bible or consulting it — because a man who never finds himself corrected by a book is not being taught by it (cf. Prov. 3:5–7; Isa. 5:21; Matt. 11:25).

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours.”

The logic is not what we expect. Paul does not say: stop boasting in men, because you have nothing to boast about. He says: stop boasting in men, because you are far too rich for that. The Corinthians are behaving like people fighting over scraps, and Paul’s answer is to open the accounts.

Look at the list, because it expands in stages. Paul, Apollos, Cephas — the very men the factions were dividing over. Each group had claimed one and rejected the others, and Paul tells them they own all three. The faction was not merely wrong; it was a self-imposed poverty. They were each clinging to a third of an inheritance that was entirely theirs.

Then the list jumps: the world. The created order itself, which belongs to those who are in Christ because the meek inherit the earth and the heirs of God are joint heirs with him (Rom. 8:17). Then life — not a lease on a few decades, but life as a possession rather than a predicament.

And then a word nobody would have put in a list of assets: death.

Death is yours. Not death is survivable, or death is temporary. It belongs to you, it is on the inventory, it is among the things you own. Which is the most extraordinary claim in the sentence, and Paul means it: the last enemy has been so thoroughly defeated that it now serves the believer. It is the servant that carries a Christian home. To die is gain (Phil. 1:21), and the thing every human being organises their life around avoiding has been reduced to an item on a list of possessions.

A guard is needed here, because this verse is regularly conscripted for something Paul is not saying. “All things are yours” has been used to underwrite a gospel of prosperity — claim your health, claim your finances, everything belongs to you. But notice what is on the list and what that does to the claim. Nobody preaching that gospel has ever quoted or death. Paul is writing to a church that is poor, socially insignificant (1:26), and about to be told that the apostles themselves are hungry, badly clothed and homeless (4:11). The riches he is describing are not being paid out in the currency such teaching demands.

And notice the last pair: the present or the future. Both. Not the future only — this is not a promise to be endured towards. The present, this month, with its unresolved situation, belongs to you as much as the glory does.

So a test for the reader who feels spiritually poor — and most of us do, most of the time. Write down what you think you are short of: standing, security, a future, a place to belong, someone in your corner. Then read the list again. The Corinthians were quarrelling over which apostle to claim while owning the world, life, death, the present and the future. It is possible to be an heir of everything and live like a man counting coins, and the only thing that has to change is that somebody tells you what is in the account (cf. Rom. 8:32; Ps. 24:1).

verseByVerse.quote: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” Nine words, and they hold the whole chapter together.

The chain runs downwards and the ownership runs upwards. All things belong to you — but you are not the top of the chain, and that is exactly what keeps v. 22 from becoming the fantasy of self-importance the Corinthians would have made of it. You own everything, and you are owned. The inheritance is real because the belonging is real, and the moment the belonging is removed the inheritance evaporates.

This is why the factions were absurd. A man who says “I am Paul’s” has swapped an infinite estate for a small allegiance, and has got the direction of ownership wrong in the bargain. You do not belong to a teacher. Teachers belong to you, and you belong to Christ.

Then the last clause, which has been the subject of long argument: “and Christ is God’s”. Read carelessly it sounds like a demotion — as though the Son were a lesser being belonging to a greater one, which is precisely what the Arians of the fourth century argued from sentences like this.

The church’s answer, hammered out at Nicaea and worth having plainly, is that Scripture speaks of the Son in two registers. As to his being, he is fully and equally God: this same Paul calls him the Lord of glory (2:8) and applies to him the covenant name from Jeremiah (1:31). As to his mission, he willingly took a place of submission — sent by the Father, doing the Father’s will, and at the end handing the kingdom over to the Father (15:24–28). Equal in nature, ordered in relation. The submission is not evidence of a lesser deity; it is the shape divine love took when it came to fetch us.

And the practical force of the chain is considerable. Everything you have depends on a link you did not make and cannot break. Your standing rests on your being Christ’s; his standing rests on nothing at all, because he is God’s eternally and by nature. There is no point in that chain at which your grip is what holds it. Which is the same comfort as 1:9, arriving by a different road.

So the chapter that opened by calling them infants ends by telling them what they own. It began with jealousy over preachers and ends with the world, life, death, the present and the future signed over to a squabbling congregation in a port city — not because they had grown up, because they plainly had not, but because they were Christ’s.

And he is God’s. He did not seize the position; he was given everything by the Father and gave it away to us, and when it is all finished he will hand the kingdom back, so that God may be all in all. There is no acquisitiveness anywhere in the Godhead. Everything the Son has, he has from the Father, and everything you have, you have from the Son — and the whole vast movement of it runs in one direction, outwards, from a God who has never once needed anything and has never stopped giving (cf. John 17:10; 1 Cor. 15:28; Phil. 2:6–11).

4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the most personal of the opening section’s chapters — Paul at his most tender and most fierce. He describes the apostolic calling as stewardship: apostles are servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, accountable not to the Corinthian audience but to the Lord who will judge on the Last Day. The Corinthians have been sitting in judgment on Paul and Apollos — evaluating their performance, weighing their merits, forming factions around their preferences. Paul challenges this from every direction: the only judge who matters has not yet rendered his verdict, and that verdict will contain surprises.

Then the chapter turns, and Paul describes what apostleship actually looks like from the inside: the apostles are a spectacle to the world, last of all, condemned to death. While the Corinthians have become kings, filled, rich, they are hungry, thirsty, poorly dressed, reviled, homeless, the scum of the world. The irony is devastating. The church that has modelled itself on the world’s standards of success looks at the apostles — weak, despised, suffering — and fails to recognise them as the authentic embodiment of the gospel they profess. Chapter 4 ends with a father’s appeal: I am not writing this to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children. Imitate me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The proper way to think about Paul and Apollos is not as competing spiritual celebrities but as servants (hypēretas — literally, under-rowers, the galley slaves at the bottom of the ship) and stewards. A steward administers someone else’s property; he has no claim on it and no right to use it for personal enrichment. His one qualification is faithfulness. This single word — “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (v. 2) — is the only criterion Paul acknowledges for apostolic evaluation. Not brilliance, not fruitfulness, not cultural impact: faithfulness.

The passage then moves into one of Paul’s most striking statements of judicial humility. He is aware of no charge against himself (v. 4) — but this does not acquit him. The judge is the Lord. Paul refuses to sit in judgment on himself because the final verdict belongs to the One who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart. The day of judgment will not merely evaluate actions; it will disclose motivations. Everything hidden — including the hidden pride and self-interest that can lurk beneath apparently faithful ministry — will be brought into the light.

Verse 7 then aims a dart with surgical precision at the root of Corinthian pride: “For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” Three questions that leave the Corinthian boaster nowhere to hide. Every gift, every capacity, every spiritual experience is received — given by grace, not earned by merit. To boast in received gifts is to claim credit for a gift, which is both ingratitude and dishonesty.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatological Judgment and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pre-judge himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism but eschatological realism. The final judgment has not yet been rendered; therefore all present judgments — including self-assessment — are provisional. Reformed theology has always warned against both false confidence (I know I am right) and false despair (I know I am condemned): both pre-empt the judgment that belongs to God alone. The practical implication is freedom: neither to be destroyed by human criticism nor to be puffed up by human praise, because neither the critic nor the flatterer is the judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were evaluating Paul and finding him wanting, not by the standard of faithfulness but by the standards of rhetorical eloquence and visible success. Paul refuses the evaluation: you are not my judge; the Lord is. Now: Ministry evaluation by attendance, public approval, or conference invitations is the contemporary equivalent. The minister who structures his ministry around what will get him praised by his peers has already chosen the wrong judge. The only evaluation that matters is the Lord’s — and it will assess what the heart actually was.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“This is how one should regard us” — Paul is issuing a correction to the lens, not to the facts. The Corinthians have the right men in view and are looking at them through the wrong instrument.

Two words replace their categories, and both are humbling. The first is hypēretēs, which originally meant an under-rower — a man on the lower bench of a galley, pulling an oar he could not see out of, in a ship whose course he had no part in setting. By Paul’s day it had broadened to mean any subordinate assistant, but the flavour remains: someone who supplies effort under someone else’s direction.

The second is oikonomos, a steward — the household manager, often a slave, who ran the estate, kept the accounts and dispensed the stores. He handled a great deal of wealth and owned none of it. That is the exact position of the man entrusted with the gospel: real responsibility, considerable trust, and no ownership whatever. What he distributes is not his, and he cannot alter the terms on which it is given out.

And what is being administered is “the mysteries of God” — which in Paul’s vocabulary never means esoteric secrets kept from ordinary people, but the thing once hidden and now announced: Christ crucified, and the nations brought in (2:7; Eph. 3:6). A steward of that has one job, which is to hand out what he was given, in the form he was given it.

Then the single criterion: “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful”. Not gifted. Not effective. Not admired. Faithful — which means simply that the master’s goods arrive where the master intended, unadulterated and undiminished.

Notice how completely that displaces every measurement the Corinthians were using. They were ranking their teachers by eloquence and impact. Paul says the only question is whether the man can be trusted with something that is not his. And a steward is not assessed by how much the household admired him, but by whether the accounts balance.

Which extends well beyond preachers, because every Christian is a steward of something. Money, time, a gift, a position, a family, a piece of knowledge somebody trusted you with. All of it is held rather than owned, and the question in each case is the same.

So a test worth running on whatever you are responsible for. Ask what you would have to change if you genuinely believed it was not yours — the money, the diary, the influence, the platform. Most of us discover we have been quietly behaving as proprietors of an estate we were only ever managing, and that the change required is not in how hard we work but in whose interests we are working (cf. Luke 12:42–44; 1 Pet. 4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you.” It sounds dismissive, and it is not. Paul is not saying their opinion is worthless; he is saying it is not the verdict. A jury’s view matters enormously until you learn they were never empanelled.

Then he goes further than anyone expects: “In fact, I do not even judge myself.” He removes his own assessment from the court as well — and then makes the most searching admission in the passage: “I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted.”

Stop on that, because it is one of the most honest sentences Paul ever wrote about self-knowledge. He has examined himself and found nothing. And he refuses to treat that as a verdict of innocence — because the examiner and the accused are the same man, and no man has full access to his own motives. We are all judges sitting on our own cases, with an interest in the outcome and incomplete evidence.

Which is precisely what the psalmist knew when he asked God to do what he could not do for himself: search me and know my heart… see if there be any grievous way in me (Ps. 139:23–24). And what Jeremiah meant by the heart being deceitful above all things — not merely that it lies to others, but that it lies to its owner (Jer. 17:9).

A guard is needed at once, because this verse can land on an anxious Christian like a sentence. If a clear conscience does not acquit me, is any assurance possible? Am I to go through life suspecting myself?

No — and the answer is in the same clause. Paul’s point is not that he is secretly condemned but that the verdict is not his to give, in either direction. He is refusing to acquit himself and equally refusing to condemn himself. Both are the Lord’s business, and the Lord has already spoken about those who are in Christ: there is no condemnation (Rom. 8:1). John says the same thing to people whose hearts were accusing them — God is greater than our heart, and knows everything (1 John 3:19–20), which cuts both ways and is meant as comfort.

So the effect of this passage is not anxiety but a strange freedom, and it is one of the most practically useful things in the letter. If the only judge who counts sees everything, then two exhausting occupations become unnecessary. You need not manage your reputation, because the verdict does not depend on what people conclude about you. And you need not run a permanent internal tribunal, because your own assessment was never authoritative either.

Which yields the test. Think of the last piece of criticism that stayed with you for days, and the last piece of praise you found yourself replaying. Ask what authority you granted to each. Most of us hand out judicial powers very freely — to a colleague, a relative, an anonymous comment — and then live under sentences passed by people who were never on the bench. There is one judge. He knows everything, including the things in your favour that nobody noticed, and he is the one who died for you (cf. Ps. 139:23–24; 2 Cor. 10:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not pronounce judgment before the time.” The fault Paul names is not judging but the timing of it — a verdict delivered before the evidence is complete and before the judge has taken his seat.

And a guard is needed immediately, because this is among the most quoted verses in the modern church and almost always for the wrong purpose. It is produced to shut down any moral assessment whatever: do not judge. But the same letter, one chapter later, has Paul pronouncing judgment on a man’s conduct (5:3), instructing the church to judge those inside it (5:12), and asking incredulously whether they are really unable to settle a dispute between brothers (6:5). Whatever v. 5 forbids, it cannot be the thing Paul does immediately afterwards.

What it forbids is the verdict only God can reach: the assessment of another person’s heart and final standing. You may say that an action is wrong — Scripture requires it. You may not say what a man is before God, or what he was really after, because you do not have the file.

That distinction is worth holding onto, because we cross it constantly and casually. It is the difference between what he said was untrue and he is a liar; between this decision was unwise and he only did it for the credit. The first is observation. The second is a ruling on the purposes of the heart, and it is reserved.

Because that is exactly what the Lord will do: he “will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart”. Not only deeds — motives. Everything done in the dark, and the reasons behind everything done in the light.

Which is a solemn prospect, and Paul means it to be. There will be no missing evidence and no successful spin. The charitable act done to be noticed, the generosity that was an investment in reputation, the service rendered to secure a position — all of it disclosed. And equally the things nobody ever knew: the kindness done anonymously, the temptation resisted in private, the years of quiet faithfulness in a place where it was never noticed.

Then the last clause, which is where this verse becomes unexpectedly wonderful. “Then each one will receive his commendation from God.” The word is epainos — praise, approval spoken aloud.

Read that again slowly. Paul has just said the Day will expose the hidden purposes of every heart, and he expects the outcome for God’s servants to be praise. Not a bare acquittal, not a relieved escape — commendation, from God, to each one. It is the same note as the master in the parable saying well done, good and faithful servant (Matt. 25:21).

That God should forgive us is grace beyond calculation. That he should then intend to praise us, having himself supplied everything he is praising, is something else again — and it is why Augustine said that when God crowns our merits he is crowning his own gifts. The judgment Christians most instinctively dread is described here as the occasion on which their Father speaks well of them out loud (cf. Rom. 2:29; 1 Pet. 1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul explains what he has been doing: he has used himself and Apollos as the worked example, so that the Corinthians may “learn by us not to go beyond what is written”.

That last phrase is genuinely obscure and honesty requires saying so — it may have been a proverb, or a schoolroom expression about a child tracing letters and not straying outside them. What is clear is the direction: Scripture sets a boundary, and the Corinthians have wandered outside it. Their factions, their rankings, their confidence about who stands where are all inventions with no warrant in anything God has said. Whatever the idiom meant precisely, the instinct behind it is sound and permanent: stop at the line, and do not construct convictions on ground Scripture has not given you.

“Puffed up” — physioō, inflated, swollen with air. It is Paul’s favourite word for this church and he uses it six times in the letter. The image is exact: something enlarged by nothing, occupying more space than its substance justifies, and requiring only a pinprick.

Then verse 7, which is one of the great sentences of the New Testament and has done more to demolish spiritual pride than any argument ever constructed. Three questions, and there is no way through them.

“Who sees anything different in you?” — what distinguishes you from the person you feel superior to? “What do you have that you did not receive?” — and the honest answer is nothing whatever. Not your intelligence, which was in your genes before you could form a preference. Not your upbringing, or the country you were born in, or the family that told you about Christ, or the health that let you work, or the temperament that makes you easier to like. Not your faith, which Paul elsewhere says is a gift (Eph. 2:8). Not one item on the list was generated by you.

“If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” The pride is not merely unattractive; it is a false claim. It is presenting a gift as an achievement, which is a form of dishonesty as well as ingratitude.

And notice how comprehensively it removes the ground for comparison, which is what the whole chapter has been about. You cannot rank yourself against another Christian on the basis of gifts you were both handed. It would be like two men quarrelling over which of them was the more distinguished for having been given a coat.

So here is the test, and it is the most useful single question in this letter for daily use. The next time you feel the small internal lift of being further on than another believer — better read, more disciplined, more sound, less of a mess — stop and ask Paul’s question in his words: what do I have that I did not receive?

Follow it honestly for thirty seconds and the lift collapses, because every single item you were about to congratulate yourself on turns out to have been handed to you. And what is left when it collapses is not humiliation but relief, and gratitude, and a strange new warmth towards the person you were just measuring (cf. Rom. 12:3; John 3:27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Here Paul employs one of his sharpest rhetorical weapons: sustained, ironic contrast. “Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!” (v. 8). The irony is biting and precise. The Corinthians have already achieved, in their own minds, the eschatological glory that belongs to the resurrection age — the riches, the reigning, the fulfilment. But the resurrection has not yet come; Christ has not yet returned; the kingdom has not yet been consummated. Their triumphalism is a premature arrival in a future that is not yet.

The contrast Paul draws is between the Corinthian experience of glory and the apostolic experience of cruciformity. Apostles are last, condemned to death, made a spectacle. While they reign, the apostles are hungry, thirsty, poorly dressed, brutally treated, homeless. While they are honoured, the apostles are reviled, persecuted, slandered. While they are wise, the apostles are fools for Christ’s sake. The pattern is deliberate: the apostolic life is shaped by the cross, not the resurrection. This age — between the first and second coming — is the age of bearing the cross, not wearing the crown.

Paul’s concluding summary is brutal: “We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things” (v. 13). Perikatharmata and peripsēma both connote the filth scraped from a surface — what is cleaned off and discarded. This is how Paul describes his apostolic credentials. Not miracles (though he has those), not visions (though he has those too), but the marks of a life shaped by the dying of Jesus. The cross is not merely Paul’s theology; it is his biography.
verseByVerse.theology:
Realized Eschatology and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Corinthians’ problem was not merely social pride but theological confusion about which age they were in. They were living as if the resurrection age had fully arrived — treating this present life as the time of reigning and riches. Paul’s corrective is eschatological: we are still in the “between the times,” the age between the first and second coming, in which the pattern of the Christian life is cruciform, not triumphant. The “not yet” of eschatology shapes the “how” of Christian living. Suffering, weakness, and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but participation in Christ’s own pattern — the pattern of resurrection that comes through, not around, the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman spectacle of condemned criminals paraded before the crowd before their execution is the image behind v. 9 (“made a spectacle”). Paul uses the imagery of the arena: God has made the apostles last, like the condemned criminals brought on at the end of the show. This was not hyperbole; Paul had been beaten, imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the contemporary version of Corinthian triumphalism: the claim that health, wealth, and success are the normal marks of Spirit-filled Christianity. Paul’s fools for Christ’s sake, hungry and homeless, are a permanent rebuke to any theology that makes suffering an anomaly rather than a participation in the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three exclamations, and every one of them is irony: “Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings!”

The repeated already is the key to the whole verse, and it identifies the Corinthians’ error with precision. They believed they had arrived. The riches, the reigning, the fullness — all the things Scripture promises for the age to come — they had claimed as present possessions. They were living as though the resurrection had happened and the kingdom had been consummated and there was nothing left to wait for.

Paul does not deny that Christians are rich; he told them in the previous chapter that all things are theirs (3:21–22). What he denies is the timing. The inheritance is certain and it has not been paid out. We are heirs in a country we have not yet entered, and to behave as though the crowns had already been distributed is not faith but confusion about which chapter of the story we are in.

And it is worth noticing that Paul uses sarcasm here, deliberately and at length. Some readers are uncomfortable with that, but Scripture is not: Elijah on Carmel suggesting Baal might be asleep or on a journey (1 Kgs. 18:27), the prophets on idols that have to be carried, the Lord himself on men who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. Irony is a legitimate instrument when someone is so pleased with himself that a straight statement will simply be absorbed. It is a way of holding a mirror at an angle the man cannot avoid.

Then the sentence turns and the irony breaks: “And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!” The wistfulness is real. Paul is saying: I wish it were true. I wish the kingdom had come and the waiting were over — because I am hungry, and cold, and in trouble, and if you were really reigning then so would I be. His complaint is not that they are too hopeful. It is that they have taken delivery of a hope that has not yet arrived, and have therefore stopped needing the cross.

Which is why this verse is a permanent rebuke to a familiar kind of teaching. Whenever Christianity is presented as the route to health, wealth, victory and constant flourishing now — with suffering treated as a malfunction, a failure of faith, or a thing to be claimed away — that is Corinthian triumphalism in modern dress. Paul’s answer is not a better argument. It is the next five verses, in which he lists what the apostles were actually enduring while the Corinthians reigned.

So a test, and it is diagnostic of something deeper than doctrine. Ask what you have quietly come to expect from God in this life — not what you would say in a Bible study, but what you actually assume when things go wrong. If a serious disappointment feels like a breach of contract rather than a hard providence, then some part of you has been living in v. 8. The Christian has everything, and the payment date is not today (cf. Rom. 8:17–18; 2 Tim. 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death.” The imagery is from the arena, and it would have been unmistakable.

A day at the games ran in an order. The best contests came in the middle, when the crowd was fullest and most attentive. And at the end, when the spectacle proper was finished, the condemned were brought out — men with no weapons and no chance, whose function was not to compete but to die in front of people. They were the item you stayed for only if you had nothing better to do.

Paul says God has placed the apostles in that slot. Last of all. The word for spectacle is theatron — he is not comparing himself to a gladiator, the professional with skill and a following, but to the man brought on at the end to be finished off.

And set that against the previous verse. The Corinthians are reigning as kings; their founding apostle describes himself as the closing act of an execution. Those are not two styles of Christianity. One of them is a misunderstanding of what age we are in.

Then the audience: “a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men”. It is an arresting detail and it is not decoration. Paul assumes that what happens to ordinary Christians is watched by the unseen order — the same assumption behind the angels who long to look into these things (1 Pet. 1:12), and behind the claim that God intended his manifold wisdom to be displayed to the rulers and authorities through the church (Eph. 3:10). Heaven is following this.

Which puts a strange dignity on the least impressive Christian life. If the arena imagery is right, then the believer who is being quietly humiliated for his faith — passed over, laughed at, thought a fool — is not in an obscure corner of an indifferent universe. He is in the middle of a lit stage, being watched by beings who understand exactly what they are looking at, even when nobody in the room does.

And it is worth asking what the angels are watching for. Not the suffering itself, which is common enough. What no angel had ever seen before the incarnation, and what they cannot see anywhere except in the church, is a creature who is losing and is not bitter — a man deprived of everything the world offers, who blesses the people taking it and does not stop trusting God. That is a phenomenon with no natural explanation, and it is precisely what the next four verses describe.

Which is where the verse quietly turns, because Paul did not invent the pattern. There was one who was exhibited last of all, sentenced to death, made a spectacle in front of a jeering crowd, with the world and the angels and men all watching. He was stripped and lifted up where everyone could see, and the whole city came out for the afternoon. The apostles are not in an unusual position for followers of that man. They are in the only position his followers have ever occupied (cf. Heb. 12:2; Col. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three contrasts, laid out with painful symmetry. We are fools — you are wise. We are weak — you are strong. You are held in honour — we in disrepute.

The rhetorical shape matters: in each pair the apostles get the worse half, and in the last one Paul reverses the order so the sentence ends on disrepute. He is not distributing blame evenly. He is drawing a line between two ways of being Christian and putting himself firmly on the side nobody wants.

“Fools for Christ’s sake” is the phrase to hold. Paul is not claiming that Christians are unintelligent, nor recommending eccentricity for its own sake. The foolishness is entirely derivative: it is what you look like when you have staked everything on a crucified man, in a world that measures by power and success. Chapter one established that the message is folly to those who are perishing (1:18); this is what it costs to be the man carrying it.

And notice the asymmetry Paul is exposing. The Corinthians had managed to hold the gospel and their social standing at the same time. They were wise, strong, honoured — respectable in Corinth and confident in church. Paul’s implication is quiet and devastating: if the message is genuinely offensive, how have you avoided all the offence?

That question has not aged. It is entirely possible to hold Christian convictions in a way that costs nothing — to believe the right things privately while ensuring that nobody at work, in the family, or among one’s friends is ever given occasion to think one odd. It is not hypocrisy exactly. It is the careful management of the parts of the faith that would look foolish if said out loud.

This verse is for the Christian who is already paying that cost, often in small and unglamorous ways. The colleague known as the religious one, whose views are treated as a harmless quirk. The student whose position on some question has quietly ended his hope of being taken seriously. The relative whose family have decided, kindly, that he has become a bit much. The person who has learned that mentioning prayer changes the temperature of a room.

None of that is persecution in the sense the early church knew, and it should not be dressed up as martyrdom. But it is real, and it wears people down precisely because it is so ordinary and so deniable. Paul’s word to such a reader is that being thought a fool for Christ’s sake is not a sign that you have handled things badly. On this evidence it is a sign you are in the apostolic line.

So a test that is easier to state than to pass. Name the belief you hold that would make you look most foolish among the people whose respect you most want. Then ask when you last said it out loud in front of them. The answer is not a verdict — there is wisdom in when and how to speak, and Paul was no boor. But if the answer is never, and the reason is not love but reputation, then the honour in this verse is in the wrong column (cf. 1 Cor. 1:18–25; Heb. 13:13).

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the catalogue, and it is deliberately physical: hunger, thirst, poor clothing, beatings, homelessness, manual labour. Paul is not recalling his early hardships from a comfortable retirement. “To the present hour” — this is his condition as he writes.

“We labour, working with our own hands” carries a sting a modern reader misses. In the Greek world manual work was contemptible; a philosopher who worked with his hands had declassed himself, and the sophists at Corinth were paid handsomely for talking. Paul made tents (Acts 18:3). Part of the Corinthian embarrassment about their apostle was straightforwardly social: their founder had a trade.

Then the three responses, and this is the heart of the passage. “When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat.”

Look at what is not there. No retaliation, no defence of reputation, no cutting reply, no campaign to set the record straight. And notice these are not passive. To bless is to actively ask God’s good for the man who has just insulted you. To entreat is to appeal — to keep the door open toward someone spreading lies about you. That is harder than a counter-attack and takes longer.

It is also exactly what Paul had been taught. Bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28). And it is what he had watched in the pattern of his Lord, who when reviled did not revile in return (1 Pet. 2:23), and who from the cross asked the Father to forgive the men driving the nails.

Then the final image, and Paul chooses the two ugliest words available. Perikatharmata — the filth scraped off when something is cleaned. Peripsēma — what is wiped away, the residue on the cloth. He is describing himself as what you find in the bucket at the end.

And this is how he lists his credentials. Not the visions, not the miracles, not the churches planted, though he had all three and mentions them elsewhere. When Paul wants to prove he is a genuine apostle to a church impressed by success, he produces his hunger and his reputation.

The practical value here is unusually direct, because the three responses are learnable and can be practised this week. Somebody will misrepresent you. Somebody will say something dismissive. The instinct will be to answer, and the answer will already be drafted in your head within about four seconds. Paul’s three verbs are the alternative, and they are specific enough to act on: ask God to do that person good, by name; stay where God has put you rather than withdrawing; keep speaking to them rather than about them.

None of it is natural, and that is the point — it is the one thing in this list the angels of v. 9 have never seen anywhere else. A man can be reduced to the scrapings of the world and still be blessing the people who put him there. Only one thing in the universe produces that, and it is not strength of character (cf. Rom. 12:14, 20–21; 1 Pet. 3:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The irony drops. Paul’s tone shifts from sharp to tender: “I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children” (v. 14). The whole chapter — the biting contrasts, the withering irony — was not the anger of an offended ego but the grief of a father watching his children go wrong. Paul is not competing with the Corinthians; he loves them. He is their father in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The implication is not that Paul has authority over them as a tyrant but that he has a claim on their hearts as a parent — and a parent’s deepest desire is not obedience but flourishing.

The appeal to imitate Paul (v. 16) is not arrogant. In a world without books, seminaries, or theological education, the primary vehicle of pastoral formation was the imitation of a living model. Paul is offering himself — specifically the pattern of cruciform ministry described in vv. 8–13 — as the template for what gospel living looks like. Timothy is being sent as Paul’s representative precisely to remind them of Paul’s ways in Christ: not his opinions but his life-pattern.

The chapter ends with a warning that reintroduces the note of apostolic authority. Some at Corinth have become arrogant, imagining that Paul will not come to deal with them. He will come — and when he does, he will find out not the talk of the arrogant but their power. The kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. Paul will come with love and a gentle spirit — if they will receive it. If not, he will come with a rod. The father’s love is real; so is the father’s authority.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fatherhood of the Apostle and Spiritual Formation by Imitation

Paul’s claim to spiritual fatherhood over the Corinthian church is grounded in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The new birth produces a spiritual parentage — and the one through whose proclamation the Spirit brought new birth to a community is, in a real sense, their spiritual father. This is not about control but about formation. Calvin, commenting on v. 16, noted that Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living embodiment of the gospel he preached: “He calls them to imitate not his person but his pattern — the pattern of the cross.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had, in Paul’s absence, developed arrogant teachers who had dismissed the apostle. Timothy is sent to embody what Paul had taught by his life — because argument alone, without the living example, is insufficient. Now: The pastoral call to “imitate me as I imitate Christ” (11:1) is the most demanding thing a minister can say — and the most necessary. Disciples need models, not merely doctrines. The church that produces only correct theology without cruciform character has missed the point of the apostolic office.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The irony stops, and the change of tone is one of the most affecting moments in the letter: “I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children.”

Everything since v. 8 — the sarcasm about kings, the arena, the scrapings of the world — has to be re-read in the light of this sentence. It was not the retaliation of a man whose pride had been injured. It was a father who could not get through to his children, doing the one thing left.

And the distinction he draws is worth pausing on, because we habitually confuse the two. Shaming and admonishing feel similar from the outside and are opposite in intent. Shame attacks the person: it aims to make him feel small, and it works, and it produces either compliance or resentment and never growth. Admonition — noutheteo, to put in mind — attacks the problem, and it aims at change, and it can only be received from someone the hearer is sure loves him.

Then the claim: “though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers.” The word for guides is paidagōgos — the household slave who walked the children to school, kept them out of trouble and enforced the rules. Useful, necessary, and hired. Not a parent. Paul is not sneering at the other teachers; he is naming a different kind of bond. “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” — the man through whose preaching you were born cannot be replaced by a better speaker, any more than a father can be replaced by a more impressive man.

Which is worth saying to a church culture in which people move between congregations for the quality of the teaching, and to anyone who has ever quietly transferred their loyalty from the person who led them to Christ to somebody more polished. The polished man may well teach you more. He will never be the one who told you first.

And there is a practical lesson here about how to correct anyone at all. Notice the order Paul uses. He speaks the hard thing first, at length, without softening it — and then makes the affection explicit. He does not open with reassurance to cushion the blow, and he does not leave the affection to be inferred. He says it: beloved children.

Most of us get this wrong in one of two directions. Either the love is assumed and never stated, so the rebuke arrives as bare criticism and lands as shame. Or the love is stated so warmly and at such length that the correction never actually gets said, and everybody leaves comfortable and nothing changes.

So the test, if there is something you need to say to someone. Ask whether they know — not whether they could reasonably infer, but whether they know, because you have told them — that you are for them. If they do not, the correction will not land however true it is. And if they do, you can say almost anything. Paul had just called them puffed-up infants playing at kings, and he could do it because they had watched him work with his hands among them and knew exactly what he had spent on them (cf. Prov. 27:6; 2 Cor. 12:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I urge you, then, be imitators of me.” It sounds, on a first reading, breathtakingly presumptuous. No modern minister would dare say it, and our instinct is to reach for a qualification.

Paul does supply one, later in the letter: “be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1). So the imitation is not of a personality but of a direction; he is a man pointing, and he is asking them to follow the pointing. But it is worth noticing that he does not soften it here, and that our discomfort with the sentence may say more about us than about him.

Because consider what he is asking them to imitate. He has just spent eight verses describing it, and it is not his eloquence, his authority or his success. It is hunger, disrepute, manual labour, and blessing people who revile you. Imitate me, in this context, means: take the lower place, work with your hands, be thought a fool, and do not retaliate. That is not a bid for a following. Nobody builds a personality cult on that material.

And there is a reason the appeal has to be to a life rather than to a syllabus. These people had no Bibles of their own, no theological education, and in most cases no literacy. Christianity had to be transmitted the way a trade is transmitted — by watching somebody do it. Which is still how most of it is actually learned. Nobody has ever become patient by reading about patience; they have watched a patient person handle something and understood, for the first time, that it was possible.

Hence Timothy: “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ”. Paul does not send a letter alone. He sends a person — and the person he sends is himself a demonstration, a man formed by exactly the pattern under dispute. The argument travels in a document; the pattern travels in a man.

“My ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church” — a quiet answer to the suggestion that Corinth was being given a harder standard than everyone else. There is one gospel and one pattern of life, and it is the same in Ephesus and Philippi and here.

So two tests, and both are uncomfortable in the right way. First: who are you actually imitating? Not who do you admire in the abstract, but whose life have you got close enough to see, and whose handling of money, marriage, disappointment and provocation is shaping yours by observation? Most Christians are being formed by somebody, and a great many are being formed at a distance by people they have only ever seen performing.

And second, harder: is there anyone who could learn Christianity by watching you? Not by asking your opinions — by watching. That is the question Paul’s sentence puts to every parent, every elder, every long-standing member of a congregation, and it cannot be answered by improving one’s doctrine. He was not afraid of it, and the reason he was not afraid of it is that what he was offering to be copied was a cross (cf. Phil. 3:17; 1 Thess. 1:6; Heb. 13:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you.” The diagnosis is shrewd, and it names something universal: people behave differently when they believe they will not be met.

The word is the puffed-up word again — physioō, inflated. And the inflation had a cause: distance. Paul was hundreds of miles away, in custody of a kind, unable to appear. So a certain confidence had grown up in Corinth, of the sort that always grows in the absence of the person who might answer back. It is the courage of the letter never sent to the man's face.

Paul’s reply is simply to announce that the absence is temporary. “But I will come to you soon” — and the whole basis of their confidence disappears with the sentence.

Notice, though, the four words he attaches: “if the Lord wills”. This is not a verbal tic. It is the settled habit of a man who genuinely does not consider his own plans self-executing — the same instinct James insists on: you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (Jas. 4:15). Paul is in the middle of asserting his authority over a rebellious church, and even here he will not say he is coming without adding that it is not finally up to him.

Which is a small thing that reveals a large one. A man who says if the Lord wills about a journey has already settled something about who runs the world, and it shows up in his diary rather than in his theology lectures. There is a useful test in that, and it needs no theology at all: listen to how you talk about next year.

Then the substance of the visit: “I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.” Two words are being set against each other — logos and dynamis. Talk and power.

And this is the question Paul intends to put when he arrives, which is worth stating plainly because it is the question the whole chapter has been building toward. He is not coming to compare rhetoric; the Corinthians would win that and it would prove nothing. He is coming to see whether anything has actually changed — whether the gospel these people discuss so fluently has produced in them the one thing it always produces where it is real.

What that is, the letter has already told us. Not miracles particularly. Chapter three said the evidence of the Spirit’s absence was jealousy and strife; chapter thirteen will say that gifts without love are nothing. So the power Paul intends to look for is not spectacular. It is whether these people have begun to love each other.

Which makes the coming inspection considerably more searching than a debate would have been, and it is the same inspection any of us would face. A man can talk about grace for thirty years with real fluency and be no easier to live with than he was at the start. Talk is cheap and endlessly available. The other thing cannot be produced on demand, which is exactly why Paul proposed to look for it (cf. Jas. 4:13–16; 1 Thess. 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.” It is the principle behind the visit, stated as a maxim, and it cuts in both directions.

Against the Corinthians: fluency is not evidence of anything. They could discuss wisdom, argue about apostles, and produce impressive religious conversation, and Paul says the kingdom is not made of that material. Words are the cheapest commodity in any church, and the ability to talk well about God has never yet transformed anybody who possessed it.

But it cuts against a certain kind of Christian defensiveness too. “Power” here is not a promise of the spectacular, and it should not be conscripted to demand signs and wonders as the proof of a genuine church. The power this letter has described is the power of God that saves fools through a message about an execution (1:18), that raises the dead, and that turns a jealous congregation into people who love each other. That is not less than miraculous; it is simply harder to photograph.

Then the final question, and Paul leaves it hanging as a question rather than a threat: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?”

The rod is real. Paul has apostolic authority and will use it — he has already told them what he expects them to do about the man in chapter five. Nothing in this chapter’s tenderness cancels the discipline; a father who cannot ever be firm is not being kind, and a church that cannot ever act is not being loving.

But notice which one he wants, and notice that the choice is not his. He has put it in their hands. This is the strangest kind of authority — a man with the right to compel, asking. He would rather arrive as a father with nothing in his hand, and whether he can depends entirely on what they do between receiving this letter and seeing him.

Which is exactly how God has dealt with his people throughout Scripture, and it is the note the chapter ends on. He warns before he acts, at length, and the warning is itself the mercy — a rod described in advance is a rod trying not to be used. Turn, and why will you die? (Ezek. 33:11). The severity in Scripture is always announced first, and always by someone who would prefer not to.

So the chapter closes where it began, with a servant. It opened with under-rowers and stewards, men who own nothing and administer everything, and it ends with one of them holding real power and asking permission not to use it. He had every right to arrive and impose order on a church that had insulted him, and what he wants is to come in gentleness.

He learned that from someone. The one who had the right to come with a rod to a world in open rebellion came instead as an infant, and worked with his hands, and was reviled and blessed, and was made a spectacle last of all — and the only rod that has yet fallen fell on him (cf. Ezek. 33:11; 2 Cor. 13:10; Isa. 53:5).

5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Chapter 5 confronts the most scandalous pastoral failure in the letter: a man is living openly with his father’s wife — a sexual relationship forbidden by both Roman law and the Torah — and the church is not only tolerating it but apparently celebrating their openness and inclusivity. Paul is appalled, not merely by the sin itself but by the community’s response to it: pride. They are “puffed up” (v. 2) when they ought to be mourning. The church that boasts in its spiritual gifts and theological sophistication has somehow become the kind of community that treats gross immorality as evidence of its broad-mindedness.

Paul’s response is a theology of church discipline rooted in the holiness of God and the meaning of the cross. The community that tolerates unrepentant sin is like unleavened bread with a lump of leaven in it: the whole loaf is compromised. Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb; therefore the community that shelters in that sacrifice must be a community of sincere integrity, not malice and evil. The exclusion of the unrepentant sinner from the community is not revenge but surgery — and not merely for the community’s sake but for the sinner’s: “that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (v. 5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The opening accusation is stark: “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans — for a man has his father’s wife.” The relationship would have violated both Mosaic law (Lev 18:8; Deut 22:30) and Roman legal norms.
