It was not merely sinful by Christian standards but scandalous by the standards of the surrounding culture. And the church was proud of it — perhaps viewing their non-judgmental acceptance of the relationship as evidence of their spiritual sophistication and gospel freedom.

Paul’s verdict is delivered with apostolic authority. As already present in spirit, he has already judged: the man is to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. This extraordinary phrase — “delivered to Satan” — means exclusion from the community of God’s people into the domain where Satan holds sway. The intention is not punitive but redemptive: “that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.” Church discipline, rightly understood, is not the church washing its hands of a sinner but performing a painful surgery designed to bring him to his senses before the Last Day.

The Passover metaphor is the theological engine of the passage. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. The Passover required the complete removal of all leaven from the household before the feast — a single lump of yeast, left in place, works through the whole batch. The community that allows tolerated immorality to remain is a Passover household with leaven in the pantry: the sacrifice has been made, but the household is not living in correspondence with it. “Let us celebrate the festival...with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (v. 8) — the ongoing moral life of the community should match the purity that the Passover sacrifice purchased.
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

The Reformed tradition has always identified church discipline as one of the marks of the true church (alongside Word and sacraments). Calvin’s Institutes III.11–14 ground discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the holiness of the community is not a human achievement but a participation in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the final word against the sinner but the penultimate word, designed to produce repentance. The church that refuses to discipline its members — in the name of grace, tolerance, or avoiding conflict — is, paradoxically, acting without grace: it is allowing the leavening of unrepentant sin to compromise the whole community and denying the sinner the painful mercy of confrontation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian pride in tolerating this relationship may reflect the influence of the “strong” in the community — those with social status and rhetorical sophistication who had reinterpreted gospel freedom as moral permissiveness. The man involved may have been a patron of the church, someone whose loss the community feared. Paul overrides all such calculations: the gospel has higher priorities than keeping wealthy members comfortable. Now: The contemporary church’s allergy to any form of discipline is well-documented and widely lamented. Churches afraid to confront unrepentant sin in their members have, ironically, become communities shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“A man has his father’s wife.” The wording is careful and it matters: not his mother, but his stepmother — the father either dead or divorced, and the relationship apparently settled and ongoing rather than a single lapse, since Paul uses the present tense.

The law of Moses forbade it explicitly (Lev. 18:8; Deut. 22:30). But Paul’s point is not that it breaks the law of Moses; it is that it breaks the standards of pagan Corinth. Roman law prohibited such a marriage outright, and Cicero records a case of it as a public scandal. Corinth was a city with a reputation for vice across the whole Mediterranean, and this was over the line even there. The church had managed to be more permissive than a port town famous for permissiveness.

And then the sentence that is the real subject of the chapter: “And you are arrogant!”

That is what Paul is writing about. Not the man — the man is dealt with in three verses. The congregation. They were not agonising over this, or divided about it, or quietly ashamed of it. They were proud.

How? The likeliest explanation runs straight out of the previous chapters. This was a church that prized its own spiritual sophistication and had a theology of freedom it was pleased with. Grace so large, liberty so complete, that it could accommodate even this — and a congregation that could take it in its stride was demonstrating how far beyond ordinary scruples it had travelled. There may have been a more sordid factor too: a man in such a marriage was likely wealthy, possibly a patron the church could not afford to lose.

Whatever the mechanism, the shape is permanent, and it is worth naming because it recurs. There is a kind of tolerance that presents itself as maturity and is actually cowardice with a theology attached.

“Ought you not rather to mourn?” The word is pentheō — the verb for grieving a death, the word used of mourners at a funeral. And this is the most instructive thing in the passage, because it names the right emotion, and it is one almost nobody reaches for.

Consider the two responses available when serious sin surfaces in a church. One is what the Corinthians did: absorb it, explain it, be relaxed about it. The other is what churches more often do: outrage, gossip, the energetic circulation of the details, and a certain relish. Paul asks for neither. He asks for grief — the response of people who have lost something they loved and are standing at a graveside.

Which is a searching test, because grief cannot be faked and cannot be enjoyed. Outrage is pleasurable; that is why it is so popular. Indifference is comfortable. Mourning is neither, and it is the only one of the three that has any love in it — you do not grieve over someone you were not attached to.

So the test, for the next time you hear that a Christian you know has done something serious. Watch the first movement of your heart in the four seconds before you have composed a response. If it is a flicker of interest, or of superiority, or of relief that it was not you — then whatever you go on to say about the sin, you have not yet reached the emotion this verse asks for. And a church full of people who cannot mourn is not qualified to do what Paul is about to command (cf. 2 Cor. 12:21; Gal. 6:1).

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Though absent in body, I am present in spirit.” It is worth saying at once what this is not. Paul is not claiming a mystical projection of himself across the Aegean, nor some special apostolic power of remote attendance. He is saying what any of us mean by being with someone in spirit — but with the added weight that his apostolic authority genuinely travels in the letter being read aloud. When they hear this document, they are hearing him.

“I have already pronounced judgment.” The verdict is not being submitted for discussion. Paul has weighed the case and reached a conclusion, and he does so from a distance because the facts are not in dispute — the thing is being openly and publicly done.

But now notice something that governs the whole doctrine of church discipline and is regularly missed: Paul does not act. He has pronounced the verdict, and the execution of it waits on something — “when you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus”.

The apostle with unquestioned authority does not remove the man by letter. He tells the congregation to gather and do it. Which means discipline in the New Testament is a corporate act, not an administrative decision taken by a leader, and this cuts in two directions at once.

It cuts against churches that will not act. The congregation cannot outsource this to the minister and then complain about him, nor can it treat a matter of this kind as somebody else’s department. Paul lays the duty on the assembly, and a church that never assembles to face anything has quietly declined a responsibility Christ gave it.

And it cuts equally against the leader who acts alone. A great deal of damage has been done in churches by men who decided a case privately and announced the outcome, and this verse gives them no cover whatever. The whole body meets. Which is the same safeguard the Lord himself built into the procedure — the escalating steps of Matthew 18, ending with tell it to the church, not tell it to the pastor.

Then the two things that make such a gathering more than a disciplinary hearing. It is “in the name of the Lord Jesus” — convened on his authority, not the church’s own. And it proceeds “with the power of our Lord Jesus” — which is precisely the promise attached in Matthew: where two or three are gathered in his name, he is there among them (Matt. 18:20). That famous sentence is not, in its context, a comfort about small prayer meetings. It is a guarantee given to a church doing this very thing, and it is the most sobering possible reason for doing it carefully.

So the practical weight of these two verses is a warning against both of the errors churches actually commit. Nothing here permits a congregation to shrug. And nothing here permits a leader to move without the body, or a body to move without Christ’s authority and in something other than the spirit of the previous verse’s grief. An assembly gathered in his name, with his power present, is not a tribunal. It is a church standing in the presence of its Lord, doing the hardest thing he ever asked of it (cf. Matt. 18:15–20; 2 Cor. 2:6).

verseByVerse.quote: you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.” It is one of the most alarming sentences in the New Testament, and every clause needs handling.

“Deliver to Satan” does not mean handing a soul over to damnation, and Paul’s own final clause forbids that reading. The whole letter has been describing two spheres: the community where Christ dwells by his Spirit (3:16), and the world outside, which lies under the power of the evil one. To be excluded from the assembly is to be put out of the first and into the second — removed from the protection, the fellowship, the sacrament and the prayers, and left in the open. Paul uses the same phrase once more, of two men who had made shipwreck of the faith (1 Tim. 1:20).

“For the destruction of the flesh” is genuinely disputed and honesty requires saying so. Some take it of physical suffering, even death, on the pattern of the judgments in Acts 5 or later in this letter (11:30). Others take flesh in Paul’s usual moral sense — the sinful nature — so that what is to be destroyed is the appetite itself, by being allowed to run to its own bitter end. The second fits Paul’s vocabulary better and fits the purpose clause far better, and it describes something we have all watched: a man protected from the consequences of what he is doing will continue; a man who is left to feel what it actually costs may come to his senses. It is the mechanism of the prodigal, who needed the pigs before he wanted the father.

And then the clause that governs everything: “so that his spirit may be saved”.

Read the sentence again with that at the front and it changes character entirely. This is not the church washing its hands of a man. It is the last available means of grace, applied because everything gentler has failed. Excommunication in the New Testament is not the opposite of seeking someone’s salvation; it is an instrument of it — the surgeon’s knife, used because the alternative is worse and used with the intention of a cure.

Which is proved by what happened next, and no treatment of this verse is honest without it. Writing to the same church a while later, Paul deals with a disciplined man — almost certainly this one. The discipline had worked. And Paul’s instruction is emphatic: the punishment has been enough, now forgive him and comfort him, reaffirm your love for him, “lest he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” — and he adds a reason that ought to be written over every church discipline case in history: do it “so that we would not be outwitted by Satan” (2 Cor. 2:5–11).

Note where Satan is in each passage. In 1 Corinthians 5 he is the instrument God uses to bring a man home. In 2 Corinthians 2 he is the danger of a church that will not let a repentant man back. The devil can work either side of this, and the second failure is the commoner one.

So the guard, and it is needed because this text has been used to justify real cruelty. Shunning as punishment, families broken up, people pursued for years, the machinery of the cult — all of it has claimed this verse. The test is the purpose clause. If a church disciplines without longing for the person’s return, without a route back, without telling him plainly what repentance would look like and how gladly he would be received, then whatever it is doing, it is not this. Paul’s aim is a man saved in the day of the Lord, and everything that does not serve that aim is somebody else’s idea.

And if you are reading this as the person who was put out: the door in this passage opens both ways, and the man it was written about walked back through it and was told to be comforted (cf. 2 Cor. 2:5–11; Luke 15:17–20; Heb. 12:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?” The image is domestic and exact, and it explains why Paul will not let this pass as one man’s private business.

Leaven works invisibly and it works completely. You cannot put a small piece in one corner of the dough and have the rest unaffected; given time it is through everything, and there is no way of taking it out again. Paul is describing what tolerated sin does to a congregation.

And it is worth being precise about the mechanism, because the danger is not that everyone in the church will commit that particular sin. It is that the standard moves. Once something serious has been publicly accommodated, it becomes the new floor. Everything less than it is now unmentionable, because how do you raise a small matter in a church that has swallowed a large one? A single unaddressed case does not produce one hypocrite; it produces a congregation in which nothing can be said about anything.

Then Paul reaches for Passover, and the metaphor is chosen with care. Before the feast, every Jewish household conducted a search — a deliberate hunt through the house for any trace of leaven, which was then removed and burned. Not a general resolve to be purer. A search, room by room, for a specific thing, undertaken because a lamb had been killed.

“Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened.” Do not hurry past that last clause, because it is the engine of all New Testament ethics and it is the reverse of how we naturally think.

Paul does not say: purify yourselves in order to become clean. He says: you are unleavened — now get the leaven out. The status comes first and the effort follows from it. The Corinthians are not working towards a holiness they might one day possess; they are being told to correspond to a holiness already given them by the sacrifice. Become what you are. Every command in this letter stands on an indicative like that one, and a Christian who reverses the order will spend his life trying to earn a thing he was given at the start.

“For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”

Everything in the chapter rests on that clause, and it is the only reason the search is worth conducting. Consider what stood behind the original feast. A night in Egypt, a lamb chosen and killed in every house, blood struck on the doorposts, and a family inside eating in haste with their belongings packed — and death moving through the streets, and passing over every door where the blood was. Nobody inside those houses was safer than anybody else because of their character. The blood was on the door or it was not.

And every Passover for fourteen centuries afterwards was a rehearsal, a nation sitting down annually to eat the meal of a rescue that had already happened, with a lamb on the table that could never actually take away anything. Then John saw Jesus walking by the Jordan and said: behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). He died at Passover, at the hour the lambs were being killed, and not a bone of him was broken — as the law required of the Passover lamb (Exod. 12:46; John 19:36).

The lamb was always him. Fourteen hundred years of dinners were pointing at one afternoon outside Jerusalem, when the blood went on the doorposts of the world and death passed over everyone who was inside (cf. Exod. 12:1–13; 1 Pet. 1:18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let us therefore celebrate the festival.” It is an unexpected way to finish a paragraph about excommunication, and the choice of image tells you a great deal about how Paul understood the Christian life.

The Passover was not a single evening. The lamb was killed, and then came seven days of unleavened bread — a whole week of feasting that flowed out of the sacrifice. Paul takes that structure and applies it: Christ has been sacrificed, once, finished; and what follows is not a fast but a festival, and the festival is now.

Which is worth pressing, because a great many Christians would describe their faith in almost any terms other than feasting. Duty, effort, struggle, a certain grimness endured in hope of better later. Paul says the sacrifice has been made and the church is therefore at a feast — and the only question on the table is what is being served with it.

Then the striking thing, and it catches every reader who is paying attention. Having spent seven verses on a case of gross sexual immorality, Paul names the leaven to be cleared out as “malice and evil”.

Not immorality. Malice. The word is kakia — ill-will, the settled disposition to want someone’s harm. Having every right to name the obvious sin, he names the one the congregation had not thought to look for, and it is the sin of the respectable. The man in v. 1 was one person. The malice was general, and it is what had made the church proud rather than grieving in the first place.

This is the pattern all through the letter and it should be expected by now. The Corinthians were exercised about spectacular failures in other people and entirely comfortable with their own settled unkindness. It is possible to be scrupulous about the sins one has no appetite for.

Against that Paul sets two words. Eilikrineia — usually rendered sincerity, and probably built from the idea of something held up to the sunlight to show there is nothing hidden in it. Unmixed, unalloyed, with no second layer. And alētheia, truth — the correspondence between what a person is and what he appears to be.

Which makes the required cleansing considerably more searching than the removal of one man. A church can conduct discipline impeccably and still be full of the leaven this verse names — can put out the immoral member and go on with its factions, its cold shoulders, its long-running grudges and its carefully maintained impressions.

So here is the search, conducted the Passover way, room by room and for something specific. Not am I broadly a decent Christian, which nobody has ever answered usefully. Rather: is there a person whose difficulty would not entirely displease me? Is there a version of myself I maintain in public that those who live with me would not recognise? Those are leaven, in the two exact categories Paul names, and this is a feast, and the householder is expected to go looking with a candle before he sits down (cf. Matt. 23:25–28; Eph. 4:31).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A clarification that Paul has apparently already needed to make once before (v. 9: “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people”). The Corinthians had apparently applied this to the world at large, concluding that they must withdraw from every immoral person in Corinth — which would have required leaving the world entirely. Paul corrects the misunderstanding with characteristic precision: the command applies to those inside the community who name the name of Christ and live in unrepentant immorality, not to unbelievers outside who make no such profession.

The logic is powerful: God judges those outside the community; the community is responsible to judge those inside. The world cannot be held to the standard of the gospel it has not received; the church member who has received the gospel and persists in unrepentant wickedness has abandoned the correspondence between profession and life that the gospel demands. To refuse judgment on such a person is not grace but confusion — treating the unrepentant church member as if they were the unbelieving neighbour.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside the community (v. 12–13) defines the scope of church discipline with precision. The church is not called to police the world; it is called to maintain the integrity of its own fellowship. “God judges those outside” — this is not indifference to the world’s sin but a recognition that the church is not the world’s court of law. The church’s mission to the world is evangelism, not judgment; its internal discipline is precisely what enables it to be a credible witness in the world it is trying to reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. Misapplied teaching on holiness tends in two directions: either becoming a withdrawal sect (refusing all contact with sinful unbelievers) or collapsing into permissiveness (refusing all internal accountability). The Corinthians had done the latter. Now: The same confusion persists: churches that are either socially withdrawn from the world (failing at evangelism) or internally undisciplined (failing at community). Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I wrote to you in my letter” — and the letter in question is not in our Bibles. Paul had written to Corinth before this, and the document is lost.

That is worth a moment, because it puzzles people. It does not follow that a page of Scripture has gone missing. What God intended to preserve for the church he preserved; Paul, like any pastor, wrote a great deal that was true and useful and not intended to be Scripture, and this was one such letter. The apostle wrote notes, made arrangements, sent greetings. Inspiration is not a claim that every sentence Paul ever penned was canonical.

What we do have is the Corinthians’ misreading of it, and the misreading is instructive. Told not to associate with the sexually immoral, they had apparently applied it to Corinth at large — and Paul’s correction is dry to the point of comedy: not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world… since then you would need to go out of the world.

He is pointing out that the policy is unworkable. In that city, a rule of no contact with immoral people would empty the market, the workshop, the street and most families. You would have to leave — which some later Christians duly tried, taking themselves off to the desert, and which every separatist movement since has attempted in some form.

And notice what Paul does not do. He does not say: it would be admirable but impractical. He rules it out as a misunderstanding of the command. The Christian is not meant to withdraw from unbelievers, and the whole New Testament is against it. The Lord himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, which was intended as an insult and was simply an accurate description of how he spent his time; and Paul will shortly be telling this church to accept dinner invitations from pagan neighbours (10:27).

Then the thing that makes this chapter permanently useful, which is the shape of the Corinthian error. They were strict where they should have been open, and open where they should have been strict. Rigorous with outsiders who had never professed anything; entirely relaxed about a member living in public sin. Precisely inverted.

That inversion is not a first-century curiosity. It is the standing temptation of religious communities, and it runs both ways. There are churches that are ferocious about the sins of the surrounding culture — well-informed, indignant, quick to denounce — and unable to have a hard conversation with one of their own. And there are churches so anxious not to seem judgmental that they have no internal accountability at all, while being quietly disdainful of the world they are supposed to be reaching.

So a test, and it is diagnostic of which error is yours. Count your actual friendships — not acquaintances, not colleagues, but people whose houses you have been in — and ask how many of them are not Christians. If the honest answer is none, you have drifted out of the world in the way this verse forbids, whatever your theology of engagement says. And then ask when you last spoke, kindly and directly, to a fellow believer about something that was doing them harm. Most of us find one of those two answers uncomfortable, and which one it is tells us which half of Paul’s correction we needed (cf. Matt. 11:19; John 17:15–18).

verseByVerse.quote: But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the command itself, and the decisive words are “anyone who bears the name of brother”. That is the whole distinction. Not the immoral of the world, who have professed nothing; the person inside, who claims to belong to Christ and whose life publicly contradicts it.

Look at the list, because it is more uncomfortable than we let it be: sexually immoral, greedy, idolater, reviler, drunkard, swindler. Sitting in the middle of that catalogue, between an idolater and a drunkard, is the man with a vicious tongue. Paul has put the church member who savages people verbally in the same list as the man in verse 1. We would never have compiled it that way, and that is the point. A congregation will act on scandal and will tolerate a reviler for thirty years.

“Not even to eat with such a one.” In that world a shared table was not a casual arrangement; it was the public sign of acceptance and common life. And the primary reference is almost certainly the church’s own meal — the gathering at which the Lord’s Supper was taken. The man is to find that the fellowship whose sign he has been receiving is closed to him, precisely so that he registers that something is wrong.

Two guards are essential here, because this verse has done real damage in careless hands.

The first: this is about the unrepentant, and not about the struggling. Nothing here touches the Christian who is fighting a sin and losing, who is ashamed, who keeps confessing and keeps failing. That person is not a candidate for this passage; he is a candidate for Galatians 6:1, restoration by the spiritual in a spirit of gentleness. The category Paul is describing is settled, public, and defended — a man who has decided, and who expects the church to accommodate it. If you are reading this with a guilty conscience about a sin you hate, this verse is not about you, and the fact that you hate it is the proof.

The second: this is the church’s corporate fellowship, not a licence to destroy natural bonds. Readers ask the hard version immediately — my son professes faith and is living in something serious; do I stop eating with my own child? Paul is regulating the assembly’s table, not abolishing the duties of a parent, and the New Testament never asks anyone to stop loving their family. Note too what he does not say. He does not say have no contact, cut him off, or refuse to speak. And when he writes about a similar case elsewhere he supplies the tone explicitly: “do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3:15).

That sentence should govern the whole practice. The aim is not to make the person feel hated; it is to make the anomaly unmistakable — to withdraw the signal that everything is fine, while leaving no doubt that he is wanted back. Which is a difficult thing to do well, and it is the reason the chapter began by asking for grief rather than outrage. Only mourners can be trusted with this. Anybody who finds it satisfying should not be doing it (cf. Gal. 6:1; 2 Thess. 3:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside.”

Paul draws the boundary in a single sentence, and it settles the jurisdiction. The church is answerable for the church. The world is answerable to God directly, and he needs no assistance.

Which is not indifference to the world’s sin — the same apostle will describe the judgment of God on human wickedness at length in Romans. It is a recognition that the church has not been appointed the world’s magistrate. Our commission to those outside is announcement, not enforcement: we tell them what God has done in Christ. Their accounts are not ours to audit.

And there is a practical release in that which many Christians need. A great deal of religious energy is spent being indignant about people who never claimed to be anything else — monitoring the culture, keeping score, maintaining a running commentary on the sins of those outside. Paul’s question is quietly deflating: what have I to do with judging outsiders? Not your court. And the hours are better spent on the one that is.

Then the closing citation, and Paul has been building towards it: “Purge the evil person from among you.” It comes from Deuteronomy, where the phrase recurs like a refrain (Deut. 13:5; 17:7; 19:19; 22:21). Israel was a nation as well as a covenant people, and there the purging was capital — the offender was put to death, and the community was cleansed by his removal from the land.

Notice what Paul does with it. He keeps the seriousness and transposes the penalty. The church is not a state, holds no sword, and executes nobody; what it can do is exclude. Which means the new covenant version of this command is at once as grave as the old and immeasurably more merciful — because a man put outside the camp can come back, and a man stoned outside the camp cannot. The whole apparatus of discipline in the New Testament is a death sentence commuted to a temporary exclusion, with the door left unlocked.

And that is not an accident of temperament. It is a consequence of the sacrifice in v. 7. The reason the church does not need to purge anybody with a stone is that the death the covenant required has already been died, by someone else, once.

Which is where this chapter finally lands, and it is worth seeing. The pattern of Deuteronomy is that the evil is taken outside the camp and destroyed there, and the people are made clean. And there was a day when someone was led out of the city, in the name of the community’s purity, and executed outside the walls between two criminals. He was not the evil person. He was the only one in the story who was not, and he went out anyway, in the place of the man in verse 1 and the arrogant congregation in verse 2 and every reader of this page.

“So Jesus also suffered outside the gate… Let us go to him outside the camp, and bear the reproach he endured” (Heb. 13:12–13). The purging that actually cleansed the people of God was not the removal of a sinner from the assembly. It was the Lamb, carried out through the gate, at Passover (cf. Deut. 17:7; Heb. 13:11–13).

5.text: <sup>1</sup>It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife.<sup>2</sup>And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.<sup>3</sup>For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing.<sup>4</sup>When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,<sup>5</sup>you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.<sup>6</sup>Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?<sup>7</sup>Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.<sup>8</sup>Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.<sup>9</sup>I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—<sup>10</sup>not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.<sup>11</sup>But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.<sup>12</sup>For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?<sup>13</sup>God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”

6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Chapter 6 addresses two more symptoms of the same disease: the Corinthians’ preference for the world’s courts over the community’s wisdom, and their confusion about what gospel freedom means in the domain of the body. The two sections are linked by the common thread of what it means that the Holy Spirit dwells in the believer — individually and corporately. If the Spirit of the living God inhabits these people, then taking one another before pagan courts is an absurd undervaluation of the wisdom God has given the community, and using the body for sexual immorality is an act of desecration against the temple of God.

The chapter reaches its climax in one of the most electrifying declarations in all of Paul: “Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” The body is not a neutral instrument for satisfying appetites; it is the dwelling place of the Spirit of the Creator. The resurrection of Christ, which will raise this same body, makes the body eternally significant. The cross, which purchased this body at infinite cost, makes the body not our own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s opening is blunt: “Does anyone of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints?” The church at Corinth — spiritually gifted, theologically sophisticated — was taking its internal disputes to pagan magistrates. Paul finds this not merely improper but absurd and shameful. The community that will one day judge the world and the angels is incapable of settling a trivial lawsuit?

The critique has two edges. The first: the church has the wisdom and authority to resolve internal disputes — and refusing to use it is a failure of community life. The second: the very existence of such lawsuits is itself a defeat. Even if the church could resolve every dispute with perfect fairness, the fact that brothers are suing brothers rather than suffering wrong and accepting being defrauded reveals a fundamental absence of the cruciform character the gospel produces. The person shaped by the cross willingly absorbs loss for the sake of the brother; the Corinthian litigant insists on his rights at the expense of the community.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul’s argument from eschatology — “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2) — is a characteristic move: the future reality of the believer’s status shapes present behaviour. The saints who will participate in Christ’s eschatological judgment (Dan 7:22; Rev 20:4) have already, in their union with Christ, been granted a dignity that makes recourse to pagan courts for petty disputes absurd. The inconsistency Paul exposes is not merely practical but theological: why would those destined for cosmic judicial authority submit their neighbourhood disputes to judges who do not acknowledge Christ?
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Going to court was not merely a legal act but a social strategy. Paul refuses the framework: the cross creates a community in which the willingness to absorb loss is a greater display of power than the ability to win in court. Now: The Christian instinct to reach for legal remedies when wronged by a fellow believer is understandable but reveals how deeply the world’s categories of justice and self-protection have shaped us. Paul’s question — “Why not rather suffer wrong?” — is among the most countercultural sentences in the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Does he dare?” The verb is tolmaō — to have the audacity, the nerve. Paul is not opening with an argument; he is opening with astonishment that anyone would think of it.

What was happening is clear enough. Members of the church were suing each other in the Corinthian courts. And to understand why Paul is so exercised, it helps to know what those courts were. Roman civil litigation in a provincial city was not primarily a search for justice; it was an arena in which social standing was asserted and rivals were damaged. The wealthy man with connections and a hired advocate generally won, and everybody knew it. Going to law was a way of using your position against somebody with less of it.

So when the Corinthians took their disputes to court, they were not merely choosing an inconvenient venue. They were importing into the church the exact mechanism by which the powerful of that city kept the weak in their place — which is what this whole letter has been about since the first chapter.

“The unrighteous” is not name-calling. It is Paul’s standing category for those outside Christ, and he uses it here to make a point about competence: these judges do not share the standard by which the case ought to be decided. They can apply Roman law. They cannot ask what love requires, or what the cross makes appropriate between two brothers.

Then the argument from the greater to the lesser: “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?”

It is a startling claim and Paul assumes they have been taught it. Its roots are in Daniel’s vision, where judgment is given to the saints of the Most High (Dan. 7:22), and in the Lord’s own promise that his followers would sit on thrones (Matt. 19:28; cf. Rev. 20:4). The believer’s participation in that judgment is not independent authority but a consequence of union with Christ: where he sits, those who are in him sit.

“Are you incompetent to try trivial cases?” The word for trivial is the smallest available. Paul’s logic is simple and unanswerable: people appointed to a share in the final assize cannot plausibly claim they are unqualified to sort out a disputed debt.

Which quietly exposes the real problem, and it was not competence. A church that could produce men wise enough to settle the matter was choosing not to, because at least one party did not want a fair settlement — he wanted to win, and the court was where winning was available.

So there is a test here for any Christian in a dispute with another. Ask whether you are looking for a resolution or for a verdict. They are not the same thing, and it is usually possible to tell which you want by noticing whether you would accept an outcome in which nobody was declared right. The Corinthians had access to brothers who could have helped them. They preferred a venue that would produce a loser (cf. Dan. 7:22; Matt. 19:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do you not know that we are to judge angels?”

Paul drops it in as though it were common knowledge, which tells us it had been part of his teaching at Corinth. It is one of the most extraordinary throwaway lines in the New Testament, and he does not stop to explain it.

Which angels? Almost certainly the fallen ones — the beings Peter describes as kept in chains of gloomy darkness until the judgment, and Jude in the same terms (2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 6). There is a day appointed for their assessment, and Paul says believers will have a part in it.

Take the measure of that for a moment. These are creatures of an order above us — older, stronger, unencumbered by bodies, with a knowledge of the created order that no human being has ever approached. The Corinthians were being intimidated in a provincial courtroom by men with money and social connections. Paul reminds them that they are destined to sit in judgment on beings beside whom a Roman magistrate is nothing whatever.

And notice how he uses it. Not to make them feel important — this whole letter is an assault on their sense of importance. He uses it to make their behaviour look absurd. “How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!” The phrase is biōtika — the ordinary business of living: money, property, contracts, boundaries. People with that future are squabbling over these things in front of pagans.

Which yields a question worth carrying about, because most of us never think in these terms at all. We have a functional sense of our own significance, and it is assembled almost entirely out of present things — the job, the income, the standing among people whose opinion we track. Scripture’s account of what a believer is destined for has almost no traction on our ordinary Tuesday.

And that is precisely the disconnection Paul is attacking. He is not asking them to feel grand. He is asking them to let the size of the future put the present in proportion — because a man who genuinely believed he would one day share in the judgment of angels would find it very hard to sustain a two-year grievance about a boundary wall.

So a test with a small scale, which is how this actually bites. Think of the thing that has most occupied your mind this week — the slight, the money worry, the argument you keep re-running. It is almost certainly a biōtikon, a matter pertaining to this life. Not unimportant; Paul does not say these things do not matter, only that they are the small end of the scale.

Then set beside it the sentence in this verse. There is a courtroom coming in which you will be seated, in Christ, over powers that have terrorised the human race since Eden. The disproportion is not meant to shame you for caring about your week. It is meant to loosen the grip of it (cf. 2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 6; Rom. 8:18).

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I say this to your shame.” Paul does not reach for that phrase often, and when he does the rebuke has reached its sharpest point. He used the opposite formula two chapters ago — I do not write these things to make you ashamed (4:14). Here he does.

And the shame is precisely targeted. “Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers?”

The irony would have been unbearable, and it is the whole point. This is the church that has spent four chapters congratulating itself on its wisdom. They had factions organised around competing teachers, they prided themselves on knowledge and eloquence, they thought of themselves as the mature. Paul has been arguing with that self-assessment since 1:18. Now he simply asks them to produce one wise man for a practical purpose — and the answer, evidently, is that they cannot.

It is the standing test of whether wisdom is real. Wisdom that can discuss the deep things of God and cannot help two brothers settle a debt is not wisdom in any sense the Bible recognises. James makes the same point from the other end: the wisdom from above is peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy — and where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, whatever else is present, it is not wisdom (Jas. 3:14–17).

“But brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers.” The last phrase carries the second injury. It is not only that the dispute exists; it is that it is being conducted in public, in front of exactly the people the church exists to reach.

Think of what a Corinthian pagan would have seen. A new religious movement claiming that its God had reconciled enemies and made one body out of Jew and Greek, slave and free — and two of its members in the basilica, arguing about money, using the same lawyers and the same tactics as everybody else. Every claim the church had made about itself was being tested in that courtroom, and it was failing.

Which is the abiding application, and it has more forms now than Paul could have imagined. Congregations split in public. Churches conduct their disagreements where anyone can read them. Christians savage one another in writing, at length, before an audience of thousands, over matters that two people of goodwill in one room could have resolved in an afternoon. The watching world does not weigh the arguments. It notices that these people cannot get on.

And notice what Paul assumes the church should have: a functioning way of settling disputes between its members. Not a court, but wise people the parties are willing to be bound by. That is a real institution and most congregations do not have it — which is why, when something serious arises, there is nowhere for it to go except outwards.

So a practical question for any church, and it is answerable in a sentence. If two members of your congregation had a genuine, sharp, money-shaped disagreement next month, who would they take it to, and would they accept the answer? If the honest reply is that there is no such person and no such process, then this passage is not describing Corinth’s problem. It is describing yours (cf. Jas. 3:13–18; Matt. 18:15–17).

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you.” The word is hēttēma — a loss, a defeat. Paul is saying that the verdict is irrelevant, because the outcome was settled the moment the case was filed. Win or lose, you have lost.

Then the two questions that are among the most countercultural sentences in the New Testament: “Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded?”

He is not asking them to pretend the wrong did not happen. The words are blunt — be wronged, be swindled — and they assume a real injury and a real loss. What he is proposing is that a Christian might decide to absorb it.

The logic is not passivity but arithmetic of a different kind. The Corinthian litigant has calculated that the disputed sum is worth more than the brother. Paul says the calculation is wrong, and that a man shaped by the cross will reach a different total — because the one he follows absorbed infinite wrong without retaliating, and when he was reviled did not revile in return (1 Pet. 2:23). It is the Sermon on the Mount applied to a courtroom: if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well (Matt. 5:40).

Now a guard is essential here, because this passage has been used to do real harm and the misuse is not hypothetical.

These verses are about property and money disputes between Christian brothers. They are not a rule that Christians must never use the law, and they cannot be stretched into one without contradicting Scripture and Paul himself. Paul invoked his Roman citizenship when he was about to be flogged (Acts 22:25), demanded a public apology from the magistrates at Philippi (Acts 16:37), and appealed to Caesar rather than be handed over (Acts 25:11). And in Romans he says the civil magistrate is God’s servant, who bears the sword for the punishment of wrongdoing (Rom. 13:4) — which is not a thing God instituted in order that his people should never make use of it.

So this text has nothing to say against reporting a crime. Nothing against protecting a child. Nothing against a victim of abuse or assault going to the police, or an employee taking a genuine grievance to a tribunal. Any leader who quotes “why not rather suffer wrong?” to persuade a victim to stay silent and keep it in the church has taken a verse about a money dispute and used it as a lid. That is not what Paul wrote and it is the opposite of what the passage intends, since the whole point is that the strong should stop using their advantage against the weak.

Then the final sentence, which is the sharpest in the paragraph: “But you yourselves wrong and defraud — even your own brothers!”

Paul has been addressing the plaintiffs. Now he turns and addresses the defendants, and the picture is complete. This is not a church of innocent parties being unfairly pursued. Some of them are doing the defrauding, and doing it to their own brothers, and are then apparently surprised to find themselves in court.

So the test cuts both ways, and it is worth running honestly. If you are the one who has been wronged, could you absorb it — genuinely, without a running account? And if you are honest, is there anyone with a legitimate grievance against you: money owed, a promise not kept, an advantage taken because you could? The chapter began by asking who would judge the case. It ends by suggesting that both men in the courtroom may need the same verdict (cf. Matt. 5:38–42; Rom. 12:17–19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Between the lawsuit passage and the sexuality passage, Paul inserts a solemn catalogue of sins that exclude from the kingdom of God. The list is not a complete inventory of all possible disqualifying sins but a selection of the specific patterns that characterise Corinthian culture: sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, homosexual behaviour, theft, greed, drunkenness, reviling, swindling. The community must not be deceived: these things exclude from the kingdom.

But the thunderclap of v. 11 follows immediately: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” Three passive verbs, three completed divine acts: washed, sanctified, justified. The people in the community who once practised these things have been transformed — not by self-improvement but by divine action in the name of Christ and through the Spirit. The catalogue of vices is not a present description but a past one: “such were some of you.” The past tense is the gospel’s answer to shame.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The triad of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — covers the full scope of soteric transformation. Reformed theology typically orders justification before sanctification logically; Paul here places sanctification before justification in the list, which suggests he is not giving a logical order but a rhetorical one: moving from the most experientially tangible (washing, cleansing from the pollution of past sin) to the most legally decisive (justification, right standing before God). All three are accomplished “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — trinitarian to the root.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street — not foreign or distant behaviour but the lives many of the congregation had lived and from which the gospel had extracted them. Paul is not writing to people who need to be warned away from exotic sins; he is reminding them of who they used to be, so they understand what they now are. Now: The church in every generation contains people whose past is on the list in vv. 9–10. The three words of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — are the most liberating words any of them will ever hear about that past. It was real; the transformation is realer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not be deceived.” The warning implies someone was doing the deceiving — and given what this letter has shown of Corinth, the likely message was that grace is so complete and freedom so total that conduct has become a secondary matter. Paul says that is a lie, and that people are believing it.

“Will not inherit the kingdom of God” is the whole weight of the sentence. Not will be less rewarded. The vocabulary is of inheritance — of having no share in the age to come.

Before anything else, read the list as a whole, because how it is read determines whether it is heard rightly. Sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, men who practise homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers, swindlers. Nine items, and only three of them are sexual. Sitting alongside them are greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse and dishonest dealing — sins that are present in every congregation that has ever existed and are almost never preached with this level of seriousness.

Paul has assembled a list on which nearly everybody appears somewhere. A church that reads it as a description of outsiders, or of one particular group, has misread it so completely that the next verse will make no sense at all.

The two Greek terms behind “men who practise homosexuality” are worth explaining, since English translations vary and readers deserve to know what is actually there. Malakoi means literally “soft ones”, and in Greco-Roman usage it commonly denoted the passive partner in male same-sex intercourse; older versions rendered it “effeminate”, which is misleading to a modern ear. Arsenokoitai is a compound — arsēn (male) and koitē (bed) — and appears to have been coined from the Greek Old Testament of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where those two words stand side by side in the prohibition. Together they cover both roles in the act.

Some scholars argue Paul has only exploitative forms in view — pederasty, or the use of slaves. The argument deserves a fair hearing and it does not finally hold: the derivation from Leviticus points to the act itself rather than to its circumstances, and Paul names both partners rather than only the exploiter, which an argument about exploitation would not require. The historic reading of the church stands.

But the grammar matters enormously, and it is where most of the pastoral damage is done. Every item in this list is a settled way of life, not an experience of temptation. Paul is describing what people are and do, habitually and without repentance — the thief who steals, the drunkard who drinks, the reviler whose tongue is his weapon.

So if you are a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction and is not acting on it — who has perhaps fought this for years, told almost nobody, and reads this verse with dread every time it is preached — understand that you are not the person described here. Temptation is not practice. A desire resisted is not a life lived. The man in this list is not fighting; he has settled. And a believer who is fighting is doing precisely what the next verse says the gospel produces, which is the opposite of what is being condemned.

The same distinction applies right along the list, and applies to everyone. Being tempted to greed is not greed. Losing your temper is not being a reviler. What Paul is warning against is not the presence of a struggle but the absence of one — the comfortable conviction that a man may practise what he likes and inherit the kingdom anyway. That is the deception, and it is why he opened with do not be deceived (cf. Gal. 5:19–21; Eph. 5:5–6).

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And such were some of you.”

Four words, and they change the temperature of the whole chapter. Paul has just written the most severe list in the letter, and his next sentence is that it is a description of the people he is writing to.

Not people outside. Not a warning about the sort of person one might meet in Corinth. Some of you. The congregation contained former idolaters, former drunkards, former thieves, men who had lived what verse 9 describes. That is who was sitting in the room when this letter was read aloud.

And the tense is the gospel. Such were — past, finished, no longer the case. Paul does not write “such are some of you, but you are forgiven.” He says the description has stopped being true.

Then three verbs, and every one of them is passive. Things done to them.

“You were washed” — the pollution removed. This is the answer to the thing sin leaves behind after the guilt is dealt with: the sense of being soiled, of carrying something that will not come off. A man may believe he is forgiven and still feel unclean, and this word is aimed at exactly that.

“You were sanctified” — set apart, made holy, transferred into God’s own sphere. Note that this is stated as an accomplished fact, not a target. It is the same thing Paul said in his opening greeting, addressing this shambles of a church as those “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” (1:2).

“You were justified” — the legal word: declared righteous, the charge dismissed, standing before God as one against whom nothing can be brought.

Notice the order, because it is not the order a theologian would choose. Logically justification comes first — God declares, and then transforms. Paul puts sanctification before it, which suggests he is not constructing a doctrinal sequence but moving from what is most felt to what is most decisive: from the dirt coming off, to belonging to God, to the verdict that settles everything.

And all three “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — the Son’s name and the Spirit’s power and the Father’s ownership, all in one clause. Nothing here was self-administered.

This is the verse for the reader who is carrying a past. Not a vague sense of having been imperfect, but something specific — the years you do not talk about, the thing you did that you cannot imagine saying out loud in a church, the pattern you were in before Christ found you, and which surfaces at three in the morning to tell you what you really are.

Paul’s answer is not that it was not serious. He has just spent two verses saying how serious it was. His answer is that it is in the past tense and that three things have happened to you since, and that not one of them depends on your assessment of yourself.

Because look at what the accusation always does: it uses the true past to establish a false present. This is what you are. And the reply is not a denial of the history but a statement about the tense. Such were some of you. You were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified.

The washing was not a rinse, and the price is named at the end of this chapter. He did not tidy up the guilty; he bought them. The list in verse 9 is an accurate description of what he purchased, and he paid for it knowing every item, and he has never once suggested he overpaid (cf. Titus 3:3–7; Rom. 8:33–34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter’s theological climax addresses the use of the body and does so through two competing slogans — slogans that some Corinthians were apparently using to justify sexual behaviour. “All things are lawful for me” (v. 12) was likely a Corinthian slogan rooted in a misunderstanding of Christian freedom: if Christ has freed us from the law, then there are no restrictions on the body. “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food” (v. 13) was the Corinthian argument for sexual indulgence: the body is a biological instrument with natural appetites; satisfying those appetites with a prostitute is no more significant than eating a meal.

Paul demolishes both slogans with theology. The body is not a neutral instrument for appetite satisfaction; it is the member of Christ, destined for resurrection, indwelt by the Holy Spirit. To take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute is to bring Christ himself into that union — because the believer is one spirit with the Lord (v. 17). The body that will be raised from the dead is the same body that is now misused; the body indwelt by the Holy Spirit is the body now being treated as a commodity.

The climax is unforgettable: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” The price was the cross — the blood of Christ. The body, bought at that price, does not belong to the believer to use as he pleases. It belongs to God, as a temple belongs to its deity — and what is done in a temple is done in the presence of, and for the honour of, the one who inhabits it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul’s argument for sexual ethics is grounded in resurrection theology: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The body is not a temporary shell to be discarded but the vehicle of the self that God will raise — the same body, transformed. This is why what we do with the body matters eternally. The body-soul dualism that dismisses bodily sins as theologically insignificant — a common Gnostic error in the ancient world — is precisely what Paul is refuting. The resurrection of the body is the theological foundation of a robust, embodied Christian ethics.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a temple prostitute in Corinth was a normal feature of social and religious life — not perceived as transgression but as participation in the city’s religious and social fabric. The Corinthian with a “strong” theology might have regarded it as religiously meaningless (the idol is nothing) and biologically natural. Paul’s counter-argument changes the frame entirely: it is not religiously meaningless because the Holy Spirit inhabits the believer’s body; the body is not yours to give away because it was bought with a price. Now: The sexual ethics of any age are shaped by whatever account it gives of the body. Paul’s account — the body as Spirit-indwelt, resurrection-destined, cross-purchased — is the most exalted account of human physicality in any worldview.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All things are lawful for me.” Paul is almost certainly quoting them — a slogan circulating at Corinth, and quite possibly a distortion of something he had taught them himself about freedom from the law.

Notice that he does not simply deny it. He could have; instead he lets it stand and puts two limits round it, which is far more useful. Christian freedom is real, and Paul will not surrender the principle even when it is being abused. What he refuses is the conclusion that freedom is the only question worth asking.

The first limit: “but not all things are helpful.” The word is sympherei — what is advantageous, what builds up, what brings something together. A thing may be entirely permitted and still be a bad idea. That distinction is missing from a great deal of Christian decision-making, which tends to stop as soon as the question is it forbidden? has been answered.

And notice what it does to the shape of the question. “Is this allowed?” is the question of a man looking for the boundary of the territory he can occupy without penalty. “Is this helpful?” is the question of a man who wants to get somewhere. The first is the question of a servant checking the rules; the second is the question of a son who shares his father’s aim.

The second limit is the more penetrating: “but I will not be dominated by anything.”

The Greek carries a wordplay that the English cannot quite hold. The slogan says all things are exestin — permitted, within my authority. Paul replies that he will not be exousiasthēsomai — brought under the authority of — anything. Same root, turned round. Everything is under my authority; I will not let anything take authority over me.

Which exposes the irony in the Corinthian position with great precision. They were using the language of freedom to justify appetites that had them by the throat. A man who insists he is free to do a thing, and cannot stop doing it, is not describing liberty. He has simply found a theological vocabulary for his slavery.

That is the permanent usefulness of this verse, because the pattern outlives its first application. It is the drinker who is emphatic about Christian liberty in the matter of alcohol. The man who defends his viewing habits on the grounds that legalism is a greater danger. The person whose spending, or phone, or ambition is plainly running him, and who has an argument ready for anyone who raises it. In every case the giveaway is not the argument but the defensiveness — because a genuinely free man does not need to justify anything at length. He can simply stop.

So here is the test, and it is the most practical one in the chapter. Take whatever you would defend on the grounds of Christian freedom, and do not argue about whether it is permitted. Put it down for a month.

What happens next is the answer. If it goes without much difficulty, the freedom was real and you have lost nothing. If you find yourself negotiating, rationalising, or unable to face the month at all, then you have discovered which way the authority is running — and Paul’s point is that you were never arguing about liberty in the first place (cf. Gal. 5:13; 2 Pet. 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another slogan, and this one is an argument: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food.”

The reasoning behind it is easy to reconstruct and it is still in use. The body has appetites. Appetites exist to be satisfied. Hunger is met with food and nobody considers it a moral event; therefore sexual desire may be met wherever it is convenient, and it is no more significant than a meal. The Corinthian who visited a prostitute was not, on this account, doing anything of consequence — merely attending to a biological function.

Paul’s reply comes in two moves, and the second is the one the older commentary here left out because the stored quotation stopped short of it.

First: “and God will destroy both one and the other.” He grants the analogy and then points out where it goes. Yes — food and the stomach belong to an order that is passing away. Digestion is a temporary arrangement; there will be no stomachs in the resurrection in the sense you now have one. If you want to argue from what is transient, then admit that the whole category you are appealing to is on its way out.

Then the reply proper, and it is one of the most remarkable sentences Paul ever wrote about the human body: “The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.”

Read the second half again. Not merely that the body is for the Lord — which we might have guessed — but that the Lord is for the body. God is committed to your physical self. He is not tolerating it, waiting for the real you to be released from it at death. He made it, he took one himself, he redeemed it, and he intends to raise it.

That is the whole answer to the slogan, and it demolishes it at the root. The Corinthian argument assumed the body was a machine with requirements. Paul says the body is a person, and the person belongs to Christ.

And it is worth seeing how completely this cuts across the instinct of the ancient world, which held that the material was inferior and the spiritual was what mattered — so that what a man did with his body was either unimportant or a distraction from higher things. Christianity has never taught that, though Christians have often absorbed it. The faith whose central claims are an incarnation, a bodily resurrection and a coming new creation cannot regard flesh as an embarrassment.

Which is why sexual ethics in the New Testament are never presented as a set of arbitrary restrictions. They follow from a doctrine of the body so high that no other worldview comes near it. You will not find a rival account — ancient or modern — that says more about your physical self than that God became one, died in one, rose in one, and intends to give you one that will not decay.

So the practical consequence is broader than the passage’s first subject. If the Lord is for the body, then what you do with yours is never spiritually neutral — not the sleep you refuse it, not the way you speak about it, not the contempt some Christians carry for their own physical selves and mistake for humility. He is for it. That is a stranger and kinder claim than most of us have let it be (cf. Rom. 12:1; Phil. 3:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power.” Paul is still answering the food-and-stomach argument, and he answers it with the resurrection.

The logic runs like this. If the body were merely a temporary container, what is done with it would matter no more than what is done with a coat. But the body has a future. The same power that brought Jesus out of the tomb is going to be applied to your physical self, and what will stand in the new creation is not a disembodied spirit but a raised person. Which means the body you are currently deciding what to do with is the body that will be there.

Then the second argument, and it moves from the future to the present: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”

Melē is the ordinary word for limbs and organs — the same word behind “members” in English. This is not a metaphor about belonging to a club. Paul means that by union with Christ, the believer’s physical self is joined to him as a hand is joined to a body.

And having said that, he draws the conclusion with deliberate brutality: “Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?”

It is meant to shock, and it should. Paul refuses to let the sin be pictured privately, as a transaction between two consenting people in a room. He insists that Christ is not absent from it. The Christian does not leave his union with the Lord at the door and pick it up on the way out; there is no such door. Whatever a believer does with his body, he does as a limb of Christ.

“Never!” — mē genoito, the strongest negative in Paul’s vocabulary, the expression he reserves for a suggestion so appalling it does not deserve an argument.

Now, the ancient application was the temple prostitute, and the modern reader is inclined to file that under practices we no longer face. It would be a mistake. The argument Paul makes is not about a particular institution; it is about what a body is. And the contemporary form of the same transaction — a screen, an image, another human being reduced to a function, entirely private and entirely deniable — is available to almost every reader of this page, at any hour, at no cost and with no witnesses.

Which is exactly why this verse is worth having. Every defence of that habit depends on its being nobody else’s business: it harms no one, nothing is happening, it is only an image. Paul’s answer is that something is happening, and that the Lord is present at it, because the man doing it is a limb of Christ and does not stop being one for the duration.

That is a heavier thought than shame, and it is also more hopeful, because shame merely tells a man what he is and leaves him there. This tells him whose he is. The argument for purity here is not that you are dirty and must clean yourself up. It is that you are joined to Christ — already, now, in the body — and that he does not withdraw when you sin, which is precisely why it matters so much what you take him into (cf. Rom. 6:12–13; 1 Cor. 12:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now explains why the food analogy fails, and he does it by quoting Genesis about a prostitute.

“He who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her. For, as it is written, ‘The two will become one flesh.’”

The citation is Genesis 2:24 — the wedding verse, the charter of marriage, spoken in Eden before the fall. And Paul applies it to a paid encounter with a stranger.

That is the whole argument, and it is devastating. The Corinthian position was that this sort of thing carries no weight — a transaction, a bodily function, nothing exchanged but money. Paul says the one-flesh bond forms regardless. It was built into the act by God at creation, and it does not wait to be authorised by the intentions of the participants. Neither party meant a union. A union occurred.

Which is why sex can never be what every generation keeps insisting it can be: a thing done with the body alone, walked away from, filed under recreation. Paul’s claim is not that casual sex is emotionally unwise, though it is. It is that there is no such thing — that the act is a covenant-shaped act whether or not a covenant exists, and that performing it outside one does not neutralise it but tears it.

And the modern evidence is not against him. People discover, repeatedly and to their own surprise, that they cannot dispose of these attachments as easily as the theory promised — that someone they were assured meant nothing turns out to be lodged in them years later. Paul told us why. Something was joined that was designed not to come apart.

Then verse 17, which is the sentence the whole argument has been building to: “But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.”

Note that Paul uses the same verb both times — kollaō, to be glued, cemented, welded. He is deliberately setting the two unions side by side in identical language, and the effect is to make them mutually intolerable. Not incompatible in the sense of being unwise together; contradictory. The man is already glued to Christ. He is proposing to be glued to somebody else.

And this is where the passage turns from prohibition to something better. Paul’s final answer to sexual sin is not a rule. It is a rival intimacy — and a greater one. The believer is one spirit with the Lord: a union closer than the one being contemplated, permanent where that is momentary, and satisfying at a depth the other cannot reach even when it delivers everything it promises.

Which is worth saying plainly to anyone fighting here, because the fight is usually lost at the level of desire rather than of information. Nobody has ever been kept pure by being told that sex is serious; they knew. What holds is knowing what you already have. Purity that is only refusal is a starvation diet, and starvation diets do not last. The Christian is not being asked to want less. He is being asked to notice that he is already joined to Someone, and to want that more — which is the only appetite strong enough to displace the other one (cf. Gen. 2:24; Eph. 5:31–32; Ps. 63:1–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Flee from sexual immorality.” One word, and it is the whole strategy.

Paul does not say resist it, or manage it, or develop a robust theology of it. Pheugō — run. And the tense is continuous: keep running, make it a habit rather than an emergency measure.

This is worth noticing because it is not how the New Testament speaks about most temptation. Elsewhere Christians are told to stand, to resist the devil, to put on armour and hold their ground (Jas. 4:7; Eph. 6:13). Here the instruction is the opposite, and the change is deliberate. In this particular fight, standing your ground to prove you can is not courage. It is how men lose.

The model is Joseph, and the detail in Genesis is exact. He does not debate with Potiphar’s wife, or reason with her, or test how much of the conversation he can survive. He runs out of the house and leaves his coat in her hand (Gen. 39:12). It cost him his reputation and his liberty, and it was the right decision.
