“Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.” The clause is genuinely difficult, and commentators divide over it — some think Paul is again quoting a Corinthian saying and qualifying it; others that he means sexual sin uniquely implicates the whole self, since it is the one act in which the body itself is the instrument, the currency and the thing given away. Whatever the precise force, the direction is clear: this sin turns inward in a way others do not, and the damage lands on the person committing it.

Now the practical shape of fleeing, because the command is useless if it stays abstract — and the modern form of this battle is not the temple precinct but a device in a pocket.

Fleeing is not what most people attempt. What most people attempt is resisting at the point of temptation, using willpower, at the exact moment when willpower is least available — late, tired, alone, discouraged. That is a fight nobody wins for long, and the repeated failure then produces the despair that makes the next failure easier.

Fleeing happens earlier and it is structural rather than heroic. It means the decision is taken at ten in the morning, not eleven at night. It means the filter installed, the device out of the bedroom, the account handed to somebody else, the route home changed, the friendship that has begun to warm quietly cooled before anyone has said anything they cannot unsay. It is unglamorous and slightly humiliating, and that is a mark in its favour: a man who is willing to look foolish about this is a man who has understood what he is dealing with.

And it means telling somebody. Nothing in this chapter grows in the dark like this does, and the single most reliable step any Christian takes here is the one that ends the secrecy — because sin that has to be reported to a friend on Thursday loses a great deal of its power on Wednesday.

So the test is simply this: name the last time you were in this fight, and identify the point at which it was actually decided. It will not have been the moment of failure. It will have been somewhere earlier and quieter, and that earlier point is where the word flee belongs (cf. Gen. 39:12; 2 Tim. 2:22; Prov. 4:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit?”

Paul said something very like this three chapters ago — but there the pronouns were plural and the temple was the congregation (3:16). Here they are singular. The church together is God’s temple, and so is the individual believer’s physical body. Both are true, and the second is the one this chapter needs.

Consider what that meant in a city like Corinth, where temples were everywhere and everyone knew how they worked. A temple was not merely a religious building; it was the place a god was held to reside, and its holiness followed entirely from that residence. Nothing about the stone was special. What made a temple a temple was the occupant.

So the argument is not that your body is impressive, or attractive, or in good order. It is that Someone lives there. And the Someone is named: the Holy Spirit, “whom you have from God” — a gift, not an achievement, and therefore not something the reader can claim to be too unworthy to have received.

“You are not your own.”

Four words that cut directly across the deepest assumption most people hold about themselves, then and now. My body, my life, my business. Paul denies it flatly. And it is worth being honest that this is not a comfortable sentence; it is a claim of ownership over the one thing every human being reserves.

But look at how he grounds it, because the ground changes everything: “for you were bought with a price”. The verb is agorazō — the marketplace word, the word for purchasing a slave. Somebody paid, and the payment transferred ownership.

Paul does not name the sum here. He does not need to; this letter has been circling it since chapter one. The price was the cross — not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18–19). And that is the answer to anyone who hears “you are not your own” as a threat to their freedom. You are owned by someone who bought you at his own cost, having assessed you accurately, and who has never once complained about the price.

Which turns the sentence into the most reassuring in the chapter rather than the most confining. If you are not your own, then you are not finally at the mercy of your own failures, your own assessment of yourself, or your own capacity to hold on. The body you have treated badly, the self you are ashamed of, the life you suspect you have wasted — none of it is yours to write off, because none of it is yours.

“So glorify God in your body.” And notice that the chapter ends on a positive command rather than a prohibition. Paul has spent eight verses on what must be fled; he finishes with what the body is actually for.

Which is a wider commission than avoiding sin. Hands that work honestly, a tongue that tells the truth and blesses rather than reviles, a face that is glad to see people, feet that go where they are needed, arms that pick up a child, a body spent in service and eventually worn out in it — all of that is what this verse asks for, and none of it is possible for a man who thinks his body is either a machine or an embarrassment.

The temple in Jerusalem was destroyed, and the God who had filled it did not become homeless. He moved into people. Into a fractious congregation in a port city, and into the bodies of men who had been on the list in verse 9 — washed, sanctified, justified, and now inhabited. He looked at what could be bought in that market, and he paid the full price without haggling, and he moved in (cf. 1 Pet. 1:18–19; John 2:19–21; Rom. 12:1).

7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is Paul’s most extended treatment of marriage, and it has been misread in every generation. It is not an argument for celibacy as the spiritually superior state, nor a concession to physical weakness, nor an expression of sexual pessimism. It is a carefully calibrated pastoral response to a specific set of questions from the Corinthian church, shaped throughout by two governing convictions: the nearness of the end (“the present form of this world is passing away,” v. 31) and the principle that each person should remain in the calling in which they were called (v. 17, 20, 24).

Paul affirms marriage fully: the husband and wife have mutual obligations to one another; neither may withhold from the other except by mutual agreement for prayer; divorce is forbidden (with one exception). He also affirms celibacy as a genuine gift from God — not a higher state but a different calling that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord. The practical advice throughout is shaped by the eschatological pressure: given the compressed nature of this age, those already in a status (married, single, slave, free) should generally remain there, serving the Lord as they are, rather than treating a change of status as a spiritual upgrade.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens by responding to a Corinthian slogan: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” Some at Corinth, apparently influenced by an ascetic theology that treated the body as spiritually inferior, had concluded that even within marriage sexual relations were to be avoided. Paul corrects this without simply contradicting it: yes, celibacy is good — but precisely because sexual desire is real, marriage is the God-given context for its fulfilment, and within marriage, mutual obligation is the governing principle.

The language of “authority” in vv. 3–4 is strikingly mutual: the husband has authority over his wife’s body, and she over his. In a culture where the husband’s authority was assumed and the wife’s was unthinkable, Paul’s symmetry is remarkable. Neither partner owns their own body exclusively; each belongs to the other. The practical implication — do not deprive each other except by mutual consent for a limited time of prayer — takes seriously both the goodness of sexual life in marriage and the value of devoted prayer.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

Reformed theology has always resisted the Catholic elevation of celibacy above marriage as the spiritually superior state. Calvin read 1 Corinthians 7 as affirming both callings as genuine gifts of God, neither intrinsically superior. Luther’s own marriage was a theological act — a public demonstration that marriage is not a second-class spiritual status. Paul’s careful handling of both callings in vv. 7–9 supports this reading: celibacy is a charisma, a grace-gift, as is marriage. Neither is commanded; both are honoured.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics who were advocating celibacy within marriage may have been influenced by the same Gnostic-adjacent body-negativity that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6 — but in the opposite direction: if the body is spiritually inferior, why give it what it desires? Paul’s answer refuses both the libertine and the ascetic extremes. Now: The Christian tradition has tended to err in one direction or the other in every generation: either treating sexuality as a dangerous force to be suppressed, or (more recently) treating it as a sovereign identity that cannot be questioned. Paul’s account makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant obligation, eschatologically relativised.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote” — the whole shape of the chapter changes here. Until now Paul has been responding to reports that reached him from Chloe’s people. From this point he is answering a letter the Corinthians sent him, question by question, and the phrase now concerning will mark each new topic through the rest of the book.

Which matters immediately, because it means the sentence that follows is very probably their words, not his. The ESV puts it in quotation marks for that reason: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” This is the slogan of a party at Corinth — and Paul is about to spend forty verses qualifying it.

That is worth getting right, because the chapter has been badly misread for centuries by people who took the slogan as Paul’s own settled view. Read that way, this becomes the passage where the New Testament grudgingly concedes that marriage is permissible for those who cannot manage better — and a great deal of unhappy teaching about sex and the body has been built on it.

Paul does not say it. What he does is more interesting: he neither endorses the slogan nor dismisses it. He will agree that singleness has real advantages, and he will insist that the ascetics have no business imposing it. This is a church, remember, that had a party for whom the body did not matter because it was disposable (ch. 6), and evidently a party for whom the body did not matter because it should be denied. Both are the same error, and Paul is refusing both.

So his answer: “because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.” Blunt and unromantic, and it is often quoted as though Paul thought marriage existed only to manage lust.

He thought no such thing, and we should not read a specific answer as a complete doctrine. Paul knows perfectly well what marriage is; he wrote the passage about a husband loving his wife as Christ loved the church (Eph. 5:25–32), and he grounds it in Genesis 2 rather than in the management of desire. Here he is answering one question from one church with one particular problem, and the answer is pitched at the problem.

But it is worth noticing that the blunt answer is also a kind answer, and it is a mark of Scripture’s realism about people. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to aspire to a purity they will not sustain. He tells them, in effect: you are not made of iron, you live in Corinth, and God has provided for this. There is no shaming in it.

Which is a note to hold for the whole chapter, because it is unusually easy to read this material and come away feeling condemned — married readers feeling second-rate, single readers feeling deficient. Paul’s tone is not that. He is a pastor answering a real letter from real people about how to live, and the strongest thing in his answer is not a standard but a refusal to bind anyone’s conscience where God has not (cf. Gen. 2:18; 1 Tim. 4:1–5).

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.” The word behind “rights” is a debt word — what is owed. Paul is describing an obligation each spouse has to the other, not a claim each has on the other, and the difference is the whole verse.

Then verse 4, which is one of the most quietly revolutionary sentences in ancient literature: “the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

Read the two halves again and notice that they are exactly symmetrical. In the Greco-Roman world the first half was unremarkable — a wife’s body was understood to be at her husband’s disposal, and no one would have argued. The second half had no parallel anywhere. A husband’s body was his own; his liberties outside the marriage were assumed and largely unpoliced. Paul says his body belongs to his wife, in precisely the terms and with precisely the force that hers belongs to him.

That single word likewise did more to dignify women than any legislation of the period. And it means the passage cannot be read as a charter for a husband’s demands, because whatever it grants him it grants her in the same breath and the same sentence.

Which is where a guard is essential, because these verses have been used to do serious harm. They have been quoted to wives — usually by husbands, occasionally by pastors who should have known better — to argue that a woman has no right to refuse, that her consent is not required, that saying no is a sin. Some women reading this page will have had this text used against them in exactly that way.

It will not carry the weight. The whole framing is mutual: two people who have each given themselves away, each responsible for the other’s good. And the very next verse governs how this works in practice, and the governing phrase there is by agreement. Paul’s model is two people deciding together, not one person exercising a right over another. A man who uses verse 4 to override his wife’s no has taken a verse about mutual self-giving and used it as a lever — and he has quietly ignored the half of it that binds him.

The positive teaching is worth having plainly, because it is more searching than the arguments people have about it. Marriage in the New Testament involves a real handing-over of the self, and it works only when both are doing it. The obligation is to give, and neither spouse is anywhere given permission to take.

So the test here is directional, and it is answerable. In your marriage, are you chiefly aware of what you are owed or of what you owe? Paul frames the entire subject in terms of a debt you carry toward the other person, and a marriage in which both are thinking that way has almost no room left for the arguments this passage usually gets dragged into (cf. Eph. 5:21, 28–29; Phil. 2:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not deprive one another.” The verb is the one used for defrauding somebody — the same root Paul used two chapters earlier of the Corinthians cheating their brothers (6:8). To withhold yourself from your spouse is treated here as a species of theft.

That is strong, and it is worth sitting with, because withholding is one of the commonest instruments in an unhappy marriage and it is almost never named. It is deniable, requires no words, and can be maintained for years while both parties pretend nothing is happening. Paul calls it fraud.

Then the single exception, and it comes with three conditions, every one of which limits it: “except perhaps by agreement, for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer”.

By agreement — both, freely. This is the phrase that settles the argument raised at v. 4: Paul’s picture is never one spouse deciding for the other. For a limited time — with an end date, agreed in advance, not an indefinite drift. And for prayer — for a positive spiritual purpose, not as leverage, punishment, or the slow retreat that most such withdrawals actually are.

“But then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.” Paul assumes the resumption; the abstinence is a parenthesis in a normal life, not a higher state to be aspired to. And he names the danger without embarrassment: a marriage in which this has been allowed to lapse is a marriage with a door left open, and there is somebody who tries doors.

Notice that he does not say because of your sin. He says because of your lack of self-control — which is simply a statement about how human beings are made, offered without condemnation. Paul is being protective, not accusing.

And there is a pastoral word owed to two different readers here, because this verse lands very differently depending on where you are standing.

To the one who has been quietly withholding — sometimes for reasons that felt entirely justified, because of hurt, or exhaustion, or a long-running grievance that was never resolved — this verse is a summons to say so out loud. Not to comply resentfully, which is not what Paul is asking for anywhere in this passage, but to stop conducting the argument in silence and have it in words.

And to the one on the other side, who has been going without and has begun to feel foolish for minding: it is not foolish, and Scripture does not treat it as a trivial want. A whole verse of the Bible exists to say that this matters and that its absence is a danger to both of you.

But hold the guard from v. 4 alongside it, because this verse is not a lever either. It is addressed to both, it requires agreement, and the man who quotes it at his wife has misunderstood it as thoroughly as the woman who ignores it. The remedy Paul prescribes is not compliance. It is a conversation the two of you have been avoiding, and quite possibly a prayer you have never prayed together (cf. 1 Pet. 3:7; Eccl. 4:9–12).

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now as a concession, not a command, I say this.” Paul stops to mark the status of what he has just written, and the habit is worth noticing because he keeps it up all chapter. He will distinguish the Lord’s charge from his own judgment (vv. 10, 12, 25), and here he flags that the preceding advice is permission rather than obligation.

What is the concession? Most likely the temporary abstinence of v. 5 — that is allowed, not required. Some take it more broadly of the marriage counsel generally. Either way, the point is that Paul is being scrupulous about not binding consciences where God has not bound them, which is a discipline in short supply among religious teachers of every century.

“I wish that all were as I myself am.” Paul is single as he writes — whether never married or, as many think likely given his background as a Pharisee and a member of a council, a widower. He does not say. And he is honest that he considers his own state advantageous, for reasons he will give at length from v. 32.

But then the sentence that stops him from making his preference into a rule, and it is the most important thing in these two verses: “each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.”

The word is charisma — a grace-gift, the same word Paul will use of the gifts of the Spirit in chapter 12. Which means marriage is a gift and singleness is a gift. Not one gift and one deficiency; two gifts, differently distributed, both from God.

That single word settles more than most of what is said about this subject in churches. A married Christian is not the standard from which single Christians are a variation, and a single Christian is not someone waiting in a corridor for real life to begin. Both are described here as people who have been handed something.

And a word is owed to a reader who finds this cold comfort, because a great deal of clumsy teaching has been built on it. Single Christians are regularly told they must have “the gift of singleness” — and the phrase is then used to mean that they should therefore not mind, and that wanting marriage is a failure to accept their gift. Many people hear this and think: then I do not have it, because I mind very much.

Notice that Paul does not describe a gift of contentment with one’s state. He describes the state itself as the gift. The single Christian who longs to be married has not thereby forfeited or misidentified anything; he is simply a person in the condition God has him in, wanting something good that he does not have. That is not a spiritual failure. It is the ordinary experience of most people alive, married and unmarried both, about something.

So the useful question is not do I have the gift? — which is unanswerable and produces only anxiety. It is the one Paul will put in v. 17: what is the life the Lord has assigned me today, and what does faithfulness in it look like? That has an answer, and it is available this morning, whatever changes or does not change later (cf. Matt. 19:11–12; 1 Cor. 12:11).

verseByVerse.quote: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am.” Paul repeats his own preference, and again as counsel rather than command.

Then the sentence everyone remembers, and it is usually quoted with a certain amusement: “if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.”

The verb is pyrousthai — to be on fire. Some have taken it of the fire of judgment, but the sense here is almost certainly the ordinary one: consuming desire that will not leave a person alone. And Paul’s judgment is entirely unembarrassed. If desire is running your life, marry; that is what it is for, and there is no virtue in a heroic celibacy you cannot sustain.

Two things need saying about it, because the verse is regularly misused in both directions.

First, it is not a low view of marriage, though it is often read as one — as though Paul regarded it as a licensed outlet for people of weak character. He is answering a question, in a context, about people who are already struggling; and his answer is the pastoral one, not the complete one. The apostle who wrote this also wrote that marriage images the union of Christ and his church, which is the highest thing anybody has ever said about it.

Second, and more urgently: it is not a promise that marriage will solve the problem. A great deal of unhappiness has been caused by young Christians who read this verse as an instruction to marry quickly in order to have their desires resolved — and who then discover that marriage does not extinguish desire, does not guarantee a satisfying sexual life, and adds a second person with her own history, tiredness and struggles. Paul says marrying is better than burning. He does not say marrying will stop the fire.

And there is an honest word owed to the reader for whom this verse offers no route at all. Paul’s advice presupposes that marriage is available. For many it is not — through circumstance, or a lack of anyone to marry, or same-sex attraction, or a spouse who is present but with whom this part of life has ended through illness. Such a reader can find this verse almost mocking: the remedy is named and the door is shut.

Scripture does not pretend that is easy, and neither should we. What it does say is that no one has ever been promised the fulfilment of every legitimate desire in this life, that the Lord who requires this of some was himself a single man who knew the whole range of human temptation and was without sin (Heb. 4:15), and that his grace is repeatedly said to be sufficient precisely where the thorn is not removed (2 Cor. 12:9).

That is not a tidy answer and it is not meant to be. But it is a great deal better than the two things such readers are usually offered, which are a demand to feel differently and a promise God has not made (cf. Matt. 19:11–12; Isa. 56:3–5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns to a question about divorce, and carefully distinguishes between the Lord’s own command (vv. 10–11, where Jesus’s teaching in the Gospels forbids divorce) and his own apostolic judgment (vv. 12–16, which addresses a situation Jesus did not directly address: the “mixed” marriage between a believer and an unbeliever). The distinction is not between authoritative Scripture and fallible opinion; it is between two levels of apostolic teaching: the direct dominical command and the apostolic application to new situations.

The “Pauline privilege” of vv. 15–16 has been much discussed. If the unbelieving spouse chooses to leave, the believer is not bound — meaning, most naturally, that the believer is not obligated to pursue, beg, or hold on. The reason Paul gives is surprising: “God has called you to peace.” The Christian life is not characterised by endless conflict to maintain a marriage that the unbeliever has already abandoned. Paul is not opening a door to easy divorce but recognising that when an unbelieving spouse has departed, the believing spouse has not failed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s careful distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” vs. “I say, not the Lord”) is a fascinating window into apostolic hermeneutics. It does not mean that vv. 12–16 are less authoritative Scripture — Paul is writing under inspiration. It means that vv. 10–11 apply a dominical teaching directly, while vv. 12–16 extend the principle to a situation Jesus did not address. Both are authoritative; they are transparent about their different relationship to the dominical tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth had a high divorce rate by ancient standards; the city’s fluid social culture made marriage instability common. The question of what to do in a mixed marriage — especially if the unbeliever wanted out — was live and urgent for many in the community. Now: The “Pauline privilege” continues to be one of the most practically significant and debated passages in NT ethics, applied to situations ranging from desertion to abuse. The governing principle — God has called you to peace — is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord).” Paul is doing something specific: he is citing the recorded teaching of Jesus. The Lord had addressed this directly — whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her (Mark 10:11–12) — and where Paul has a word from Christ he says so and rests on it.

The charge itself is stated in two directions, and both are unusual for the period: “the wife should not separate from her husband… and the husband should not divorce his wife.” Under Roman law at Corinth a woman could initiate divorce, which she could not under Jewish law — so Paul addresses her first and directly, as a person with agency and responsibility.

Then the parenthesis, and it is the most practically important clause in the passage: “but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband”.

Notice what that concedes. Paul states the rule and then, in the same breath, deals realistically with its being broken. He does not pretend that a command settles what people will actually do. There will be separations; here is what to do when there has been one. And the door he leaves open is reconciliation — the situation is not treated as closed.

Now the larger question, since a reader will be asking it: does this forbid divorce absolutely?

Taken alone this passage says no exceptions. But it is not alone. The Lord himself, in Matthew’s record, adds one: except for sexual immorality (Matt. 19:9). And Paul is about to add another in v. 15, where a believer is deserted by an unbelieving spouse. So the historic Protestant position — that Scripture permits divorce on those two grounds and no others — is built from the whole of what is written rather than from any one text, and it is the reading this commentary follows.

What the passage will not support is the assumption most people actually operate on, which is that a marriage may be ended because it has failed — because the love has gone, or the parties have grown apart, or one of them is unhappy. Scripture never treats marriage as a contract that lapses when it stops delivering. Christ’s own reason is that God joined them, and what God has joined man must not separate (Mark 10:9).

And now the pastoral word, which matters more than the argument, because of who actually reads a page like this.

If you are divorced — and particularly if you look back and know that your own sin was part of why — understand what this passage is and is not doing. It is telling the church what marriage is. It is not a sentence passed on you, and it does not put you outside the reach of what this letter has already said: such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (6:11). That verse was written to people whose past included the things in the list, and it is not amended for the divorced.

There is no category of sin in the New Testament that is forgiven except this one. A divorce is not a permanent second-class standing before God, and any teaching that leaves a repentant believer with that impression has strayed from the gospel this same letter preaches. The command in v. 10 is for a marriage you are in. The mercy in 6:11 is for a life you have already lived (cf. Mark 10:2–12; Matt. 19:3–9).

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“To the rest I say (I, not the Lord).” The phrase alarms some readers, so it is worth being clear about what it does and does not mean.

It does not mean that this paragraph is less inspired, or that Paul is offering a private opinion the church may take or leave. Paul is drawing a distinction between two kinds of material: teaching where he can cite a saying of Jesus (v. 10), and teaching where he cannot, because the Lord did not address this particular case during his ministry. In the second kind he must apply the mind of Christ to a new question — and he does so as an apostle, closing this very chapter with the claim that he too has the Spirit of God (v. 40).

So the distinction is about the source of the teaching, not its authority. And its presence is a mark of Paul’s honesty: a lesser man would simply have asserted that the Lord had said it.

The case itself had no precedent because it could not have arisen in Galilee. In a city like Corinth people were converted out of pagan households, and very often one spouse believed and the other did not. What then? The believer is now joined for life to someone who does not share the thing that has become the centre of their life.

Paul’s answer is emphatic and it runs in one direction: stay. “If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her” — and then the identical instruction to the woman, in the same words, because the situation and the duty are symmetrical.

The condition is the only one: if she consents to live with him. The believer is not to initiate the ending. If the unbeliever is content to remain in the marriage, the marriage remains.

And the force of this is easy to miss unless you know what had happened before. There was an Old Testament precedent for exactly this situation, and it went the other way. When the returned exiles were found to have married foreign wives, Ezra had them put away — wives and children both — as an act of covenant faithfulness (Ezra 10). Any Jewish believer at Corinth would have known that story, and might reasonably have concluded that the holy thing to do was to end a marriage to a pagan.

Paul reverses it. Under the new covenant the direction of contamination has changed, and the next verse will say why. Holiness is no longer a fragile thing to be protected by separation; it is a stronger thing that spreads.

Which is a real word for a reader in that marriage now — and there are many, including some who became Christians after they married. The instruction is not to look for an exit, and not to treat the marriage as a mistake to be corrected. It is to stay, and to be the sort of husband or wife that the rest of the New Testament describes, and to leave the outcome where v. 16 will put it.

That is a hard assignment and it is not a hopeless one. Peter writes to precisely this reader and does not tell her to argue: they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives (1 Pet. 3:1–2). The marriage is not an obstacle to your discipleship. In God’s providence it may well be the field of it (cf. Ezra 10:1–3; 1 Pet. 3:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife… Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.”

This is the reason the believer is to stay, and it is a startling one. It is also widely misunderstood, so the first thing to establish is what it cannot mean.

It does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved. Paul settles that himself two verses later, where he wonders whether the believing partner may yet save their spouse (v. 16) — which would be an odd thing to wonder about someone already saved. Nobody is redeemed by marriage. Salvation is not transmitted by association, and every person stands before God on their own.

So what does “made holy” mean? The word is the ordinary one for sanctified — set apart. And Paul’s point is about the marriage and the household rather than the individual’s standing before God. The believing spouse was evidently worried that the union itself was defiling — that living with a pagan, sharing a bed and a table with someone outside the covenant, made the whole thing unclean and the children along with it.

Paul says the influence runs the other way. In the new covenant, holiness is not a delicate condition that contamination destroys; it is the stronger force in the room. The presence of one believer sets the household apart and puts it within the sphere of God’s covenant dealing. The marriage is a real marriage, honourable and undefiled. The children are not outsiders.

That reversal is worth pausing on, because it runs all through the Gospels. Under the old order, touching a leper made you unclean. When Jesus touched one, the leper was made clean (Mark 1:41). The direction of transfer changed when he arrived, and this verse is that same change applied to a mixed marriage in a Greek city.

A note on a long-running debate, since readers meet it here. The clause about the children being holy is used in discussions of infant baptism — taken by paedobaptists as evidence that the children of a believer stand within the covenant community, and answered by those who baptise believers only on the grounds that the same word is used of the unbelieving spouse, who is certainly not baptised on that basis. Both sides make a fair point; the verse is genuinely used by both, and it was not written to settle the question. Christians who love the same Lord differ here, and it should not become the thing this chapter is about.

What the verse is actually for is the comfort of an anxious believer, and that is how it should be preached.

If you are the only Christian in your house, you have almost certainly wondered whether your family is somehow outside — whether your children are at a disadvantage, whether your marriage is a compromise God tolerates rather than blesses, whether the whole arrangement is second-best.

Paul’s answer is that your household is set apart because you are in it. Your presence there is not a problem to be managed; it is the reason the place is holy. God has put one of his own in that house, and he did not do it by accident, and the direction of influence is not what you fear (cf. Mark 1:40–42; Rom. 11:16).

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.”

Paul has spent three verses telling the believer to stay. Now he deals with the case where staying is not in their power, and the tone changes entirely.

“Let it be so” — let them go. The believer is not to pursue, obstruct, or fight to hold a marriage the other person has ended. That is a hard permission, and it is a permission, not an instruction to give up easily; the whole preceding paragraph assumes the believer wants the marriage to continue.

Then the crucial clause: “the brother or sister is not enslaved” — ou dedoulōtai, not bound as a slave is bound.

What is the deserted believer freed from? At minimum, from the obligation to keep the marriage going — they are not under a duty to chase, or to remain in limbo indefinitely waiting.

But the historic Protestant reading has taken it further, and with good reason: the freedom includes freedom to remarry. The argument is straightforward. Paul uses a different word here from the one he uses of the binding of marriage in v. 39, where a wife is bound as long as her husband lives and is free to be married when he dies; and to say a deserted person is “not enslaved” while still holding them to a bond they cannot escape and did not break would be a strange kind of freedom. The Reformers read it this way, and it is what this commentary holds. Others read it more narrowly, and they are not to be dismissed — but the reading matters enormously to real people, and it should not be left vague.

“God has called you to peace.” This is the clause that governs the whole verse and it is easily hurried past.

It means that where reconciliation is genuinely impossible — where the other person has gone and will not come back — God is not requiring you to conduct a war, or to live permanently in an unresolved conflict, or to keep hold of something that is being pulled out of your hands. There is a kind of pious tenacity that looks like faithfulness and is actually a refusal to accept a loss God has permitted. Paul releases the deserted believer from it.

And a word to that reader, because this is one of the loneliest situations in church life. The person who has been left often carries a double burden: the desertion itself, and a persistent sense that a better Christian would have held the marriage together. They watch other people’s marriages, and they wonder what they failed to do.

Read the verse again. Paul does not ask what you might have done differently. He does not treat the departure as evidence about you. He addresses you as someone who has had something done to them, releases you from the obligation to fix what you did not break, and tells you that the God who called you called you to peace — which is precisely what you have been unable to feel, and precisely what he intends you to have (cf. Rom. 12:18; Matt. 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?”

The sentence can be read two ways, and both are grammatically possible. Commentators have divided over it for centuries, and it is worth setting out honestly because the pastoral force differs.

Read hopefully, it is an argument for staying, attached to vv. 12–14: who knows — you may be the means of your spouse’s salvation, so do not leave.

Read soberly, it is a comfort for letting go, attached to v. 15: how can you know that you will save them? You cannot — so do not hold a departing spouse hostage to a hope you have no way of guaranteeing.

The immediate context favours the second. Verse 15 has just released the deserted believer, and this verse gives the reason: you are not able to promise yourself the outcome that would justify clinging on. But the first reading is not wrong either, and Paul may well have intended both to be heard by the two different readers who would need them.

What is beyond dispute is the astonishing thing the verse takes for granted: that a Christian may be the human means by which their own husband or wife comes to Christ. Paul does not say it is likely. He says it is possible, and he says it in a way that assumes his readers have seen it happen.

And that possibility is worth holding carefully, because it can be turned into a burden it was never meant to be. The verse says how do you know? — which is a question, not a promise. It does not guarantee that a faithful wife will win her husband. Some do; some pray for forty years and bury a man who never came. To promise otherwise is to make the verse say what it explicitly refuses to say.

But it also forbids the opposite conclusion, which is the one most people in that situation eventually drift into: that it is settled, that he will never change, that after this many years there is no point. You do not know that either. The verse cuts against certainty in both directions, and leaves the outcome where it belongs.

So how does a believer live in that marriage? Not by campaigning. Peter’s instruction to precisely this reader is that a husband may be won without a word, by conduct (1 Pet. 3:1–2) — which is not a ban on ever speaking, but a warning that the sermon delivered over dinner for the fifteenth time is not the instrument God is most likely to use.

What is being asked of you is a long, unspectacular faithfulness in the same house: to be someone whose Christianity has visibly made them kinder, more patient, less easily provoked, more generous than they were before — and to keep asking God for the one thing you cannot do yourself.

You are not able to save your husband. Paul’s question makes that plain, and it is a mercy that he does, because it lifts off you a weight you were never given. Someone else saves people. Your part is to be in the house, and to ask (cf. 1 Pet. 3:1–2; 1 Cor. 3:6–7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The governing principle of the chapter appears three times like a refrain: remain in the calling in which you were called (vv. 17, 20, 24). Paul applies it to two examples — circumcision and slavery — to make a point that transcends both: a change of social or physical status is not a spiritual upgrade. The Corinthians appear to have been anxious about their pre-conversion status: the circumcised wondering if they should undo it; the uncircumcised wondering if they should be circumcised; slaves wondering if they should seek freedom. Paul’s counsel is essentially: the gospel does not require a change of external status; it transforms the meaning of the status you are in.

The application to slavery in vv. 21–23 is nuanced. Paul does not command slaves to remain enslaved as a theological principle — “if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity” (v. 21). But he does relativise the difference: the slave who belongs to Christ is the Lord’s freedman; the free person who belongs to Christ is Christ’s slave. The cross inverts and relativises every social category without immediately abolishing them. “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (v. 23) — the one who belongs to Christ in the ultimate sense is not defined by any lesser master.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Relativisation of Social Status by the Gospel

Paul’s refrain — remain as you are — is not social conservatism but theological prioritisation. The gospel relativises every earthly status by subjecting it to a higher identity: in Christ. This does not mean social structures are indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good), but that the gospel’s transformative work operates from the inside out, transforming the meaning of every condition before changing the condition itself. This is the seed from which the ultimate abolition of slavery grew in Christian history: not immediate political revolution but the recognition that the slave is Christ’s freedman, which eventually made the institution of slavery theologically intolerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. The question of whether conversion required a change of social status was real and practically urgent. Paul’s answer guards against two errors: treating social change as spiritually necessary (legalism applied to status), and treating social change as spiritually forbidden (quietism about injustice). Now: The principle “remain as you are” guards against the modern Christian anxiety that effectiveness for God requires a different job, a different social location, a different cultural context. You were placed where you are by Providence; bloom there.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.”

Here is the governing principle of the whole chapter, and Paul says he teaches it everywhere. Everything else — the married, the single, the widowed, the mixed marriage, the slave — is an application of this one sentence.

Notice the two verbs. The Lord has assigned; God has called. Your circumstances are not an accident you must escape before your real Christian life can begin. They are a distribution, made by someone, on purpose.

Which is why Paul reaches for the test case of circumcision, and it is a shrewd choice because it was the most emotionally loaded status marker in his world. A Jewish believer might feel his circumcision now embarrassing among Gentiles; there was even a surgical procedure to disguise it, undertaken by Jews who wanted to compete in the gymnasium without being marked out. A Gentile convert, on the other hand, might feel a second-class member of a faith with Jewish roots, and be tempted to acquire the mark. Paul says: stay as you are. The identity you brought with you is not the problem.

“For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.” It is a startling sentence from the man who fought the circumcision party to a standstill in Galatia. He is not contradicting himself. What he denies is that the mark carries any standing; what he affirms is that obedience does — not as the ground of acceptance, but as the substance of a life that has been accepted.

And the practical force of the principle is considerable, because most of us are quietly convinced that our circumstances are the obstacle. If I were married. If I were single. If I had the other job, the other health, the other family, the other church — then I could serve God properly.

Paul’s answer is that the life you are in is the life you were assigned, and that faithfulness in it is not a holding pattern until the real thing starts. There is no arrangement of circumstances in which obedience becomes easy, and no set in which it becomes impossible.

One guard, because this verse can be misheard as fatalism, and Paul will correct that himself in two verses. “Remain as you are” is not a prohibition on ever changing anything. He is about to tell a slave to take his freedom if he can get it (v. 21), and he has already told the burning single person to marry (v. 9). The principle is contentment, not paralysis. You may change your circumstances; what you may not do is treat your present circumstances as a reason to postpone obedience.

So the test is a simple substitution, and it is answerable today. Take the sentence you most often say to yourself about what is missing — when I have X, I will be able to Y. Then ask what obedience actually looks like this week, in the life you have, with the people who are already in it. That question has an answer, and the other one never has (cf. Phil. 4:11–12; 1 Tim. 6:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called.” The principle is restated, and then applied to the hardest case in that society.

“Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it.”

It is a jarring sentence to a modern ear, and it should not be softened prematurely. Perhaps a third of Corinth was enslaved, and the church contained many such people. Paul tells them not to let it trouble them — and he can say that only because of what he is about to say in the next verse about who they actually are.

But notice the parenthesis, because it changes the whole tone: “But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.”

The Greek here is genuinely elliptical — it says something like “rather use”, without stating what is to be used, and a minority of interpreters have taken it to mean rather make use of your condition as a slave. The ESV takes the majority reading, and rightly: take the freedom. Manumission was common in that world, and Paul tells a Christian slave who gets the chance to take it without hesitation.

So this is not quietism, and it is not indifference to injustice. Paul does not say slavery is good, or that a slave should refuse liberty out of piety. He says two things at once, and both are needed: your condition does not define you, and if you can be free, be free.

Which is the balance the whole passage is holding, and it is a difficult one to keep. Lose the first half and you get a Christianity in which nothing can be borne until it is fixed — in which a believer’s peace depends entirely on his circumstances improving. Lose the second and you get the far uglier thing that has actually happened in history: this text quoted by slaveholders to tell slaves that Christianity required them to stay put and be content. It required nothing of the kind, and the parenthesis in this verse is the refutation of it.

And it is worth being clear that the New Testament’s way with this institution was not endorsement but undermining. Paul lists slave-traders among the worst of sinners (1 Tim. 1:10). He sends a runaway back to his master with instructions to receive him “no longer as a bondservant but… as a beloved brother” (Philem. 16). And he tells masters in another letter that they have a Master in heaven who shows no partiality (Eph. 6:9). Those sentences, believed, dissolve the thing from within, and eventually did.

For the ordinary reader the transfer is straightforward, and it applies to any circumstance you did not choose and may not be able to change: the job you are stuck in, the illness, the family situation, the years that are not going the way you planned.

Paul’s counsel is neither resignation nor restlessness. Do not let it define you — and if a door opens, walk through it without guilt. Contentment is not the refusal of a better situation. It is the freedom to live well in this one while the door stays shut (cf. Philem. 15–16; Eph. 6:5–9).

verseByVerse.quote: For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul explains why a slave need not be consumed by his status, and the explanation is one of the great paradoxes of the New Testament.

“He who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ.”

Both halves are conversions of status, and they run in opposite directions. The slave in the congregation — who owns nothing, whose time is not his own, who may be sold next month — is a freedman: manumitted by Christ, and therefore in the only sense that finally matters a free man sitting in that room. And the free man beside him, the citizen with property and standing, has been bought and now belongs to somebody.

Which means that within the church the two most important social categories in Corinth had been not merely relativised but crossed over. Each man had received what the other had. There was, in the end, nothing left to rank.

Then: “You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men.”

Paul used that phrase one chapter earlier, of the body (6:20). Here he uses it of the self, and draws a different conclusion. Because you are owned by Christ, you must not let yourself be owned by anybody else.

And notice that this is addressed to people who were, in the plainest legal sense, already owned by other men. Paul is not talking about their legal position; he is talking about the interior one. A slave may belong to a master in Corinth and be, in his soul, a free man who serves Christ. A free citizen may be legally answerable to nobody and be entirely enslaved — to opinion, to advancement, to the fear of what people will think.

Which is where this reaches most readers, because almost nobody reading it is legally owned and almost everybody is servile about something. The commonest form is the one Paul names elsewhere as its own snare: the fear of man (Prov. 29:25). It is the settled habit of arranging your life around other people’s approval — saying the thing that will land well, softening a conviction because of who is listening, taking on more than you should because you cannot bear to disappoint, measuring yourself daily by an audience whose opinion you did not choose and cannot control.

That is what Paul forbids, and he forbids it on the ground of ownership rather than of self-respect. The argument is not you are worth more than that. It is you are not for sale, because you have already been bought.

So the test is one you can run on your week. Find the point at which you were not honest, or not obedient, or not generous, because of what somebody would think. Then ask who your master was at that moment. The name will be a person, or a group, or a version of your reputation you are maintaining — and the verse’s reply is that whoever it was, they did not pay for you.

Somebody else did, at a price named at the end of chapter six, and having paid it he set a slave free and made a free man his own, and in his church the two of them sit down together and neither can any longer say what he used to be (cf. Gal. 1:10; Prov. 29:25; Rom. 6:17–18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul extends his principles to the specific cases of betrothed virgins and widows, but the thread running through the entire section is the eschatological urgency introduced in v. 26: “in view of the present distress.” Whether this refers to a specific local crisis (famine, persecution) or to the general eschatological pressure of the “last times” is debated; either way, Paul’s counsel is shaped by the sense that the present order is passing (v. 31) and that undivided devotion to the Lord is a genuine good.

The famous “as if not” passage of vv. 29–31 is not a call to emotional detachment or worldly withdrawal but an eschatological relativisation: those who mourn as if not mourning, those who rejoice as if not rejoicing, those who buy as if not possessing. The present is real but not ultimate; the world is passing away. This is not Stoic apathy but the freedom of a person who knows that the ultimate good is secured in Christ and therefore holds all penultimate goods with an open hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eschatological Relativisation and Christian Freedom

Paul’s “as if not” framework is one of the most pastorally liberating texts in the NT for the believer under pressure. It is not an ascetic refusal of the world’s goods but an insistence that no good and no loss in this age has the last word. Marriage, mourning, rejoicing, buying — all are real; none are final. The person who holds them “as if not” is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their ultimate security is not invested in any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress” — the compressed time between the first and second coming, with its attendant pressures. He is not issuing universal commands but pastorally calibrated counsel. Now: The eschatological urgency has not diminished — we are closer to the end than Paul’s Corinth was. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, is not less relevant but more.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now concerning the betrothed” — the marker again, and a new question from their letter.

“I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.” Paul is careful in exactly the way he was at v. 12, and the carefulness itself teaches something. There is a difference between what God has clearly commanded and the wise application of Christian principle to a situation Scripture does not directly address — and a teacher who blurs the two, presenting his own judgment with the authority of a command, is doing something Paul refuses to do even when he is confident.

“By the Lord’s mercy” is worth noticing too. Paul’s trustworthiness is not a quality he claims for himself; it is mercy received — from the Lord who found him on the Damascus road doing the opposite.

“I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.”

What distress? Paul does not say, and interpreters have suggested several things: a famine known to have affected Greece around this period; the pressure of hostility toward the young church; or, more broadly, the whole character of the age between Christ’s coming and his return, which the next paragraph will describe as short and passing.

The honest answer is that we cannot be certain, and it matters less than it seems, because Paul’s reasoning holds under any of them. He is not laying down a timeless rule that Christians should not marry. He is giving situational counsel — in view of a particular pressure — and the word he uses of it is one that elsewhere describes hardship and persecution.

Which is a useful thing to see, because it models something we are generally poor at: pastoral advice that is explicitly tied to circumstances and does not pretend to be universal. Paul is not saying marriage is inferior. He is saying that in a season of acute difficulty, adding the responsibilities and vulnerabilities of a family is a real consideration, and a Christian is free to weigh it.

And there is a quiet permission in this for anyone facing a decision Scripture does not settle. A great many of the choices that actually shape a life — whom to marry, whether to marry, which work, where to live, when to move — are not commanded either way. Christians often want them to be, and go looking for a verse or a sign that will remove the responsibility of choosing.

Paul’s example is more freeing than that. He weighs the circumstances, applies the principles, reaches a judgment, states it as a judgment, and leaves the other person free. That is what wisdom looks like when there is no command — and it is what Christian maturity is largely made of, since most of life is lived in exactly that territory (cf. Rom. 14:5; Phil. 1:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.” The principle of v. 17 applied once more: do not make a project of changing your situation.

Then, immediately, the qualification — and it is emphatic, because Paul knows exactly how his counsel is likely to be heard: “But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned.”

He says it twice, once for each party. This is a man who has just spent twenty-six verses commending singleness, and who is now anxious that nobody should conclude that marrying is a failure. He will not have his preference turned into a burden on anyone’s conscience.

That instinct runs through the whole chapter and it is worth naming, because it is rare. Paul holds a strong personal conviction, states it plainly, argues for it — and then repeatedly and deliberately protects the freedom of those who will decide differently. Very few teachers manage that. The usual pattern is to state a preference and then let the weight of one’s authority do the rest.

“Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.”

The word is thlipsis — pressure, affliction, the word used of persecution and hardship. And this is Paul being honest in a way that Christian teaching about marriage often is not.

Because marriage is regularly commended to young believers as the destination, the completion, the arrival — and the sermon usually stops at the wedding. Paul says plainly that it brings trouble. Not that it is a mistake; he has just said twice that it is no sin. But it doubles the number of people whose suffering you feel as your own. It introduces the possibility of losses you would not otherwise have been exposed to. Every married person eventually discovers that they have given hostages.

“I would spare you that” is affection, not disparagement. It is a pastor who has watched people carry things, wishing they did not have to.

And the honesty is a kindness in two directions. To the single reader, it removes the fantasy that marriage is where the difficulty ends — which is worth knowing, because that fantasy makes singleness far heavier than it needs to be, and makes marriages far more disappointing than they need to be.

To the married reader who is currently in the middle of the trouble — the illness, the strain, the years of difficulty with someone you cannot walk away from — it says that you have not discovered a defect in your marriage. Paul told you this would be part of it, in writing, in advance. What you are carrying is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is what he meant (cf. Prov. 18:22; 1 Cor. 7:35).

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The appointed time has grown very short.” The word is kairos — the decisive season rather than clock time — and the verb is a nautical one: sails furled, canvas taken in. The remaining stretch has been shortened.

Then five clauses in the same startling form. Let those who have wives live as though they had none; those who mourn as though not mourning; those who rejoice as though not rejoicing; those who buy as though they had no goods; those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it.

Taken flatly this would be monstrous, and it must not be taken flatly. Paul cannot mean neglect your wife — he has just spent five verses insisting that spouses owe each other everything they have, and elsewhere tells husbands to love as Christ loved the church. He cannot mean suppress your grief, when Scripture is full of lament and he himself writes of sorrow upon sorrow (Phil. 2:27). He cannot mean refuse to be glad, in a Bible that commands rejoicing more often than almost anything else.

What he is doing is relativising, not abolishing. The Greek idiom here sets everything under the shadow of the coming end, and the sense is: hold all of it in an open hand. Marry, grieve, celebrate, buy, work — and do not let any of it become the thing you are ultimately living for, because none of it is going to survive in its present form.

Which is exactly what the last clause says: “the present form of this world is passing away”. The word is schēma — shape, outward arrangement, the way things are currently configured. Not that the world is worthless or that matter is evil; the arrangement is temporary. What is passing is the shape, not the substance.

And the practical effect of believing that is not detachment but proportion. A man who holds his possessions loosely can still enjoy them; he simply does not panic when they go. A woman who holds her plans loosely can still make them; she is not destroyed when they change.

Notice, too, that Paul includes both the sorrows and the joys in his list, and that the inclusion of mourning is the tenderest thing in the paragraph. Grief is not exempted because grief is unimportant; it is included because grief, too, has a horizon. The thing you are mourning is real and the mourning is right, and it is not the last word about the person you have lost. There will be a morning when the arrangement in which that loss was possible has passed away.

So a test that fits in a sentence. Take the thing that currently has the most power to make or ruin your year — the outcome you are waiting for, the possession, the relationship, the plan. Ask what would remain of your life if it were removed tomorrow.

If the honest answer is nothing much, then that thing has moved from being a gift to being a foundation, and Paul’s five clauses are aimed precisely at it. The sails have been taken in. Everything on this ship is worth having and none of it is worth building on, because the port is close (cf. Ps. 39:4–6; Col. 3:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I want you to be free from anxieties.” That is Paul’s stated motive for everything he has been saying about singleness, and it should govern how the rest is heard. He is not trying to recruit ascetics. He is trying to spare people worry.

Then the argument itself, and it is refreshingly unspiritual. “The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife.”

Notice that Paul does not say the married man is anxious about sinful things. Pleasing your wife is not a worldly ambition in any pejorative sense; it is a Christian duty, and the same apostle commands it. “Worldly” here simply means belonging to this present arrangement — the ordinary, legitimate, time-consuming business of a shared life.

So the point is not that marriage is spiritually inferior. It is that marriage takes attention, and attention is finite. The single Christian has one set of claims on his time; the married Christian has two, and the second one is a person with her own needs, opinions, tiredness and hopes. That is not a defect in marriage. It is marriage.

And Paul’s observation is simply accurate, as any honest married Christian will confirm. There are decisions a single believer can take alone and quickly — where to live, how much to give away, what risk to run, how much time to spend in service — that a married one cannot take at all without agreement, and often cannot take.

Which is worth saying to both readers, because each tends to misread the other’s situation.

To the single reader, particularly one who did not choose it: this is Paul naming something real that you already possess, and it is not a consolation prize. You have a freedom of movement and attention that is genuinely useful to God, and a great deal of the church’s most demanding work has always been done by people who were free to do it. That does not remove the loneliness. But it means your situation is not merely an absence; there is something in your hands.

To the married reader: the division of interests is not a failure of devotion that you should be repenting of. The attention you give your wife or husband is not stolen from God. It is the form your obedience takes, and Paul is not calling you back from it.

What he is doing is asking you to be honest that the cost exists. Many married Christians drift for years without ever admitting that their capacity for other things has genuinely narrowed, and then feel a low-grade guilt about it that they never examine.

So the useful question for either reader is the same, and it is Paul’s own: where is my anxiety actually going this week? Not which state is better, which is unanswerable and not the question he is asking. Simply: what am I currently worried about, and does the list look like the life of somebody who belongs to Christ in the situation he has assigned me? (cf. Matt. 6:33; Luke 10:41–42).

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul completes the argument by applying it to women in the same terms, which is itself worth noticing — the unmarried woman is described as “anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit”, exactly parallel to the man. In a world that defined a woman almost entirely by her household, Paul assumes an unmarried Christian woman has her own devotion to the Lord, her own concerns, and her own spiritual vocation.

Then the sentence that governs the entire chapter and rescues it from every misuse it has suffered: “I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.”

The word behind “restraint” is vivid: brochos, a noose or a snare — the loop thrown over an animal to bring it under control. Paul is saying he has no intention of putting a rope round anybody’s neck.

That is the safeguard he has been building toward since v. 6, and it is what makes this chapter safe to read. Everything Paul has said about the advantages of singleness is offered as counsel for the reader’s benefit, not as a standard by which anyone is to be measured, and certainly not as a rule the church may impose.

Which is precisely what happened anyway, for centuries. The chapter was read as establishing celibacy as the higher path, marriage as the concession for the weak, and a two-tier Christianity with the unmarried at the top. Whole systems of spirituality were built on it. Paul wrote this sentence to prevent exactly that, and it was ignored.

And the same danger runs in the opposite direction now, which is why the verse still matters. In many churches the noose is thrown over the single. There are congregations in which an unmarried adult is treated as a problem to be solved, is asked with wearying regularity whether there is anyone, is quietly excluded from the real business of church life which is assumed to be families, and is made to feel that his or her life has not properly started. That is a restraint Paul forbids just as firmly, and it is far commoner among us than enforced celibacy.

“Undivided devotion to the Lord” is where the paragraph lands, and the phrase is the goal of the whole chapter. Not singleness. Not marriage. Devotion — and the word suggests waiting close by, attending on someone.

Which reframes the question every reader of this chapter has been asking. The right question was never which state is superior? Paul has refused that question repeatedly and in as many ways as he can find. The question is what undivided devotion looks like for the person you actually are, in the situation the Lord has assigned you.

For one reader that will mean a freedom of time and movement to be spent rather than hoarded. For another it will mean loving one person faithfully for forty years in a way nobody outside the house will ever see. Neither is the higher path. Both are the same devotion, and the God who assigned them is not comparing (cf. Luke 10:39; Ps. 27:4).

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These three verses are among the more obscure in the letter, and honesty requires saying so before anything else.

The difficulty is that the Greek does not make explicit who the parties are. Two readings have held the field. The older one takes it of a father and his unmarried daughter — a man deciding whether to give her in marriage, which in that culture was his decision to make. The other, which the ESV follows, takes it of a man and the woman he is engaged to — a couple deciding whether to proceed with the marriage or remain betrothed without consummating it.

The second reading fits the immediate context better, since Paul announced at v. 25 that he was turning to “the betrothed”, and it fits the language of strong passions more naturally. But the question is not finally settled, and a reader who meets a different rendering in another Bible is not meeting an error.

What is beyond doubt is the substance, and it is entirely consistent with everything Paul has said. There are two options; neither is a sin; one has practical advantages in the present circumstances; and the decision belongs to the people involved.

“If his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry — it is no sin.” Once more Paul removes the guilt from the decision before anyone can attach it. He has been doing this all chapter, and it is a striking pastoral instinct: every time he commends the harder path, he immediately protects those who will not take it.

“But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control… he will do well.” The conditions are worth reading closely, because they are all internal and all mark a free decision rather than a suppressed one. Firmly established — settled, not wavering. Under no necessity — not driven to it by pressure from anyone. Having his desire under control — genuinely able, not merely determined to try.

Which quietly rules out a great deal of what has passed for celibacy in the history of the church. Paul’s version is chosen freely, from a settled heart, by someone under no compulsion and not fighting a losing battle. Vows extracted from the young, or imposed by an institution, or undertaken as a spiritual achievement, meet none of his three conditions.

“So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage does even better.”

Both are commended, and it is important that both verbs are positive. Paul is not contrasting a good decision with a bad one, or even a good one with a neutral one. He is contrasting good with better — and the “better” is not moral superiority but the practical advantage he set out in vv. 32–35, in the circumstances he named in v. 26.

And there is something freeing in the whole shape of it for anyone facing a decision of this kind now. Scripture here does not tell you which to choose. It tells you that both roads are open, that neither is sin, that the practical considerations are real and worth weighing — and then it puts the decision in your hands and refuses to make you feel guilty about it either way (cf. Rom. 14:22–23; 1 Cor. 7:35).

verseByVerse.quote: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
