“A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives.” Paul restates the permanence of marriage in a single clause, and the verb is the binding word — the one he pointedly did not use of the deserted believer in v. 15.

“But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes.” Death ends the marriage. The widow is not still bound; she is free, and Paul says so without qualification or any suggestion that remarriage would be a lesser choice. He says the same thing in Romans, using marriage as an illustration precisely because the principle is so clear (Rom. 7:2–3).

That deserves saying plainly, because widows have often been made to feel otherwise — that remarrying would be a betrayal of the person they buried, or a failure of devotion. Scripture attaches no such shame to it. Paul elsewhere positively counsels younger widows to marry (1 Tim. 5:14).

Then the three words that carry the weight: “only in the Lord.”

The freedom is real and it has one boundary. She may marry whom she wishes, provided he belongs to Christ. It is stated almost in passing, as something Paul assumes his readers already accept, and it is the New Testament’s consistent position — the same principle behind the warning against being unequally yoked with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6:14).

And the reason is not snobbery about outsiders, which would sit very oddly in a letter that has just told believers to stay married to unbelievers and to accept dinner invitations from pagans. The reason is what marriage is. If it is a union of two whole persons at every level, then a marriage in which the deepest thing about one of them is not shared by the other is divided at the root — not impossible, not without love, but permanently unable to be what marriage is for.

Which is worth putting concretely, because this is one of the decisions on which young Christians most often reason badly. It means that the person you marry will be the one you cannot pray with about your child’s illness. It means every Sunday is negotiated. It means the thing that matters most to you is a subject you learn to leave alone, and that leaving it alone becomes a habit, and that habits of that kind do not stay confined to Sundays.

Notice too the difference between this verse and vv. 12–13, because they are often confused and the distinction is the whole point. If you are already married to an unbeliever — whether you married before conversion or after — Paul’s instruction is emphatically to stay, and God’s blessing is on that household (v. 14). What he addresses here is a decision still to be made. The first is a providence to be lived faithfully; the second is a choice, and the choice has a rule.

So this is one of the few places in the chapter where Paul does give a command rather than a judgment, and it is the more striking for the freedom that surrounds it. Whom you marry, when you marry, whether you marry — all left open, all yours, all no sin either way. One boundary, stated in three words, and it is the only one he draws (cf. 2 Cor. 6:14–15; Rom. 7:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is.” Paul gives his opinion one last time, and one last time he labels it as an opinion.

Note the word he chooses: happier — makariōtera, the comparative of the word behind the Beatitudes, blessed. Not holier. Not more useful. Not more pleasing to God. He thinks she will be more blessed, given the circumstances he described at v. 26 and the undivided attention he described at v. 35 — and he says so as a man who wants her happiness rather than as one imposing a standard.

Then the final sentence of the chapter, and it is gently disarming: “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

There is a touch of irony in it. The Corinthians were the great claimants of the Spirit — the party of spiritual people, confident of their insight, quick to assess their apostle and find him wanting. Paul, having just spent forty verses declining to bind anybody’s conscience, ends by remarking mildly that he too has the Spirit, thank you.

But it is not merely irony, and the sentence does real work. Paul has been careful all chapter to distinguish the Lord’s command from his own judgment (vv. 10, 12, 25, 40), and a reader might reasonably conclude that the judgment parts are simply Paul’s private view, take it or leave it. This last clause forbids that. His considered pastoral counsel is not less than Spirit-given wisdom. He is claiming, quietly, that the whole chapter is apostolic.

Which is a fair place to look back from, because the chapter is one of the most humane in the Bible and it is worth seeing what it has done.

It has told a church full of people at every stage of life — married, single, widowed, divorced, deserted, enslaved, engaged, married to unbelievers — that not one of them is in the wrong place. It has repeatedly refused to make one state superior to another. It has said “you have not sinned” to those who marry, “you are not enslaved” to those who were left, “you are holy” to those who feared their household was not, “do not be concerned” to those who owned nothing, and “I lay no restraint upon you” to everybody.

And behind all of it stands the single sentence at its centre: let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him (v. 17). Assigned. Called. Not left over, not settled for, not what remains after the plan failed.

The circumstances you are in this evening — the marriage that is hard work, the house that is quiet, the person you are still waiting for, the person you have buried — were distributed by someone who knows exactly what he is doing and who has never yet given anybody the wrong life. The Lord of this chapter did not marry, had nowhere to lay his head, was deserted by everyone he loved, and died single and childless at thirty-three. He is not asking anyone here to accept a smaller portion than he took himself (cf. Isa. 53:2–3; Heb. 4:15; 1 Cor. 7:17).

8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
Chapter 8 begins a three-chapter discussion of food offered to idols — one of the most practically complex ethical questions facing first-century Christians in a pagan city. Meat sold in Corinthian markets had typically been offered to a god in the course of slaughter; temple festivals provided occasions for social meals at which the food served had been formally dedicated to a deity; invitations to dinner at a friend’s house might involve food similarly offered. For the Gentile Christian who had been converted from paganism, the question of whether eating such food was spiritually compromising — or whether it was an act of continued idolatry — was urgent and divisive.

Paul’s answer unfolds over three chapters and is more nuanced than either extreme: the “strong” (who know the idol is nothing and eat freely) are correct in their theology but wrong in their love; the “weak” (whose conscience is troubled by the association with idolatry) are incorrect in their theology but are being damaged by the strong’s exercise of freedom. The governing principle that Paul introduces in chapter 8 is the priority of love over knowledge: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (v. 1). Correct theology that ignores its effect on the weaker brother is not mature but immature — the immaturity of knowledge without love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens by granting the Corinthians’ theological premise: “we all possess knowledge.” They were right that an idol is nothing, that there is only one God, and that therefore the food offered to an idol has no spiritual contamination. Paul affirms the monotheism of vv. 4–6 wholeheartedly: “there is no God but one,” and the “gods many and lords many” of paganism have no genuine existence. The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is one of the most beautiful christological expansions of the Shema in the NT: the one God of Israel is now confessed as Father from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. The Lordship of Christ is inserted into the centre of Jewish monotheism as its fulfilment.

But — and here is Paul’s first move — knowledge of this kind inflates the one who possesses it. “Knowledge puffs up” (phusioi — the same word used for Corinthian pride throughout the letter). The “strong” in Corinth knew their theology; they also knew they were theologically superior to the weak. And that superiority — the smug confidence that comes from having got it right while others are still confused — is not a sign of spiritual maturity but a sign of having missed the point. “Love builds up” (oikodomei — the building metaphor of ch. 3): the measure of genuine spiritual maturity is not the correctness of your theology but the constructiveness of your love.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Christological Shema and the One Lordship

The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is a watershed in NT christology. Paul takes the foundational monotheistic confession of Israel — “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deut 6:4) — and distributes it between the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. God the Father receives the title “one God” with the phrase “from whom are all things and for whom we exist”; Jesus Christ receives the title “one Lord” with the phrase “through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” Both titles draw on the divine prerogative of creation. This is not bitheism or subordinationism; it is the Shema expanded to include the Son within the identity of the one God of Israel — which is exactly what Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically sophisticated — probably a mix of those with a Jewish background (who knew the idol was nothing) and educated Gentiles who had absorbed the Stoic critique of popular religion. Their knowledge was real. Their pride was realer. Now: The Reformed tradition is not immune to the Corinthian disease of knowledge-pride. The person who has worked through the doctrines of grace and arrived at the Reformation’s conclusions is in real danger of making theological correctness a platform for contempt of those still confused. Paul’s question applies: have you been known by God? (v. 3). That is the only knowledge that ultimately matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now concerning food offered to idols” — another question from their letter, and it needs setting in its world before the argument can be followed.

Most meat sold in a city like Corinth had passed through a temple. Animals were sacrificed, a portion was burned, the priests took their share, and the rest went to the market or was served at banquets held in the temple dining rooms. Civic life, trade guilds, family celebrations and religious observance were not separate departments; a man who refused all such meat was withdrawing from a great deal of ordinary social existence.

So the question was live and it divided the church. And Paul opens not by answering it but by quoting the confident party’s slogan: “all of us possess knowledge.”

Then the sentence that governs the next three chapters: “This ‘knowledge’ puffs up, but love builds up.”

The two verbs are chosen with care and they are opposites in a particular way. Physioō is the inflation word Paul has used repeatedly of this church — something swollen with air, larger than its substance justifies. Oikodomeō is the building word from chapter three — laying one course on another until something stands.

Both make a thing bigger. Only one of them makes it stronger. Inflation is quick and impressive and there is nothing inside it; construction is slow and unglamorous and it holds weight. That is Paul’s judgment on knowledge held without love, and it is not a criticism of knowledge. He is about to affirm that the strong party’s theology is entirely correct.

“If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.” The trap here is exquisite and inescapable. The very confidence that you have understood a matter is itself the evidence that you have not understood it as you should — because knowing as one ought includes knowing what knowledge is for, and a man using his theology to feel superior has missed that entirely, however accurate his conclusions.

Which is a warning that lands with peculiar force on readers of a commentary like this one. There is a version of the Christian life that consists almost entirely of acquiring correct positions — on grace, on election, on baptism, on whatever the current dispute is — and then holding them against people who have not yet arrived. It can be sustained for decades. It feels like maturity, because information is accumulating. And it is precisely what Paul is describing.

The Reformed tradition is not exempt; if anything it is exposed, because its doctrines are genuinely clarifying and the clarity is genuinely enjoyable, and a man who has worked through them can very easily begin to regard other Christians as the not-yet-arrived. Paul’s verdict on that man is not that his doctrine is wrong. It is that he does not yet know as he ought.

So a test, and it is uncomfortably easy to run. Take the doctrinal position you hold most firmly and most enjoy holding. Then ask what it has actually built — not what it has settled in your own mind, but who has been strengthened by your holding it. Name a person.

If nobody comes to mind, the thing may still be true and you may still be right, and it has been inflating rather than building (cf. 1 Cor. 13:2; Rom. 14:19).

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.”

The sentence does not go where the grammar leads you to expect. Paul has been talking about knowledge; the natural completion is if anyone loves God, he knows God. Instead the direction reverses, and the subject changes. You were expecting a statement about your knowing. You get a statement about God’s.

It is one of the great turns in Paul, and he does it elsewhere too. Writing to the Galatians he begins the same way and corrects himself mid-sentence: “now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God” (Gal. 4:9). He evidently could not leave the first formulation standing.

And the reason is that it puts the weight in the right place. Knowledge that puffs up is knowledge of which I am the subject — my grasp, my understanding, my position, my achievement. The moment the sentence turns round, the whole basis of that inflation is removed. What is fundamental is not that I have understood God but that he has known me.

“Known” here carries the full Hebrew weight. It is not the possession of information about somebody; it is the language of relationship, of choosing, of intimate acquaintance. It is what God says to Jeremiah — before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jer. 1:5) — and what he says of Israel, you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Being known by God is being loved, chosen, and dealt with personally.

Which makes this one of the most comforting sentences in the letter, and it is aimed at a particular kind of reader.

Some Christians live with a low, persistent anxiety about the quality of their grasp of God. They read, and forget what they read. Their theology feels thin next to other people’s. They could not defend the faith if pressed, cannot follow the arguments, are not sure they have understood justification properly even after years. And somewhere underneath is the suspicion that their standing with God is proportional to how well they have got hold of him — and that their hold is not very good.

This verse addresses that directly and takes the whole question away. The security of your relationship with God has never rested on the firmness of your grip. It rests on his. You are known, and you were known before you knew anything, and nothing about the quality of your understanding alters it.

And notice the one condition Paul does attach, which is not knowledge at all: if anyone loves God. That is the mark he is looking for. Not the ability to articulate, not theological sophistication, not having arrived at the correct position on the disputed question of the day. Love.

Which is answerable by the plainest believer in the room and often is not answerable by the most learned one. And it is, at bottom, why the confident party at Corinth were in the wrong even while being right: they had a great deal of information about a God who knew them, and had not noticed that being known was the whole of it (cf. Gal. 4:9; Ps. 139:1–6; 2 Tim. 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul states the theology, and it is worth registering that he agrees with the strong party without reservation.

“An idol has no real existence” — another of their slogans, and he endorses it. The wooden thing in the temple is not a god. It represents nothing; there is nobody behind it; the meat that passed in front of it has not been altered in any way. “There is no God but one” — the bedrock of Israel’s faith, and now of the church’s.

Then a careful qualification: “although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth — as indeed there are many ‘gods’ and many ‘lords’…”

Paul is granting that these beings are real as objects of worship. The pantheon existed in the sense that people believed in it, temples were built for it, and lives were organised around it. Zeus had no existence; the worship of Zeus was one of the most powerful forces in that society. Both things are true at once.

But there is a tension here that a careful reader will notice, and it should not be smoothed over. Two chapters later Paul will say something that sounds like the opposite: what pagans sacrifice, “they offer to demons and not to God”, and he does not want them to be participants with demons (10:20).

So which is it — nothing, or demons?

Both, and the two statements answer different questions. Ontologically, the idol is nothing: no deity corresponds to it, and the food is not contaminated. But spiritually, idolatry is not therefore harmless, because a real enemy is happy to occupy the space a false god vacates. The image is empty; the worship is not. Which is why Paul can say in chapter eight that the meat is neutral and in chapter ten that attending the temple feast is participation in something evil. It was never the meat.

And that distinction has a great deal of modern use, because it is exactly how idolatry works now. Nobody reading this is tempted by a statue. But the things we organise our lives around — money, career, a child’s success, the good opinion of others, a political cause — are in themselves nothing whatever, and the devotion given to them is real, and it does real damage.

An idol is not a rival god. It is a good thing that has been asked to do a job only God can do, and it always fails, and the failing is what wrecks people. The money does not steady you. The career does not justify you. The child cannot bear the weight of being your reason for living. There was nothing there to bear it, exactly as Paul says.

Which is why Scripture’s mockery of idols is not merely polemic but pastoral. Isaiah’s carpenter cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner, and bows down to the other half asking it to save him (Isa. 44:14–17). It is comic, and the point of the comedy is compassion: a man is asking a piece of firewood to do for him what only God can do, and he will not be answered (cf. Ps. 115:4–8; Isa. 44:9–20).

verseByVerse.quote: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.”

This is one of the most remarkable sentences in the New Testament, and its force is invisible unless you know what Paul is quoting.

Every Jew recited the Shema twice daily: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deut. 6:4). It was the confession that separated Israel from every nation around her, the thing Jews had died rather than compromise. In Greek it contains two crucial words — theos, God, and kyrios, Lord, the standard rendering of the divine name YHWH.

Paul takes that sentence and opens it up. One God — the Father. One Lord — Jesus Christ. He has not added a second deity alongside the first; that would be the abandonment of monotheism, and he has just insisted in the previous verse that there is no God but one. He has put Jesus inside the confession, distributing its own words between Father and Son.

Nothing prepares you for a first-century Jew doing that. Whatever else Paul thought about Jesus of Nazareth, he thought the divine name belonged to him — and he thought it so naturally that he can say it in passing, in the middle of a discussion about meat, without pausing to defend it.

Then the prepositions, and they are not decoration. Of the Father: from whom are all things and for whom we exist — the source and the goal. Of Christ: through whom are all things and through whom we exist — the agent of creation and of our new existence. Creation is the exclusive prerogative of God in the Old Testament, and it is here assigned to Jesus without qualification.

Which is where this connects to the argument, because Paul is not making a doctrinal excursion. The strong party’s freedom rests on this: if all things are from the Father and through the Son, then a piece of meat cannot belong to anybody else. It was made by Christ. Passing it in front of a carved image does not transfer the title.

And that is worth carrying about, because it is a more cheerful doctrine of creation than most Christians actually hold. There is a strain of piety that treats the physical world as spiritually suspect — food, pleasure, beauty, the body — as though holiness consisted in wariness. Paul’s answer is that every good thing came through Christ and belongs to him, and that the enemy has never made anything and cannot own what he did not make.

So the last word here is not about meat. There is one God and he is a Father. There is one Lord and he is the carpenter from Nazareth, through whom the universe was made and through whom the people at Corinth were now alive — the same hands. The gods of that city had temples on every hill and had made nothing, not one blade of grass, and could not answer when spoken to. And the God who made all of it, and owns all of it, was known to that fractious little congregation by name, and had died for them (cf. Deut. 6:4; John 1:3; Col. 1:16–17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The strong have correct theology; but not everyone has this knowledge. Some Corinthians, whose prior devotion had been given to these gods, had not yet made the psychological and spiritual transition to full confidence in the idol’s nonentity. When they eat food offered to idols, they eat it “with consciousness of the idol” — their conscience is troubled, not by correct theological reasoning but by the association with their former religious life. And a conscience troubled in this way, when violated by eating, is a conscience defiled — the person is wounded, not strengthened.

Paul’s principle is clear: the freedom to eat is real, but it is not the supreme value. The weak brother for whom Christ died outweighs the freedom of the strong. “If food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble” (v. 13) — the voluntary limitation of genuine freedom out of love for the weaker brother is Paul’s model and the governing ethic of chapters 8–10. Freedom is real; love is the criterion for when and how to use it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The category of “weak brother” in Paul is not a permanent spiritual classification but a pastoral description of someone whose conscience is not yet formed to the level of theological maturity the gospel makes possible. The strong are not forbidden to exercise their freedom; they are required to consider the effect of their freedom on those still developing. This is not a silencing of the theologically mature but a school in cruciform love: the pattern of Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake became poor” (2 Cor 8:9), is the paradigm for the voluntary limitation of legitimate freedom in love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific situation — food offered to idols in a pagan temple context — is culturally remote for most Western Christians. But the principle is not: the more mature members of any community regularly face the question of how to use their freedom in ways that do not damage those who are less free. Now: The contemporary applications range from alcohol (where an alcoholic is in the room) to entertainment choices (where a recovering addict might be triggered) to musical styles in worship (where real spiritual associations exist for some). The principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“However, not all possess this knowledge.” The theology of vv. 4–6 is correct and Paul has just endorsed it. He now points out that correct theology is not evenly distributed, and that this fact is itself a pastoral reality the strong must reckon with.

“Some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.”

Notice the reason: former association. These are converts out of paganism, and not long out. For most of their lives that meat had been part of a religious act they participated in — the procession, the temple, the smell of it, the sense of being in the presence of a god. Their minds now accept that the idol is nothing. Their instincts have not caught up, and instincts formed over thirty years do not dissolve because a doctrine has been explained.

So when such a man eats, he does not experience it as neutral nutrition. He experiences it as going back — and something in him registers the act as a betrayal.

Which is where the doctrine of conscience needs stating plainly, because it is widely misunderstood.

The conscience is not infallible. It is the faculty that judges our actions against the standard we actually hold, and that standard can be badly formed, over-scrupulous, or simply mistaken — as it is here, since the food is genuinely harmless. Paul says so in the next breath: “food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.”

And yet — and this is the crucial point — a conscience that is wrong must still not be violated. The man who eats while believing it wrong is defiled, not because the food defiled him but because he has trained himself to act against his own conviction. What he has learned is that his conscience can be overruled when it is inconvenient, and that lesson does not stay confined to meat. A man who has taught himself to proceed against his conscience once will do it again, in a matter where the conscience was right.

So the way to deal with a mistaken conscience is not to override it but to instruct it. It is educated by Scripture, slowly, until conviction and truth line up — and until then it is to be respected even in its error.

Which yields a practical rule with wide application. There are Christians who cannot do things that other Christians do freely — a drink, a film, a Sunday activity, a form of music — not because Scripture forbids it but because their history makes it impossible for them. The mature response is neither to mock the scruple nor to pretend it is a command of God. It is to recognise that a real person is carrying a real formation, and to be gentle with it.

And the honest personal question is worth asking too: is there something you have talked yourself into doing while a small voice was still objecting? Paul’s concern in this passage is not chiefly the act. It is what happens to a man who learns to proceed anyway (cf. Rom. 14:22–23; 1 Tim. 1:5, 19).

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.”

The word is exousia — authority, liberty, a genuine entitlement. Paul concedes it is theirs. He has spent five verses establishing that they are correct, and he does not now take it back. What he questions is not whether they may, but what happens when they do.

“Stumbling block” is proskomma — something in the path that trips a man who did not see it. And the image is exact, because nobody sets out to trip anyone. The strong Corinthian is not trying to damage his weaker brother; he is simply exercising a liberty in front of him without thinking about the effect.

Then the scenario, and it is specific: “if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple…”

This is not the marketplace and it is not a private dinner — both of which Paul will permit in chapter ten. It is the temple dining room, the most public and most religiously loaded venue available. The strong believer is sitting there, entirely convinced that the god is nothing, enjoying his freedom and quite possibly enjoying the demonstration of it.

And the weak brother walks past and sees him.

“Will he not be encouraged… to eat food offered to idols?” The verb is literally built up — the same word Paul used in verse 1 for what love does, now used with bitter irony. The weak man is indeed built up: emboldened to do a thing his conscience still condemns, on the strength of another Christian’s example. He has been constructed into a wall that will fall on him.

Which identifies the mechanism precisely, and it is worth naming because it operates everywhere. The damage is not done by argument. Nobody persuaded the weak brother of anything. He simply watched somebody he respected doing it, and concluded it must be all right, and did it against his own conviction.

That is how influence actually works, and it means every Christian is teaching all the time, whether or not they intend to. The younger believer in your church is not principally learning from what you say about holiness. He is learning from what he watches you do with your evenings, your money, your speech when you are annoyed, and your freedom.

So the question this passage puts is not am I entitled to do this? The strong were entitled and Paul says so twice. The question is who is watching, and what will they conclude?

And notice that it cannot be answered in the abstract, which is why Paul gives no list. The same action is fine in one setting and destructive in another, and the only way to tell is to know the people you are among — which is to say that love here requires attention. The strong Corinthian’s failure was not chiefly theological. He had not looked round the room (cf. Rom. 14:13–15, 21).

verseByVerse.quote: And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.”

The word is apollytai — the ruin word, the one used of perishing. Paul is not describing embarrassment or a setback. He is describing a man being wrecked.

The mechanism was set out in the previous verse: the weak believer, emboldened by watching a stronger one, acts against his conscience; and having done it once he does it again; and the habit of overriding conviction spreads to matters where the conviction was right; and a man who has learned that his conscience may be silenced when it is inconvenient is on a road that leads somewhere. That is how people are destroyed — not usually by a decision, but by a series of small permissions.

Then the phrase that ends the argument: “the brother for whom Christ died”.

Set the two things side by side, which is exactly what Paul is doing. On one side, a man’s liberty to eat a particular piece of meat — genuine, defensible, correct. On the other, a person so valuable that the Son of God went to a cross for him.

The strong Corinthian had never framed it that way. He was thinking about a principle, and he was right about the principle. He was not thinking about a person, and the person had a price attached that made the principle look very small.

Which is the permanent use of this verse, and it applies well beyond food. Whenever a Christian is about to insist on being right at another believer’s expense — in an argument, in a church meeting, in a family — this sentence is the corrective. Not are you right?, but: what did the person you are about to run over cost him?

“Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.”

And there is the last step, which the Corinthians would not have anticipated at all. The offence does not terminate on the brother. It travels.

Paul has said this before in the letter — believers are members of Christ, limbs of his body (6:15) — and the logic follows: you cannot damage a limb without the head registering it. It is the same thing the risen Christ said to Saul of Tarsus on the Damascus road, and Saul never got over it. He had never touched Jesus of Nazareth. He had been arresting Christians in Damascus, and the voice said: why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

The man who wrote this verse had been on the wrong side of that sentence, and it is quite possibly why he puts it so strongly here.

So the sobering conclusion is that there is no such thing as a private injury within the church. The sharp remark, the cold shoulder maintained for two years, the person you have quietly written off — none of it stops with them. Christ counts what is done to his people as done to himself, which is a terrifying thought for the offender and an immeasurably comforting one for anyone who has been on the receiving end (cf. Acts 9:4; Matt. 25:40, 45; Rom. 14:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.”

Paul does not conclude with a policy. He concludes with himself, and with a statement so absolute that it settles the matter by example rather than by rule. Not I will be careful. Not I will use discretion. Never — and the Greek construction is as emphatic as the English, reaching to the end of the age.

Notice too that he has moved from the second person to the first. He has spent twelve verses telling the strong what they should consider; he ends by telling them what he himself will do. It is much harder to resent a man who has already gone further than he is asking you to go.

And it costs him something real. Meat was not an everyday item for most people, but for the man who could afford it, giving it up permanently was a genuine loss — and Paul volunteers it without hesitation, for the sake of one weaker Christian whose name he does not even know.

Now a guard is needed, because this verse can be turned into an instrument of exactly the opposite kind, and frequently has been.

Read carelessly, it puts the most easily-offended person in any congregation in complete control. If anyone’s disapproval obliges everyone else to stop, then the church is governed by whoever is prepared to be upset — and every genuine liberty can be shut down by someone announcing that they find it a stumbling block.

That is not what Paul is describing, and the difference is in the passage. His “weak brother” is not someone who disapproves; he is someone in danger of being led into sin against his own conscience and destroyed by it (vv. 10–11). Being scandalised is not the same as being tripped. A man who says I disapprove of what you are doing is making a criticism; a man who is about to act against his own convictions because of your example is in danger, and only the second is in view here.

Nor does Paul suggest the weak should stay weak. The whole letter is aimed at growing people up, and Romans 14 — the fullest treatment of the same question — puts obligations on both sides: the strong must not despise the weak, and the weak must not pass judgment on the strong (Rom. 14:3). Neither is given the whip hand.

What is left, when both errors are excluded, is something harder than a rule and better: a willingness to lose a genuine right for the sake of a particular person, decided case by case, by people who are paying attention to each other.

And the pattern is not Paul’s invention. He is doing in miniature what his Lord did entirely. One who had every right — to glory, to be served, to be spared — did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). The strong at Corinth were asked to give up beef for a brother. He gave up heaven for enemies, and never once mentioned his rights (cf. Rom. 14:13–21; Phil. 2:4–8).

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.<sup>2</sup>If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.<sup>3</sup>But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.<sup>4</sup>Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.”<sup>5</sup>For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—<sup>6</sup>yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.<sup>7</sup>However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.<sup>8</sup>Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.<sup>9</sup>But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.<sup>10</sup>For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?<sup>11</sup>And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.<sup>12</sup>Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is Paul’s longest and most personal argument for the principle he stated in chapter 8: voluntary limitation of genuine freedom out of love for others. He uses himself as the exhibit. He has apostolic rights — the right to be supported financially by the churches he serves, the right to travel with a believing wife, the right to be exempt from manual labour. These rights are real; Paul defends them at length from Scripture, common sense, and analogy. And then he announces that he has used none of them. He preaches the gospel free of charge, works with his own hands, and makes himself a slave to everyone in order to win as many as possible.

The chapter is therefore both the longest example in the letter of the principle of self-limitation in love and a defence of Paul’s ministry against those at Corinth who questioned his apostleship on the grounds that he did not accept financial support. The two are connected: the very thing they criticise him for — refusing payment — is the thing that demonstrates the principle he is asking them to follow. He is not asking them to do something he is unwilling to do himself. The chapter ends with the image of the athlete: the runner who submits to severe self-discipline in order to win the race. The Christian life is not passive; it requires the kind of focused, costly self-discipline that any serious competitor knows.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul establishes his apostolic credentials and defends his rights with a series of arguments: analogy (soldiers, farmers, shepherds all receive the fruit of their work), Scripture (the ox treading grain must not be muzzled — Deut 25:4), common sense (the one who ploughs should plough in hope), and the Lord’s own command (those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel, v. 14). By the time he has finished, the right of the apostle to financial support is as well-established as any right in the letter.

The purpose of this lengthy defence is not to claim the right but to set up its voluntary surrender. Paul builds the case meticulously so that when he says “I have made no use of any of these rights” (v. 15), the reader understands what has been surrendered. The magnitude of the renunciation corresponds to the length of the defence. This is not Paul being merely practical (I prefer to earn my own income); it is a deliberately chosen posture of love that refuses to let anything — even a legitimate financial right — become an obstacle to the gospel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Right of Ministers to Financial Support

Paul’s argument from Deuteronomy 25:4 (“Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain”) follows a characteristic pattern in his hermeneutics: the OT command for the benefit of animals carries an “how much more” application to human ministers of the gospel. The principle that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7, quoted by Paul in 1 Tim 5:18) is embedded in the creation order and confirmed by the Lord’s own command. The Reformed tradition has always insisted on adequate financial support for ordained ministry as a matter of justice, not charity — grounded precisely in passages like this.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The travelling sophist in Corinth charged fees for his teaching; the apostle who did not was, paradoxically, suspected of being less legitimate — not worth paying. Paul’s refusal to accept payment actually undermined his status in the eyes of some Corinthians, which is why he defends the right even while refusing to exercise it. Now: The principle cuts in two directions: congregations should support their ministers generously; ministers should never let financial considerations drive their preaching agenda. The apostle who can preach without anxiety about whether his congregation will like what they hear is the freest preacher in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. This is my defense to those who would examine me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four rapid questions, each asserting a fundamental truth. Freedom — he is a free person, not obligated to anyone. Apostleship — he carries the commission of the risen Christ. Seeing the Lord — the basis of his apostolic claim is the Damascus road appearance, as real and defining as the appearances to the Twelve. And the Corinthians themselves — “the seal of my apostleship.” If any evidence were needed that Paul’s ministry was authentic, the very existence of the Corinthian church — converted through his preaching — provides it. The people questioning his credentials were themselves his credentials.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
verseByVerse.commentary: Three analogies from daily life — soldier, farmer, shepherd — all making the same point: in every sphere of human work, the worker has a right to benefit from his labour. The reference to Peter (“Cephas”) travelling with his wife implies that the married apostle’s wife was supported by the churches — a standard arrangement that Paul and Barnabas, who supported themselves by manual labour, did not use. Paul is not criticising Peter; he is pointing out that Peter’s accepted practice (financial support, travelling wife) was the norm from which he and Barnabas were the exception.

verseByVerse.quote: Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop. If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul’s hermeneutical aside — “Is it for oxen that God is concerned?” — is not a dismissal of animal welfare but a recognition that Torah instructions often have a typological or analogical reach beyond their immediate application. The law about the ox is simultaneously a law about human labourers: those who work should share in the fruit of their work. Paul then applies this “how much more”: if material work deserves material reward, surely spiritual work (sowing spiritual things) deserves material support. And then the turn: “nevertheless, we have not made use of this right.” The argument for the right makes the voluntary surrender of it more striking.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final argument appeals to the temple service (Num 18:8–20; Deut 18:1–8) and to the Lord’s own command — most likely the teaching of Luke 10:7 (“the labourer deserves his wages”). The principle is embedded in God’s own ordering of both old covenant worship and new covenant ministry: those who serve the community of God’s people in spiritual work deserve material support from those they serve. This is not optional generosity but covenantal justice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Becoming All Things to All People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his rights at length, Paul now announces he has used none of them — and explains why with a passion that comes close to breathlessness. His reason for refusing support is not humility or legal caution; it is his “reward” — the joy of offering the gospel free of charge, the glory of making the good news cost the listener nothing by absorbing the cost himself. He preaches under compulsion (v. 16: “woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!”) but he has made the free offering of it his personal commission within that compulsion.

The famous passage on becoming all things to all people (vv. 19–23) is not a counsel of spinelessness or strategic dishonesty. Paul is describing a principle of missional identification: the willingness to enter the world of the person you are trying to reach, to adopt their framework, speak their language, meet them where they are. To the Jew he becomes as a Jew; to those under the law, as under the law; to those outside the law, as outside the law; to the weak, as weak. The flexibility is real and costly; the gospel content is never negotiated. The goal is always the same: win some.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missional Identification and the Integrity of the Gospel

Paul’s “all things to all people” has been both one of the most misused and most important principles in Christian mission. Misused, it becomes a pretext for theological drift — adjusting the content of the gospel to make it more acceptable. Properly understood, it describes the willingness to adjust the container — cultural form, communicative register, social entry point — while keeping the content constant. Keller’s ministry in Manhattan was an extended application of this principle: enter the cultural world of the highly educated secular professional, learn to speak their language, earn the right to challenge their assumptions — and preach the same crucified Christ that Paul preached in Corinth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s concrete examples — becoming as a Jew, as under the law, as outside the law, as weak — map onto the social divisions within his own missionary world. He was not fixed in one cultural mode but radically adaptable in form while immovable in content. The Damascus road encounter made him a prisoner of the message; everything else was negotiable. Now: Contextualisation is the ongoing challenge of every missionary enterprise. The line between appropriate adaptation and compromising capitulation is real and requires constant discernment; but the failure to contextualise — treating one’s own cultural form of Christianity as the gospel itself — is at least as dangerous as over-adaptation.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
verseByVerse.commentary: “I would rather die” — the intensity is not rhetorical; Paul is describing something he has genuinely chosen to protect. His “boasting” here is not pride but the deep joy of offering the gospel without charge — the satisfaction of a sacrifice freely made. “Necessity is laid upon me” — anankē, compulsion: the preaching is not optional, not something Paul chose as a career. It was chosen for him by the one who arrested him on the Damascus road. But within the compulsion, the free offering is Paul’s own contribution — his gift to the gospel. “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel” is one of the most urgent self-descriptions in the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The paradox is subtle: Paul preaches under compulsion (not of his own will) — so the preaching itself earns no credit. But within the compulsion he has chosen to offer it free of charge — and that choice is his reward. The reward is not payment but the joy of the freely given sacrifice. This is a deeply revealing window into Paul’s interior life: he is not a mercenary preacher working for pay, nor a resentful conscript resenting his orders. He is a man who has found within the necessity that was imposed on him a freedom that he exercises with joy — the freedom of sacrificial love.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews... To those outside the law I became as one outside the law... To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
verseByVerse.commentary: The pattern is consistent: free from obligation to all, Paul voluntarily enslaved himself to all — the same logic as Christ who, though in the form of God, took the form of a servant (Phil 2:6–7). Each adaptation is a form of self-giving: entering the world of the other, surrendering the comfort of one’s own cultural vantage point, becoming vulnerable to the other’s concerns. “That I might win” — the verb kerdēsō (win, gain) echoes the financial metaphor: Paul is an investor in souls, gladly spending himself to gain others for Christ. “By all means...save some” — the universal aspiration tempered by a realistic acknowledgement that not all will respond.

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Share with them in its blessings” — Paul is not merely a dispenser of the gospel but a co-beneficiary. He runs the same race he is inviting others to run; he aims for the same crown he calls others to seek; the blessings of the gospel are as much for him as for those he wins. This prevents the apostolic ministry from becoming a professional transaction: Paul is not delivering a product he does not personally consume. He is living inside the gospel he preaches, which is what makes the preaching credible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with the athletic metaphor that grounds the principle of self-discipline in the logic of purposeful effort. The Isthmian Games, held near Corinth every two years, were the second-most prestigious games in the ancient world; the image of the runner and the boxer would have been immediately vivid to the Corinthian reader. Paul uses the image to describe the kind of disciplined self-denial that purposeful Christian living requires — not the harsh asceticism of the body-hating Gnostic but the focused self-management of the athlete who wants to win.

The force of the passage is partly eschatological: the athlete’s crown is perishable (a wreath of celery or laurel that wilted within days); the Christian’s crown is imperishable. And partly it is deeply personal: “I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (v. 27). Paul is not claiming security in his own self-discipline; he is claiming that genuine discipleship requires disciplined effort. The apostle who preaches freedom is also the apostle who runs hard, boxes purposefully, and keeps his body under control — because the prize is real, and the possibility of disqualification is real.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and Effort: The Perseverance of the Saints

The warning of v. 27 — “lest I myself should be disqualified” — has been debated in relation to the doctrine of perseverance. Reformed theology does not take this as a threat to genuine believers’ final security but as the description of the means by which that security is maintained: the God who sovereignly keeps his people does so through their own disciplined effort, not instead of it. The warning is the mechanism of perseverance: those who are genuinely elect will take the warning seriously, run hard, and thereby demonstrate and maintain their calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the Isthmian Games and would have immediately understood the competitive imagery. Paul makes the comparison in order to shame them slightly: the athletes prepare with greater earnestness for a temporary prize than the Corinthians apply to an eternal one. Now: The contemporary church has, in many quarters, lost the language of spiritual discipline entirely — afraid that any emphasis on effort sounds like works-righteousness. Paul’s athletic imagery corrects this: grace produces effort; the free gift of the gospel generates the runner’s willingness to run hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Run that you may obtain it” — the imperative is urgent and purposeful: not casual jogging but the focused effort of a competitor who intends to win. “Exercises self-control in all things” — the Greek athlete’s training regimen was famously rigorous: ten months of strict diet, abstinence, and punishing physical preparation. And all of this for a crown of celery that would wilt before the week was out. How much more, Paul implies, should the Christian’s self-discipline be motivated by the eternal prize that will not fade.

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Not aimlessly” and “not beating the air” — the contrast is with purposeless effort: running without direction, shadowboxing without an opponent. Paul runs with a clear goal and hits with real punches. “I discipline my body” — hypōpiazō literally means “to give a black eye to”: vivid, physical, almost brutal. The body is not the enemy, but its appetites, if left undisciplined, become the enemy of the race. “Disqualified” (adokimos) — the same word as the “debased mind” of Romans 1:28: rejected, failed the test. Paul is sobered by the possibility of his own failure, and that sobriety produces effort.

10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Chapter 10 deploys Israel’s wilderness history as a theological warning against the Corinthian assumption that spiritual privilege guarantees spiritual safety. Israel had extraordinary covenant advantages — cloud, sea, spiritual food and drink, the presence of Christ — and they still fell. Four catastrophic failures are cited: idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, and grumbling. These are not ancient curiosities; they are “written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come” (v. 11). The Corinthians who were confident they could attend temple meals without danger were flattering themselves into disaster.

Paul then draws the sharpest line in the letter about idol worship: the cup of blessing and the bread of the Lord’s Supper are participations in the blood and body of Christ; the cup of demons and the table of demons are genuine spiritual participations in the demonic. You cannot be at the Lord’s table and the demons’ table simultaneously. The chapter closes with the most comprehensive positive principle in Paul’s ethics: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” Every act of ordinary life is capable of being an act of worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “for” that opens chapter 10 links back to Paul’s warning about disqualification in 9:27: the Corinthians need to take the possibility of spiritual failure seriously, and Israel’s wilderness history provides the case study. The parallel Paul draws is deliberate and pointed. Israel was baptised in the cloud and the sea — immersed in the presence and power of God. They ate supernatural food and drank supernatural drink — the manna and the water from the rock. And the rock that followed them, providing spiritual drink, was Christ himself (v. 4). This is not a typological embellishment; it is Paul’s claim that the pre-incarnate Son was the mediator of God’s sustaining grace in the wilderness.

Yet Israel fell. Despite their spiritual advantages, despite their sacramental participation, despite their proximity to the divine glory — they were struck down in the wilderness because of idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, and grumbling. Paul’s point to the Corinthians is precise: you have spiritual advantages too — baptism, the Lord’s Supper, the indwelling Spirit. These are not security guarantees. They are resources for running the race; they do not exempt anyone from the possibility of disqualification.

Verse 13 is one of the great pastoral promises in the NT: “No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” The promise is not that temptations will be light but that they will be manageable — that divine faithfulness will always supply a path through that the believer is genuinely capable of taking.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Existent Christ and the Typology of the Wilderness

Paul’s identification of the rock in the wilderness as Christ (v. 4) is a claim that the Son of God was the agent of God’s sustaining grace before the incarnation — the “Angel of the LORD” tradition of the OT now understood christologically. This is christological pre-existence applied to redemptive history: the same Christ who died on the cross was present and active in the wilderness, providing the spiritual sustenance that Israel squandered. Reformed typology has always read the OT this way: Christ is not absent from the old covenant; he is present as promise, type, and mediator.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were attending temple meals — eating idol food in an actual pagan temple — needed to hear that spiritual confidence is not the same as spiritual safety. Israel had more obvious privileges than any of them and still fell. Now: The sacramental Christian who trusts in regular communion and baptism as automatic guarantees of spiritual health — without the disciplined effort, the watchful sobriety, the dependency on God that Paul describes — is making exactly the Israelite mistake. The sacraments are genuine means of grace, not magic shields.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fivefold “all” is emphatic: every Israelite shared in these extraordinary privileges. None were excluded from the baptism into Moses, the spiritual food, the spiritual drink. The christological identification of the rock with Christ is bold and precise: the pre-incarnate Son was the mediating agent of God’s sustaining grace in the wilderness. The rabbis had a tradition that the rock of Exodus 17 followed Israel through the wilderness — Paul appropriates and radicalises this: the rock was not merely a miraculous physical object but the presence of Christ himself, providing the spiritual drink that sustained life.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things took place as examples for us, so that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Most of them” — of the 600,000 who left Egypt, only Caleb and Joshua entered the land. The staggering attrition rate is the whole point: spiritual privilege does not guarantee spiritual survival. “Examples” (typoi) — the events of the wilderness were typed, stamped, shaped so as to serve as patterns of warning for later generations. This is not allegory or fanciful interpretation; it is Paul’s understanding of how God has structured redemptive history: the wilderness generation is a mirror in which later generations are meant to see themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.” We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day. We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents, nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four specific wilderness failures, each directly relevant to Corinthian temptations. The idolatry of Exodus 32 (the golden calf, with its eating, drinking, and “playing”) maps onto the temple meals. The sexual immorality of Numbers 25 maps onto chapter 5’s crisis and the general sexual permissiveness of Corinthian culture. The testing of Christ in Numbers 21 maps onto the Corinthians’ questioning of apostolic authority. The grumbling of Numbers 14 and 16 maps onto the factionalism of chapters 1–4. The catalogue is not random; it is a precise typological diagnosis of the Corinthian community.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come. Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary: “On whom the end of the ages has come” — the Christian community stands at the fulfilment of the ages toward which Israel’s history was moving. This location in redemptive history makes the warnings more urgent, not less: we are closer to the judgment than Israel was, and the clarity of revelation we have received makes our accountability greater. “Let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” — the warning is aimed precisely at the self-confident: the strong who are sure their knowledge exempts them from danger, the spiritual who are certain their gifts secure them.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise is not immunity but proportionality: every temptation the Corinthians face is within the range of human experience (“common to man” — anthrōpinos, human-sized). And God is faithful — the same phrase that closed the thanksgiving of 1:9. His faithfulness means he will not allow the test to exceed what the tested person can bear, and will always provide a way through. The “way of escape” is not necessarily removal of the temptation but the provision of the capacity to endure it. Begg: “God is not guaranteeing a comfortable exit; he is guaranteeing a navigable path.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry” — the same verb used in 6:18 for sexual immorality: not engage, not manage, not negotiate. Flee. The reason Paul now gives is the most theologically serious argument in the three-chapter discussion of idol food. Eating at the Lord’s table is a genuine participation (koinōnia) in the blood and body of Christ. The cup of blessing is not merely a symbol; it is a sharing in Christ’s own death. And eating at a pagan temple feast is not merely a neutral social act: it is a participation in what the sacrifice is offered to — not to the idol (which is nothing) but to the demonic powers behind the idol.

The argument does not depend on the idol having genuine divine existence; it depends on the demonic powers having genuine existence. Paul believes in demons (cf. Eph 6:12; 1 Tim 4:1); he believes that pagan worship, whatever its conscious intent, operates in a sphere of spiritual reality that the strong Corinthians, with their confident monotheism, are underestimating. You cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — not because the idol is real but because the demons are real, and fellowship with them is incompatible with fellowship with Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Participation

Paul’s use of koinōnia in vv. 16–17 — the cup of blessing is a koinōnia in the blood of Christ; the bread is a koinōnia in the body of Christ — is the most precise language of eucharistic participation in the NT. It does not specify the mode of Christ’s presence, but it insists on its reality: something genuinely happens in the Supper that is a real sharing in what Christ accomplished. Reformed eucharistic theology (following Calvin rather than Zwingli) has insisted on this real spiritual presence: Christ is truly present in the Supper, giving himself to be received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Attending a civic dinner at a Corinthian temple was not optional for many members of the social elite; it was part of the patronage network on which their livelihood depended. Paul’s “flee idolatry” would have carried genuine social cost. Now: The situations where Christian participation in cultural or civic life involves implicit participation in what is spiritually incompatible are multiple and not always obvious. Paul’s principle — you cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — is the test: what are you actually participating in when you participate in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary: “My beloved” — a term of endearment that sharpens the authority of what follows: these are not the words of a distant teacher but of a father who loves his children into difficult obedience. The two questions about the cup and the bread are rhetorical: of course they are participations. The Lord’s Supper is not merely a memory exercise or a pledge of loyalty; it is a genuine sharing in Christ’s own body and blood — a participation in the covenant-sealing death that purchased the community. And because there is one loaf, the many who eat become one body — the eucharistic logic of ecclesial unity that will be important in chapter 11.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary: The OT analogy (Israel’s sacrificial system) confirms the participatory principle: eating the sacrifice is participating in the altar and what it represents. For Israel this was participation in the covenant with the living God; for pagan worshippers, Paul now argues, it is participation in the demonic realm — not because the idol exists but because something does exist behind the idol, and that something is demonic. The conclusion is categorical: the Lord’s table and the demons’ table are mutually exclusive. “Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” — echoing Deut 32:21, the covenant God whose jealousy is the jealousy of a husband for an unfaithful wife. “Are we stronger than he?” is the rhetorical slap: be careful what you provoke.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with a nuanced set of practical guidelines for the specific situations the Corinthians face: buying meat in the market (eat freely, ask no questions), dining at a non-believer’s house (eat what is served, ask no questions), being told the food was offered to idols (don’t eat, for the sake of the one who told you). The practical wisdom is shaped by two principles: freedom from unnecessary scruples in ordinary life, and sensitivity to conscience — both the weak person’s conscience and the unbeliever’s perception.

The governing positive principle — “do all to the glory of God” (v. 31) — is the comprehensive positive statement of Christian ethics that underlies everything in chapters 8–10. It applies to eating and drinking; it applies to everything else. Every ordinary act of human life is capable of being an act of glorification when performed in dependence on God, in gratitude for his gifts, and in awareness of his presence. This is the Reformed vision of the sanctified life: not the withdrawal from ordinary life into monasticism but the consecration of ordinary life to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Soli Deo Gloria Applied to Ordinary Life

The Reformation’s fifth great watchword — soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory — finds its Pauline root in v. 31. Every meal, every conversation, every commercial transaction, every athletic effort is capable of being an act of worship when performed in the right spirit and with the right orientation. Calvin’s “all of life is worship” is the systematic development of this verse. The “sacred/secular divide” is not merely unhelpful; by Paul’s logic it is theologically incoherent: all of life, including the most mundane, is lived before the face of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The practical guidelines of vv. 25–28 gave the Corinthians actionable wisdom for the specific daily situations they faced. The principle of “ask no questions” at the market protected them from unnecessary scrupulosity; the principle of sensitivity at the dinner table protected the weak and the unbeliever. Both together are shaped by the glory of God, not by personal preference. Now: “Do all to the glory of God” is not a cliché but a practice — a habit of asking, in any situation: how can this moment, this act, this conversation, be a participation in the glorification of God?

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Corinthian slogan (“all things are lawful”) is again cited and qualified. The qualifications are two: helpfulness and edification. Freedom is real; it is not the only or the primary criterion. “Let no one seek his own good” — the personal application of chapter 8’s principle: the neighbour’s flourishing takes precedence over personal freedom. “The earth is the Lord’s” (Ps 24:1) — the theological ground of freedom at the market: God created all things good, and the meat has not been made permanently impure by passing through an idol’s hands. God’s ownership supersedes the idol’s association.

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience— I do not mean your conscience, but his.
verseByVerse.commentary: The practical wisdom is subtle: at the unbeliever’s dinner, eat freely (you are a guest and the meal’s religious history is not your responsibility). But if the host draws attention to the religious origin of the food, then the conscience of the person who told you is at stake — whether they are a weak believer testing you, or an unbeliever observing whether your Christian profession makes any practical difference. In either case, the freedom to eat is overridden by the impact on the other person’s conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Whether you eat or drink” — the most mundane acts of daily subsistence are named first, to establish that the principle covers everything without exception. “Do all to the glory of God” — the comprehensive positive principle that resolves every ethical question not by a list of rules but by a single orientation. Paul’s personal example — “I try to please everyone in everything” — is not people-pleasing but the self-expenditure of love: not seeking his own advantage, but the salvation of many. The apostle who will not eat meat so that his brother will not stumble and the apostle who does all things to the glory of God are the same person, living the same life, shaped by the same cross.

11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Chapter 11 addresses two worship practices at Corinth, both of which reveal something about the community’s understanding of order, dignity, and the meaning of the gospel. The head covering discussion (vv. 2–16) is one of the most culturally complex passages in the NT, rooted in first-century practices of gender expression in public worship that do not translate directly into any modern context. The Lord’s Supper passage (vv. 17–34) is one of the most urgently pastoral: the Corinthians have turned the church’s central act of communion into an occasion for social humiliation, and Paul responds with the most solemn institution narrative in the NT.

The link between the two sections is the concept of order in worship — an order that reflects the character of the God being worshipped and the relationships that his gospel creates. Both the head covering practice and the Lord’s Supper abuse are symptoms of the same Corinthian disorder: the failure to take seriously the social and theological implications of what it means to worship the God who became a servant and who died for the poor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens with a remarkable verse that has been separated from what follows by modern chapter divisions: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” This is the hermeneutical key to the head covering discussion. The imitation Paul calls for is the imitation of the pattern of Christ — who, as the Son, submitted to the Father; who, as the Lord, humbled himself for the church; who, in his very personhood, is the image of God. The theological structure Paul draws on in vv. 3–12 is an ordered sequence of relationships: God is the head of Christ; Christ is the head of the man; man is the head of the woman. This is not a hierarchy of value or dignity (v. 11 insists on mutual dependence) but a structural ordering within relationships of genuine equality.

The specific practice Paul discusses — women covering their heads in worship, men not covering theirs — was a culturally specific expression of this theological reality in the first-century Greco-Roman context.
