The resurrection of Christ from the dead is not an appendix to the gospel; it is the gospel. And the resurrection of the body is not a peripheral eschatological detail; it is the goal toward which all of creation is moving.

Some at Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead — not necessarily the resurrection of Christ (which they apparently accepted as historical) but the future bodily resurrection of believers. Paul treats this as the most catastrophic doctrinal error possible: “if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (v. 14). The resurrection is the structural load-bearing wall of the entire Christian building. Remove it and nothing stands.

Paul’s response moves in three great movements: the historical certainty of Christ’s resurrection, established by testimony (vv. 1–11); the logical and theological necessity of the resurrection for the whole Christian faith (vv. 12–34); and the nature of the resurrection body, answering the philosophical objections about how the dead are raised (vv. 35–58). The chapter ends with one of the most electrifying doxologies in Scripture: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Resurrection of Christ: The Apostolic Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins with the most important word in this chapter: “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received.” En prōtois — of first importance, of primary significance: not first in a sequence of equally important things but first because everything else depends on it. The resurrection of Christ is not one doctrine among many; it is the doctrine from which all others derive their force. And Paul has both received it (from the tradition, from the Lord himself) and delivered it (to the Corinthians, faithfully, without alteration).

The content of the tradition is the gospel in miniature: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures; he was buried (confirming the reality of the death); he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures; he appeared to Peter, then to the Twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers, then to James, then to all the apostles, then to Paul himself. The list of appearances is a legal brief — evidence gathered from multiple witnesses, most of whom are still alive and can be questioned. Paul is not asking for faith without evidence; he is pointing to the evidence and asking for faith proportionate to it.

Paul’s self-description in vv. 9–10 is the most concentrated theological autobiography in his letters: the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church of God; yet what he is, he is by the grace of God, and the grace was not in vain — he worked harder than all of them, yet not he but the grace of God that was with him. The paradox of grace and effort, of unworthiness and productivity, of receiving and working, is compressed into two verses that describe every genuine Christian life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Foundation of Salvation

Paul’s phrase “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” is the earliest creedal formulation we possess, pre-dating the letter (Paul received it). The resurrection “in accordance with the Scriptures” grounds both events in OT prophecy — Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53, Hosea 6:2 being the primary candidates. The conjunction of death and resurrection is crucial: the resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the divine vindication of the atoning death. Without the resurrection, the death has no declared meaning; without the death, the resurrection has no redemptive content. Together they constitute the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek philosophical tradition was deeply ambivalent about bodily resurrection. The famous scene in Acts 17:32 — when Paul mentions the resurrection, some mock and some are interested — captures the standard Hellenistic reaction. The Platonic tradition prized the release of the soul from the body; the idea of the body being raised was not an upgrade but a retrogression to the bodily existence the soul was trying to escape. Paul’s case for the resurrection runs directly against this deeply embedded cultural instinct. Now: The modern version of the Greek objection is not philosophical but scientific: dead bodies do not rise. Paul’s answer is the same: the evidence of the witnesses. The question is not whether bodies normally rise but whether this specific body, on this specific morning, was raised by the God who created bodies in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you— unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary: The four verbs of vv. 1–2 describe the gospel’s complete relationship to the believer: preached (it came as announcement), received (it was accepted by faith), standing (the current posture of the Christian life), being saved (the ongoing process). Then the content: four facts, each load-bearing. Died — the substitutionary reality (for our sins). Buried — confirming the death’s finality (he was really dead). Raised — the miraculous divine reversal. On the third day — a specific, datable event, in accordance with Scriptures (Hosea 6:2; perhaps Jonah 1:17). The “in accordance with the Scriptures” appears twice: the death and resurrection are not accidents of history but the fulfilment of God’s ancient promises.

verseByVerse.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Six appearances, listed with almost legal precision. The note about the five hundred — “most of whom are still alive” — is a challenge to the reader: go and check. Paul is writing around AD 55, within twenty-five years of the resurrection; the eyewitnesses are still available. “One untimely born” (ektrōmati) is a striking self-description: the word refers to a premature or stillborn child — someone who arrived before the normal time, incomplete and unexpected. Paul was arrested into apostleship without the three years of preparation the Twelve had; he arrived, as it were, prematurely into the apostolic body.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.commentary: “By the grace of God I am what I am” — one of the most theologically compressed sentences Paul ever wrote. It holds together two truths in exact tension: grace is the entire ground of what Paul is (not his effort, his zeal, his intelligence); and what Paul is, is real (grace does not produce nothing, or a puppet, but a genuine human person transformed and activated by divine power). “I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God” — full effort, full grace, simultaneously. This is the grammar of the Christian life: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Phil 2:12–13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Christ Has Not Been Raised
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now deploys the logical consequences of denying the resurrection with a series of devastating conditional arguments. If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised. If Christ has not been raised, then the preaching is empty, the faith is empty, the apostolic witness is false, no one’s sins have been forgiven, those who have died in Christ have perished, and Christians are, of all people, most to be pitied.

The argument is a reductio ad absurdum of the Corinthian position. The Corinthians apparently wanted to accept Christ’s resurrection as a unique event while denying the general resurrection of the dead. Paul shows that this is incoherent: the two stand or fall together, because Christ’s resurrection is of the same kind as the general resurrection, not a different kind of event. If the general resurrection is impossible, then Christ’s resurrection is impossible; and if Christ’s resurrection is impossible, then everything the Corinthians claim to believe has no foundation.

“You are still in your sins” (v. 17) — this is the pastoral heart of the argument. The resurrection is not merely a fact about Jesus’s fate after death; it is the evidence that the atonement was accepted. If the Father accepted the Son’s sacrifice, the verdict is the resurrection. If there is no resurrection, there is no verdict; if there is no verdict, the atonement is unconfirmed; if the atonement is unconfirmed, sins are not forgiven. The resurrection is not a bonus feature of the gospel; it is the receipt that proves the transaction was completed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Confirmation of the Atonement

Paul’s logic in v. 17 — “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” — grounds the significance of the resurrection in its relationship to the atonement. The death of Christ atones; the resurrection of Christ confirms and declares the atonement accepted. This is why Romans 4:25 says Christ “was raised for our justification”: the resurrection is the Father’s “yes” to the Son’s atoning sacrifice. Without the resurrection, Good Friday is a tragedy; with the resurrection, Good Friday is the pivot of history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian denial of bodily resurrection was probably influenced by Platonic body-soul dualism: if the soul is what matters, and it survives death, why would God re-attach it to a body? Paul’s argument is that this misunderstands both what salvation means (the redemption of the whole person, body and soul) and what happened to Christ (his body was raised, not merely his spirit). Now: The contemporary version of the Corinthian position often appears in Christian thinking that treats the soul’s going to heaven as the whole story and the resurrection as an afterthought. Paul’s insistence is that the resurrection body is the destination, and the intermediate state (soul in God’s presence before the resurrection) is the waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary: The logical trap is sprung with precision: the Corinthian position (accepting Christ’s resurrection while denying general resurrection) is self-refuting. The resurrection of the dead is the category; Christ’s resurrection is an instance of that category. Deny the category and you deny the instance. Paul does not soften this: the implications are total. “Preaching in vain” — empty, hollow, void of content, a waste of breath. “Faith in vain” — the faith has no object with any reality; it is misplaced trust in an unconfirmed claim. The consequence is nothing less than the total collapse of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Misrepresenting God” — false witnesses against God: the apostles’ testimony would be not merely incorrect but a slander against the divine name, a false report of a divine act that never occurred. “Still in your sins” — the word is shattering: not merely theoretically unforgiven but actually, now, under the weight of unresolved guilt before the holy God. The cross without the resurrection means the sacrifice was made but the verdict is unknown; the sins may or may not be accepted. The resurrection is the declaration that they are.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Those who have fallen asleep in Christ” — the Corinthians had lost members of their community to death; the question of their fate was personal and painful. If there is no resurrection, the dead have simply ceased to exist — “perished.” And if the Christian hope is only for this present life (moral improvement, community, spiritual experience), then the Christian who has sacrificed the world’s pleasures, the world’s honours, and sometimes the world’s safety for the sake of Christ, and then dies — has made the worst bargain possible. “Most to be pitied” — the emphasis is total. MacArthur: “If there is no resurrection, then every martyr was a fool, every missionary a waste, every act of self-denial for Christ a tragedy.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” The “but in fact” (nyn de) is the most powerful two-word pivot in the chapter — possibly in the Bible. After the devastating catalogue of what follows if Christ is not raised, Paul turns the corner with the simplest assertion of the most important fact in history. He is raised. Firstfruits.

The firstfruits metaphor is drawn from the OT harvest liturgy: the first sheaf of grain, brought to the temple on the day after the Sabbath following Passover, was the pledge of the whole harvest to come. Christ’s resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the first instalment of a harvest that includes all who belong to him. His resurrection is not complete until theirs is complete; his rising is the beginning of a general rising in which all who are in him will participate.

The Adam/Christ typology of vv. 21–22 is one of the most compressed and profound theological arguments in the NT. As through one man (Adam) death came into the world and spread to all who are in him, so through one man (Christ) resurrection from the dead comes to those who are in him. The parallel is structural: two representative heads, two realms of existence, two destinies. Everyone is in one or the other — either in Adam (under death) or in Christ (under resurrection). The question is which solidarity defines you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Adam/Christ Typology and the Scope of Redemption

The Adam/Christ typology here (cf. Rom 5:12–21) is the cornerstone of Paul’s understanding of both sin and salvation. Adam’s representative headship means that his sin brought death to all who are “in Adam” — which is every human being by natural birth. Christ’s representative headship means that his obedience, death, and resurrection bring life to all who are “in Christ” — which is every believer by the new birth. The scope is parallel but not identical: “in Christ shall all be made alive” refers to all who are in Christ, not to every human being universally. The typology demands that the domain of redemption be at least as real and significant as the domain of death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had lost members to death needed to know that those deaths were not permanent losses but sleeps awaiting a harvest. The firstfruits language gave them a specific, liturgically resonant image: the resurrection of Christ is God’s pledge that the full harvest of resurrection is coming. Now: The Christian stands at the graveside of a believer with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared; the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who made the pledge. The resurrection is not a hope against hope but a certainty grounded in a historical event.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Firstfruits” — aparché: the initial portion that both represents and guarantees the whole. Christ’s resurrection is not merely the first chronologically but the first in a sequence that his rising has made certain. The Adam/Christ structure: Adam introduced death as a universal solidarity; Christ introduces life as a new solidarity. Both operate through representative headship: not merely as examples to be imitated but as heads whose fate is shared by all who are incorporated in them. “In Adam all die” — by natural birth. “In Christ shall all be made alive” — by the new birth, by faith, by union with the risen Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Each in his own order” — there is a sequence: firstfruits first (Christ), then the harvest at the Parousia (those who belong to Christ). The eschatological programme Paul sketches is focused on the subjugation of every opposing power — the “rule, authority, and power” of the present age, which includes not merely political powers but the spiritual forces that hold creation in bondage. Death is the last and greatest enemy: the final expression of sin’s dominion over creation, the last thing that will be defeated before the consummated kingdom is delivered to the Father. When death dies, the victory is total.

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary: The citation from Psalm 8:6 — originally about human dominion over creation — is applied christologically: Christ, as the true Human, the last Adam, fulfils the dominion mandate that Adam forfeited. The subjection of all things to the Son does not include the Father (v. 27’s clarification). And when the mission is complete, the Son delivers the kingdom to the Father and himself takes his place in the cosmic order of subjection — not as a diminished or reduced Lord but as the eternal Son in his eternal filial relation to the Father. The end is “God all in all” — the fullness of divine presence permeating the new creation without mediation or remainder.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now makes two arguments for the resurrection from the logic of Christian behaviour. First, an obscure and much-debated reference to baptism for the dead (v. 29): if the dead are not raised, why are people being baptised for them? Whatever the practice was, Paul uses it ad hominem — not endorsing it but pointing out that even by their own behaviour, the Corinthians reveal a belief in resurrection. Second, Paul’s own apostolic suffering: “I die every day!” (v. 31). If there is no resurrection, Paul’s life of constant danger, daily exposure to death, fighting with beasts at Ephesus — all of it is pointless self-destruction. If the dead are not raised, “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” The Epicurean counsel of hedonism is the only rational alternative to resurrection hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Rational Grounds of Christian Ethics

Paul’s argument here anticipates the famous wager logic: if there is no resurrection, Christian ethics (self-denial, risk, suffering for others) is irrational. The person who lives as if the resurrection were true is either right (and has invested wisely) or wrong (and has lived a meaningful but ultimately futile life). The Epicurean is consistent: if there is no resurrection, maximise pleasure now. Paul’s whole life is a living argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes no sense on any other hypothesis.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s reference to “fighting with beasts at Ephesus” may be literal (arena animals) or metaphorical (violent opponents); either way it describes the real mortal danger of apostolic ministry. The question is: for what purpose? If the dead are not raised, the purpose has no transcendent ground. Now: Every Christian who chooses a harder path for the sake of the gospel — the missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who refuses to compromise his convictions, the layperson who sacrifices career advancement for integrity — is making an implicit resurrection bet. Their lives only make sense if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour? I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The baptism for the dead (v. 29) — baptizomenoi hyper tōn nekrōn — remains one of the most exegetically obscure verses in the New Testament; over forty interpretations have been proposed. Three are most widely discussed. The first, and the most natural reading of the Greek, is proxy baptism: some Corinthians were being baptised on behalf of deceased relatives who had died without baptism, in the belief that the rite could benefit the dead. Chrysostom and other early fathers condemned the practice; the LDS church still performs it today on the basis of this verse. A second reading takes hyper as causal rather than substitutionary: living converts were baptised “because of” the dead — moved by the example of believers whose deaths bore witness to resurrection hope. A third takes it as baptism “with a view to” one’s own coming death and resurrection. Most favour the first. But the precise identification of the practice matters far less than Paul’s rhetorical point, and on this we must be clear: he neither endorses nor condemns it — he simply uses the Corinthians’ own behaviour as evidence that they implicitly affirm the very resurrection they verbally deny. Any such practice presupposes that the dead matter — a conviction that is incoherent if the dead will never be raised. “I die every day” — not metaphor but daily exposure to mortal danger, which Paul swears by the Corinthians’ own value to him (his “pride” in them) is his literal condition. “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” — the Isaiah 22:13 citation captures the logical endpoint of denying the resurrection: if this life is all there is, optimise it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary: The famous line — “bad company ruins good morals” — is a citation from the Greek poet Menander, one of the very few times Paul quotes a pagan literary source approvingly. The practical point: those who deny the resurrection at Corinth are not merely theologically confused; their error has a moral context and a social influence. Spending time with those who deny the resurrection will corrupt the faith of those who hold it. “No knowledge of God” — the most serious possible diagnosis: the resurrection-denier does not merely have incorrect eschatology; they have missed who God is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The objection Paul now addresses is philosophical: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” He calls the questioner a fool — not for asking but for assuming the objection is unanswerable. The answer comes in two parts: the seed analogy (vv. 36–44) and the Adam/Christ typology applied to the body (vv. 45–49).

The seed analogy is brilliant in its simplicity and precision. When you plant a seed, you do not plant the body that will grow; you plant a bare seed, and God gives it a body as he wills. The same is true of the resurrection: what is buried is the seed; what is raised is the fruit of that seed — the same organism, transformed. The continuity is real (it is the same seed that becomes the same plant); the transformation is radical (no one looking at a wheat seed would predict the wheat stalk). So with the resurrection body: continuous with the buried body (it is the same person raised), but transformed into a glory undreamt of by the buried condition.

The contrast of vv. 42–44 is fourfold: perishable/imperishable, dishonour/glory, weakness/power, natural body/spiritual body. Each contrast is between a condition appropriate to the present age (subject to entropy, subject to sin, subject to mortality) and a condition appropriate to the age to come (freed from all these). The “spiritual body” is not an immaterial ghost; it is a body animated and organised by the Holy Spirit, as the present body is animated and organised by the natural life principle (psychē). It is more physical than the present body, not less — fully embodied, fully alive, fully free from everything that degrades the present embodiment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The Reformed tradition has insisted, against all forms of Gnosticism and spiritual idealism, on the bodily nature of the resurrection. The creeds confess “the resurrection of the body” — not the survival of the soul. Paul’s seed analogy establishes both poles: continuity (the seed and the plant are the same organism in different stages) and transformation (the glory of the plant exceeds anything visible in the seed). The specific body that is buried — your body, with its particular history, its particular wounds, its particular scars — is the body that will be raised. This is why the bodily resurrection of Christ is the paradigm: the same body that was crucified was raised — still bearing the wounds (John 20:27), yet transformed into resurrection glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek objection to bodily resurrection was that the body is the problem, not the solution; the soul’s liberation from the body is the goal, not its resurrection. Paul refuses this framing entirely: the body is God’s creation, declared good, destined for resurrection. The problem is not embodiment but mortality, not physicality but corruption. The resurrection is the redemption of the body, not its abolition. Now: Every theology that treats the goal of salvation as the soul going to heaven (leaving the body behind) has the Corinthian problem. The goal is the new creation, the resurrection body, the renewed earth — the full embodied flourishing of redeemed humanity in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Foolish person” (aphrōn) — not an insult but a theological category: the one who reasons without attending to what God has actually said and done. The seed analogy is drawn from everyday agricultural observation, which makes it accessible but does not diminish its force. The death of the seed is necessary: “it does not come to life unless it dies.” There is no resurrection path that bypasses death; the very thing that seems to make resurrection impossible (death, burial, dissolution) is the precondition of the new life. “God gives it a body as he has chosen” — the resurrection body is not a human achievement or a natural process but a sovereign divine gift, as unexpected and as gloriously appropriate as the wheat stalk is to the wheat seed.

verseByVerse.quote: Not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul extends the analogies into cosmology: the diversity of bodies across the created order demonstrates that “body” is not a single thing. The flesh of a human, an animal, a bird, a fish — all different expressions of embodied life. The glory of the sun, the moon, individual stars — all different expressions of heavenly existence. This cataloguing of diversity prepares for the argument: there is no reason why the resurrection body cannot be radically different in kind from the present body while still being genuinely bodily. The seed and the plant demonstrate the principle within a single organism; the star-to-star diversity demonstrates it within a single category of created things.

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourfold contrast is the most precise description of resurrection transformation in the NT. Perishable/imperishable: the present body is subject to entropy, decay, and death; the resurrection body is free from all of these — not because it is immaterial but because it is redeemed from mortality. Dishonour/glory: the present body is subject to humiliation, pain, and death; the resurrection body shares the glory of Christ’s resurrection body (Phil 3:21). Weakness/power: the present body is limited, fragile, unable; the resurrection body is fully equipped for the life of the new creation. Natural/spiritual (psychikon/pneumatikon): animated by the natural life principle now; animated by the Holy Spirit then. Each contrast is a promise: everything the present body lacks, the resurrection body will supply.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit... The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Genesis citation (2:7) describes Adam: “became a living being” — he received life, he did not generate it. Christ, the last Adam: “became a life-giving spirit” — he not only lives but gives life. The sequence (first natural, then spiritual) is creation’s own order: the animal, earthly life comes first; the Spirit-renewed, heavenly life comes through death and resurrection. “We shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” — present bearing of the dust-image (mortality, fallenness, limitation); future bearing of the heavenly image (the glory of the risen Christ). This is the telos of redemption: conformity to the image of the Son (Rom 8:29) fully realised in the resurrection body.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Behold! I tell you a mystery.” Paul announces a revelation: not all Christians will die before the Parousia, but all will be transformed. The change will be instantaneous — “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.” The dead will be raised imperishable; the living will be changed. This is not an optional upgrade but a necessary transformation: “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.” The present bodily condition, however good and however beloved of God, is not fitted for the new creation; it must be transformed into what God intends.

Then the doxology — the most triumphant sentences Paul ever wrote, perhaps the most triumphant sentences in Scripture. Death has been swallowed up in victory. The taunt against death: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The answer: nowhere. The sting of death is sin; the power of sin is the law; but God gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Death has been robbed of its sting because sin has been atoned for; sin has been dealt with because the law’s demands have been met in Christ; Christ’s resurrection has declared the victory. The enemy still exists — the last enemy will be destroyed (v. 26) — but it has already been defeated in principle. The resurrection of Christ is the down payment on a victory that is as certain as God himself.

The conclusion drawn from the entire chapter (v. 58) is one of Paul’s most bracing practical statements: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labour is not in vain.” The resurrection is not an academic doctrine about the afterlife; it is the foundation of present, costly, patient, unstoppable labour for the Lord. Because the resurrection is certain, no act of faithfulness in this life is lost, no sacrifice is wasted, no patient endurance is pointless. In the Lord your labour is not in vain. This is the word the church has been waiting for throughout sixteen chapters of rebuke, correction, and instruction. It is the word that makes everything else possible.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The practical conclusion of the resurrection argument — “your labour is not in vain” (v. 58) — is the most comprehensive positive statement about Christian ethics in the letter. The resurrection does not merely give hope for the future; it validates the present. Every act of love, faithfulness, service, and endurance that has been poured out for Christ is stored up in a creation that will be renewed, not discarded. Herman Bavinck stated it with characteristic precision: Grace restores nature. The resurrection does not annul creation — it redeems and glorifies it. Every act of love, faithfulness, and service done in Christ’s name is not lost but transformed into the fabric of the new creation. Anthony Hoekema, in The Bible and the Future, makes the same point: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed. The resurrection does not make the present world irrelevant; it makes it eternally significant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that the deaths of their beloved dead were not permanent losses, that their own present labour was not ultimately futile, and that the God who raised Christ had the power and the intention to complete what he had begun in them. The resurrection doctrine is not abstract comfort; it is the concrete ground of the community’s ability to bear all things, believe all things, hope all things, endure all things (ch. 13). Now: Every generation of the church faces the question that faces every human being: does my life mean anything beyond this brief span? Paul’s answer is the most radical possible: yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the God who inhabits your story, and he wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Flesh and blood” in Paul signifies not the material body in itself but the present mortal, perishable condition of embodied life. The kingdom of God — the fully consummated new creation — requires a transformed body, not because physicality is bad but because perishability is incompatible with the imperishable new creation. The mystery: not all will die, but all will be transformed. The instantaneity — “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” — is not a promise of painlessness but of absolute divine sovereignty: the transformation will happen without warning, without process, in the blink of an eye, at the signal of God’s own trumpet call.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary: “Must put on” (dei endysasthai) — a divine necessity. The transformation is not optional or arbitrary but the fulfilment of God’s purpose in creation and redemption. “Death is swallowed up in victory” — the citation from Isaiah 25:8, the eschatological banquet text: the God who swallows up death forever, who wipes away every tear. When the resurrection body puts on immortality, the last enemy has been defeated in the experience of God’s people as well as in principle. The victory announced on Easter morning will be consummated in the resurrection of all who are in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The taunt against death — drawn from Hosea 13:14 and transformed into a triumphant provocation — is addressed to death as if it were a defeated enemy being mocked in its humiliation. “Where is your victory?” Nowhere; Christ rose. “Where is your sting?” Gone; sin is atoned for. The metaphysics of death’s defeat is compressed into two sentences: the sting of death (what makes death spiritually dangerous) is sin (the guilt that makes death a judgment rather than merely a biological event); the power of sin is the law (which defines sin and pronounces the sentence). But God in Christ has dealt with sin (by the atonement) and fulfilled the law (by Christ’s perfect obedience). Death still occurs; its sting is removed. Begg: “Death for the Christian is not the enemy winning — it is the moment when the enemy who has already lost finally releases his grip.”

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Therefore” — the resurrection of the body is the ground of everything that follows. “Steadfast, immovable” — two words meaning the same thing with increasing force: rooted in the earth, unshakeable. “Always abounding in the work of the Lord” — the resurrection is not a reason for passive waiting but for active, lavish, overflowing investment in the work of the kingdom. “Your labour is not in vain” — the final words of the longest chapter in the letter are words of absolute assurance about the value of every act of faithfulness. Every prayer, every act of service, every sacrifice, every patient endurance that has been offered to the Lord is preserved in the resurrection hope — because the God who raised Christ is the God who has counted every tear and will redeem every loss. Not in vain. Not ever.

16.title: The Collection, the Plans, and the Farewell
16.overview:
After fifteen chapters of theological depth and pastoral intensity, chapter 16 lands with the practicality of a man who has finished his sermon and is now talking about arrangements. The collection for the Jerusalem poor, travel plans, commendations of colleagues, personal greetings — these are the ordinary textures of Christian community life, and Paul handles them with the same theological seriousness as the great arguments of chapters 1–15. The ordinary and the transcendent are not separated in Paul’s world; the collection for the poor is a gospel act; the greeting of a colleague is a theological act; the closing benediction is a doxological act.

The letter closes not with law but with grace. “My love be with you all in Christ Jesus” — the apostle who has rebuked, corrected, warned, and argued for sixteen chapters ends with love. And between the final warning and the final love comes the great cry of the early church: Maranatha — “Our Lord, come!” The pulse of the apostolic community beats with eschatological longing: come, Lord Jesus. Everything that has been argued in this letter — the cross, the resurrection, love, order, holiness, community — points forward to the moment when he who died and rose and is coming again will make all things new.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Collection for the Saints
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The collection for the Jerusalem poor was one of the major projects of Paul’s apostolic ministry — a gathering of financial support from the Gentile churches for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem, which Paul saw as both a practical act of mercy and a symbolic expression of the unity of the one body of Christ across ethnic and geographic lines. He addresses it with practical wisdom: on the first day of every week, each person sets aside whatever they can afford, accumulating it so that there is no need for a last-minute collection when Paul arrives.

The regularity (“on the first day of every week”), the proportionality (“as he may prosper”), and the discipline (“each of you...put something aside”) are the marks of Paul’s teaching on financial generosity across his letters. Systematic, proportionate, habitual giving is not merely a fundraising strategy; it is a spiritual discipline that keeps money in its proper place as a servant of the kingdom rather than a master of the heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Collection as a Gospel Act

Paul’s collection theology, most fully developed in 2 Corinthians 8–9, grounds financial generosity in the grace of Christ: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Cor 8:9). The collection is not a tax but a participation in the logic of the cross — the voluntary sharing of material blessing across economic and ethnic lines that enacts the gospel’s claim that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The Gentile churches supporting the Jewish church in Jerusalem is the financial expression of Romans 15:27: “if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church was impoverished, possibly as a result of the famine of Acts 11:28 or the social cost of Jewish Christians being excluded from economic networks following their conversion. The collection was an act of solidarity across the most significant social divide of the ancient world. Now: The principle of systematic, proportionate, habitual giving as a spiritual discipline remains the most practically effective and most theologically grounded approach to Christian financial stewardship. The “first day of every week” rhythm connects giving to worship — it is part of how the community orients itself toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The collection for the saints” — the word logia may suggest an official, organised collection rather than casual giving. “The first day of every week” — the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection. The timing is theological: giving is part of resurrection-day worship. “As he may prosper” — the proportionality principle: the amount is relative to income, not fixed. This prevents both the wealthy feeling let off with a small token and the poor feeling crushed by an unaffordable demand. The prior accumulation — “so that there will be no collecting when I come” — is pastoral wisdom: the moment of Paul’s arrival should not be associated with a frantic financial scramble.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.
verseByVerse.commentary: The financial accountability structure is notable: Paul does not handle the money himself but sends those whom the Corinthians themselves accredit. This is the principle Paul articulates in 2 Corinthians 8:20–21: “taking precautions so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.” Financial transparency and accountability are not modern governance innovations but apostolic principles. The integrity of Christian ministry requires the same careful financial administration as any trustworthy institution.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s travel plans reveal the missionary network of the early church and the genuine relationships that sustained it. He plans to come to Corinth via Macedonia, possibly spending the winter there — a significant stay, not a brief visit. Timothy will come first as his representative; Paul asks the Corinthians to receive him without intimidation, because Timothy is doing the Lord’s work. Apollos, Paul reports, was urged to visit but was not willing to come now — an interesting note that Apollos is not Paul’s rival but his colleague, acting on his own judgment about timing.

The passage is a window into the texture of early Christian community: genuine relationships, real disagreements about timing and priorities, mutual encouragement across distance. The Apollos note is particularly significant: Paul, who has spent chapters resisting the faction that followed Apollos against him, here speaks warmly of Apollos as a brother, regrets his absence, and trusts his judgment. There is no rancour, no competition, no theological warfare — only two men jointly serving the same Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Missionary Network and the Unity of the Gospel

Paul’s travel plans are not merely logistical; they reflect the theology of the one body of Christ extended across geography. The early church was not a collection of independent local congregations operating in isolation; it was a network of communities bound together by the gospel, by apostolic ministry, by financial sharing, and by personal relationship. Paul’s letters are themselves the literary expression of this network — the apostle’s presence extended across distance through writing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ease with which Paul mentions Timothy and Apollos as co-workers, and the genuine care he shows for Timothy’s reception, models the pastoral culture of the early church: mutual submission, personal warmth, collaborative ministry. Now: The temptation to treat Christian ministry as competitive rather than collaborative is ancient and persistent. Paul’s warmth toward Apollos — the man whose followers had been used as a weapon against him — is a lesson in the largeness of a gospel-formed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go... But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary: “A wide door for effective work has opened” — the missionary opportunity and the opposition are presented together, not as contradiction but as correlation. Paul does not flee the adversaries; he stays for the door. The open door and the adversaries are characteristic of genuine gospel advance: where the Spirit is at work, resistance follows. Remaining in Ephesus until Pentecost — the harvest feast — is missionally motivated: Paul will not leave while the field is ripe, regardless of personal cost.

verseByVerse.quote: When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers. Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Let no one despise him” — the same word Paul uses in 1 Timothy 4:12 (“let no one despise your youth”). Timothy was apparently young and not naturally imposing; Paul is protecting him in advance from the Corinthian community’s tendency to evaluate people by the wrong criteria. The Apollos note is warm and relaxed: Paul’s strong urging was not enough to bring Apollos; Apollos made his own decision. Paul accepts this without apparent frustration. The man who preached Apollos as a servant of the Lord accepts his servant’s independent judgment with pastoral grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final exhortations are compressed, powerful, and perfectly sequenced. “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong.” Four imperatives that read like a military order of the day — vigilance, stability, courage, strength — followed immediately by the fifth and greatest: “Let all that you do be done in love.” The four imperatives without the fifth would be cold and harsh; the fifth without the four would be sentimental and weak. Together they describe the full character of the community Paul has been trying to form throughout the letter: strong and loving, firm and warm, courageous and gentle.

The commendation of Stephanas and his household is Paul’s closing tribute to those who have served the community faithfully. They were the firstfruits of Achaia; they had devoted themselves to service; they had come to Paul in Ephesus and refreshed his spirit. Paul asks the Corinthians to give recognition to such people — not as flattery but as the appropriate honour due to those who have given themselves for the community.
verseByVerse.theology:
Courage and Love: The Paradox of Gospel Character

The sequence of imperatives in v. 13–14 — watchful, firm, courageous, strong, then loving — captures the full paradox of the Christian character that Paul has been cultivating throughout the letter. The cross demands both: the courage to stand for truth (as Paul has done in every hard section of this letter) and the love that is patient, kind, and bears all things (as chapter 13 demands). Neither without the other is Christian; together they describe the character of Christ himself, who drove the money-changers from the temple and wept at Lazarus’s tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed all five imperatives in exactly the order Paul gave them. They needed watchfulness against the false teachings threatening them; firmness against the cultural pressure to conform; courage to exercise church discipline; strength to endure the costs of faithful community. And they needed all of this wrapped in love, or it would produce the cold and harsh community that pride produces rather than the warm and strong community that grace produces. Now: Every generation of the church needs the same five imperatives in the same order. The church that is watchful and firm but unloving is a fortress, not a family. The church that is loving but not watchful and firm is a sentimentality, not a community.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.
verseByVerse.commentary: Five imperatives in two verses — the distilled pastoral vision of the entire letter. “Watchful” (grēgoreite) — the vigilance of a sentry: alert to threats, not sleepy. “Stand firm in the faith” — the stability of a soldier holding his post against pressure: the faith is not negotiable or adjustable to cultural taste. “Act like men” (andrizesthe) — be courageous, be mature, be the adults in the room rather than the spiritual infants of chapter 3. “Be strong” — the strength is not self-generated (cf. Eph 6:10: “be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might”). “Let all that you do be done in love” — the supreme criterion of chapter 13 applied to everything: not just to the exercise of spiritual gifts but to every act, every decision, every word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I urge you, brothers— you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints— be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer. I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence. For they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Devoted themselves to the service of the saints” — the word etaxan means they appointed themselves, volunteered themselves, to this ministry. No one required them; they saw what needed to be done and did it. This is the pattern of ministry Paul commends: voluntary, servant-hearted, other-directed. “Be subject to such as these” — the community is asked to recognise and submit to those who have demonstrated, by their service, a genuine apostolic character. Authority in Paul’s churches was not primarily formal but functional: earned by service, not merely conferred by position. “Refreshed my spirit” — the apostle who has poured himself out across sixteen chapters of argument was refreshed by the presence of these brothers. Ministry is mutual.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter closes with a network of greetings that map the early church’s relational geography: the churches of Asia, Aquila and Prisca (Paul’s most frequent co-workers), the church that meets in their house, all the brothers. The early church was a house-church movement — communities gathered in the homes of those with enough space to host them — and the home of Aquila and Prisca was evidently one of the centres of Christian life wherever Paul worked.

Paul’s personal closing — written in his own hand after the letter dictated to a secretary — contains two of the most theologically charged farewell statements in the NT. The anathema against those who do not love the Lord Jesus — “let him be accursed” — is not vindictiveness but the flip side of the gospel’s demand: the Lord Jesus must be loved, not merely acknowledged. And then Maranatha — the Aramaic prayer of the early church: “Our Lord, come.” This prayer, preserved in its Aramaic form even in a Greek letter to a Greek-speaking church, is evidence of its antiquity and universality. The whole church, from its earliest days, prayed this prayer. And then grace, and then love — the final words of a letter that began with grace and peace, ends with grace and love in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Maranatha: The Eschatological Pulse of the Church

“Maranatha” is either maran atha (“Our Lord has come,” a declaration of the incarnation) or marana tha (“Our Lord, come!” a prayer for the Parousia). The context — following the anathema, preceding the benediction, echoing Revelation 22:20’s “Come, Lord Jesus” — strongly favours the prayer. The church that lives with the cross at its centre (ch. 1–2), that loves without condition (ch. 13), that proclaims the resurrection (ch. 15), lives with this prayer on its lips: come. The present is not all there is; the best is yet to come; the One who died and rose is coming again. Maranatha is the heartbeat of the community that has understood what Paul has been saying all letter long.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church’s Aramaic prayer preserved in a Greek letter to a Gentile church is a small but moving piece of evidence for the unity of the early church across language and culture. Jewish and Gentile believers shared the same prayer in the same words. Now: The prayer “Come, Lord Jesus” is the one prayer that every Christian, in every tradition, in every century, has prayed. It is the prayer that the Revelation ends with; it is the prayer that this letter ends with. To pray it is to join the whole church across time — to live, with Paul, as one on whom the end of the ages has come, watching and waiting for the One whose coming makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
verseByVerse.commentary: The network of greetings maps the early church’s relational geography: churches plural across Asia Minor, the household community of Aquila and Prisca, and “all the brothers” in Ephesus where Paul is writing. Aquila and Prisca appear in Acts 18 as the couple who sheltered Paul in Corinth after his arrival from Athens; they had accompanied him to Ephesus; they had risked their lives for him (Rom 16:4). The “holy kiss” is the physical expression of the community’s unity — not merely a cultural greeting but a sign of the bond created by the Spirit across social barriers.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: The shift to Paul’s own handwriting — authenticated by the physical distinctiveness of his hand compared to the secretary’s — is a mark of personal investment in the closing words. Everything in the letter has been Paul’s; the final lines are visibly Paul’s. In an age of forgeries and pseudonymous letters, this personal authentication was also a practical guarantee of the letter’s apostolic origin.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: “No love for the Lord” — who is without genuine affection for Christ. The anathema is not aimed at sincere doubt or weakness of faith but at the fundamental absence of love for Jesus Christ — the indifference or hostility that refuses him. Maranatha — “Our Lord, come!” The most ancient prayer of the church, translated but not explained, needing no explanation. Then grace — the first word of every genuine Christian community. Then “my love be with you all in Christ Jesus” — the letter that has rebuked, warned, corrected, and argued, ends with love. Not love as a sentimental closure but love as the deepest reality: the apostle’s love for a fractious, difficult, spectacular, beloved community — and through his love, the love of Christ for his own. Amen.
